# CHAPTER 11 

## Learning with Hidden Variables

In many models some variables are not directly observed, but are latent or 'hidden'. This can also occur when some data are not observed. In this chapter we discuss methods for learning in the presence of such missing information, and in particular develop the Expectation-Maximisation algorithm and related variants.

### 11.1 Hidden Variables and Missing Data

In practice data entries are often missing resulting in incomplete information to specify a likelihood. Observational variables may be split into visible (those for which we actually know the state) and missing (those whose states would nominally be known but are missing for a particular datapoint).

Another scenario in which not all variables in the model are observed are the so-called hidden or latent variable models. In this case there are variables which are essential for the model description but never observed. For example, the underlying physics of a model may contain latent processes which are essential to describe the model, but cannot be directly measured.

### 11.1.1 Why hidden/missing variables can complicate proceedings

In learning the parameters of models as previously described in chapter(9), we assumed we have complete information to define all variables of the joint model of the data $p(x \mid \theta)$. Consider the Asbestos-SmokingCancer network of section(9.3). Using the multivariate variable $x=(a, s, c)$, if patient $n$ has a complete record, the likelihood of this record is

$$
p\left(x^{n} \mid \theta\right)=p\left(a^{n}, s^{n}, c^{n} \mid \theta\right)=p\left(c^{n} \mid a^{n}, s^{n}, \theta_{c}\right) p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right) p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right)
$$

which is factorised in terms of the table entry parameters. We exploited this property to show that table entries $\theta$ can be learned by considering only local information, both in the maximum likelihood and Bayesian frameworks.

Now consider the case that for some of the patients, only partial information is available. For example, for patient $n$ with incomplete record $x^{n}=(c=1, s=1)$ it is known that the patient has cancer and is a smoker, but whether or not they had exposure to asbestos is unknown. Since we can only use the 'visible' available information it would seem reasonable (see section(11.1.2)) to assess parameters using the marginal likelihood

$$
p\left(x^{n} \mid \theta\right)=\sum_{a} p\left(a, s^{n}, c^{n} \mid \theta\right)=\sum_{a} p\left(c^{n} \mid a, s^{n}, \theta_{c}\right) p\left(a \mid \theta_{a}\right) p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right)
$$

![img-144.jpeg](img-144.jpeg)
(a)
![img-145.jpeg](img-145.jpeg)
(b)

Figure 11.1: (a): Missing at random assumption. The mechanism that generates the missing data does not depend on either the parameter $\theta$ of the model, or on the value of the missing data. (b): Missing completely at random assumption. The mechanism generating the missing data is completely independent of the model. Note that in both cases the direction of the arrow between $x_{v i s}$ and $x_{i n v}$ is irrelevant.

Using the marginal likelihood, however, may result in computational difficulties since the likelihood equation (11.1.2) cannot now be factorised into a product of the separate table parameters of the form $f_{s}\left(\theta_{s}\right) f_{a}\left(\theta_{a}\right) f_{c}\left(\theta_{c}\right)$. In this case the maximisation of the likelihood is more complex since the parameters of different tables are coupled.

A similar complication holds for Bayesian learning. As we saw in section(9.4.1), under a prior factorised over each CPT $\theta$, the posterior is also factorised. However, the missing variable introduces dependencies in the posterior parameter distribution, making the posterior more complex. In both the maximum likelihood and Bayesian cases, one has a well defined likelihood function of the table parameters/posterior.
Note that missing data does not always make the parameter posterior non-factorised. For example, if the cancer state is unobserved above, because cancer is a collider with no descendants, the conditional distribution simply sums to 1 , and one is left with a factor dependent on $a$ and another on $s$.

# 11.1.2 The missing at random assumption 

Under what circumstances is it valid to use the marginal likelihood to assess parameters? We partition the variables $x$ into those that are 'visible', $x_{v i s}$ and 'invisible', $x_{i n v}$, so that the set of all variables can be written $x=\left[x_{v i s}, x_{i n v}\right]$. For the visible variables we have an observed state $x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}$, whereas the state of the invisible variables is unknown. To complete the picture we also need to model the process that informs when data will be missing. We use an indicator $m_{\text {inv }}=1$ to denote that the state of the invisible variables is unknown and require then a model $p\left(m_{i n v} \mid x_{v i s}, x_{i n v}, \theta\right)$. Then for a datapoint which contains both visible and invisible information,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, m_{i n v}=1 \mid \theta\right) & =\sum_{x_{i n v}} p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{i n v}, m_{i n v}=1 \mid \theta\right) \\
& =\sum_{x_{i n v}} p\left(m_{i n v}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{i n v}, \theta\right) p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{i n v} \mid \theta\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

If we assume that the mechanism which generates invisible data is independent of the parameter and the missing value $x_{\text {inv }}$

$$
p\left(m_{i n v}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{i n v}, \theta\right)=p\left(m_{i n v}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}\right)
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, m_{i n v}=1 \mid \theta\right) & =p\left(m_{i n v}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}\right) \sum_{x_{i n v}} p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{i n v} \mid \theta\right) \\
& =p\left(m_{i n v}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}\right) p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v} \mid \theta\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Only the term $p\left(x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v} \mid \theta\right)$ conveys information about the parameter $\theta$ of the model. Therefore, provided the mechanism by which the data is missing depends only on the visible states, we may simply use the marginal likelihood to assess parameters. This is called the missing at random (MAR) assumption, see fig(11.1).

Example 11.1 (Not missing at random). EZsurvey.org stop men on the street and ask them their favourite colour. All men whose favourite colour is pink decline to respond to the question - for any other colour, all men respond to the question. Based on the data, EZsurvey.org produce a histogram of men's favourite colour, based on the likelihood of the visible data alone, confidently stating that none of them likes pink. For simplicity, we assume there are only three colours, blue, green and pink. EZsurvey.org attempts to find the histogram with probabilities $\theta_{b}, \theta_{g}, \theta_{p}$ with $\theta_{b}+\theta_{g}+\theta_{p}=1$. Each respondent produces a visible response $x$ with $\operatorname{dom}(x)=\{$ blue, green, pink $\}$, otherwise $m=1$ if there is no response. Three men are asked their favourite colour, giving data

$$
\left\{x^{1}, x^{2}, x^{3}\right\}=\{\text { blue }, \text { missing }, \text { green }\}
$$

Based on the likelihood of the visible data alone we have the log likelihood for i.i.d. data

$$
L\left(\theta_{b}, \theta_{g}, \theta_{p}\right)=\log \theta_{b}+\log \theta_{g}+\lambda\left(1-\theta_{b}-\theta_{g}-\theta_{p}\right)
$$

where the last Lagrange term ensures normalisation. Maximising the expression we arrive at

$$
\theta_{b}=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \theta_{g}=\frac{1}{2}, \quad \theta_{p}=0
$$

Hence EZsurvey.org arrive at the erroneous conclusion that no men like pink, even though the reality is that some men like pink - they just don't want to say so. The unreasonable result that EZsurvey.org produce is due to not accounting correctly for the mechanism which produces the data. In this case the data is not MAR since whether or not the data is missing depends on the state of the missing variable.

The correct mechanism that generates the data (including the missing data is)

$$
p\left(x^{1}=\operatorname{blue} \mid \theta\right) p\left(m^{2}=1 \mid \theta\right) p\left(x^{3}=\operatorname{green} \mid \theta\right)=\theta_{b} \theta_{p} \theta_{g}=\theta_{b}\left(1-\theta_{b}-\theta_{g}\right) \theta_{g}
$$

where we used $p\left(m^{2}=1 \mid \theta\right)=\theta_{p}$ since the probability that a datapoint is missing is the same as the probability that the favourite colour is pink. Maximising the likelihood, we arrive at

$$
\theta_{b}=\frac{1}{3}, \theta_{g}=\frac{1}{3}, \theta_{p}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

as we would expect. On the other hand if there is another visible variable, $t$, denoting the time of day, and the probability that men respond to the question depends only on the time $t$ alone (for example the probability of having missing data is high during rush hour), then we may indeed treat the missing data as missing at random.

A stronger assumption than MAR is that the missing data mechanism is completely independent of all other model processes

$$
p\left(m_{\text {inv }}=1 \mid x_{v i s}=\mathrm{v}, x_{\text {inv }}, \theta\right)=p\left(m_{\text {inv }}=1\right)
$$

which is called missing completely at random. This applies for example to latent variable models in which the variable state is always missing, independent of anything else.

# 11.1.3 Maximum likelihood 

Throughout the remaining discussion we will assume any missing data is MAR or missing completely at random. We partition the variables into 'visible variables $v$ for which we know the states and 'hidden' variables $h$ whose states will not be observed. For maximum likelihood we may then learn model parameters $\theta$ by optimising the on the visible variables alone

$$
p(v \mid \theta)=\sum_{h} p(v, h \mid \theta)
$$

with respect to $\theta$.

# 11.1.4 Identifiability issues 

The marginal likelihood objective function depends on the parameters only through $p(v \mid \theta)$, so that equivalent parameter solutions may exist. For example, consider a latent variable model with distribution

$$
p\left(x_{1}, x_{2} \mid \theta\right)=\theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}
$$

in which variable $x_{2}$ is never observed. This means that the marginal likelihood only depends on the entry $p\left(x_{1} \mid \theta\right)=\sum_{x_{2}} \theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}$. Given a maximum likelihood solution $\theta^{*}$, we can then always find an equivalent maximum likelihood solution $\theta^{\prime}$ provided (see exercise(11.9))

$$
\sum_{x_{2}} \theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}^{\prime}=\sum_{x_{2}} \theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}^{*}
$$

In other cases there is an inherent symmetry in the parameter space of the marginal likelihood. For example, consider the network over binary variables

$$
p(c, a, s)=p(c \mid a, s) p(a) p(s)
$$

We assume we know the table for $p(s)$ and that our aim is to learn the asbestos table $\hat{p}(a=1)$ and cancer tables

$$
\hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=1), \quad \hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=0), \quad \hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1), \quad \hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=0)
$$

where we used a ' ' to denote that these are parameter estimates.

We assume that we have missing data such that the states of variable $a$ are never observed. In this case an equivalent solution (in the sense that it has the same marginal likelihood) is given by interchanging the states of $a$ :

$$
\hat{p}^{\prime}(a=0)=\hat{p}(a=1)
$$

and the four tables

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\hat{p}^{\prime}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)=\hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=1), & \hat{p}^{\prime}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=0)=\hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=0) \\
\hat{p}^{\prime}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=1)=\hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1), & \hat{p}^{\prime}(c=1 \mid a=1, s=0)=\hat{p}(c=1 \mid a=0, s=0)
\end{array}
$$

A similar situation occurs in a more general setting in which the state of a variable is consistently unobserved (mixture models are a case in point) yielding an inherent symmetry in the solution space. A well known characteristic of maximum likelihood algorithms is that 'jostling' occurs in the initial stages of training in which these symmetric solutions compete.

### 11.2 Expectation Maximisation

The EM algorithm is a convenient and general purpose iterative approach to maximising the likelihood under missing data/hidden variables[84, 202]. It is generally straightforward to implement and can achieve large jumps in parameter space, particularly in the initial iterations.

### 11.2.1 Variational EM

The key feature of the EM algorithm is to form an alternative objective function for which the parameter coupling effect discussed in section(11.1.1) is removed, meaning that individual parameter updates can be achieved, akin to the case of fully observed data. The way this works is to replace the marginal likelihood with a lower bound - it is this lower bound that has the useful decoupled form.

We first consider a single variable pair $(v, h)$, where $v$ stands for 'visible' and $h$ for 'hidden'. The model of the data is then $p(v, h \mid \theta)$ and our interest is to set $\theta$ by maximising the marginal likelihood $p(v \mid \theta)$. To derive the

Algorithm 11.1 Expectation Maximisation. Compute Maximum Likelihood value for data with hidden variables. Input: a distribution $p(x \mid \theta)$ and dataset $\mathcal{V}$. Returns ML candidate $\theta$.

```
\(t=0\)
    Choose an initial setting for the parameters \(\theta^{0}\).
    while \(\theta\) not converged (or likelihood not converged) do
        \(t \leftarrow t+1\)
        for \(n=1\) to \(N\) do
            \(q_{t}^{n}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta^{t-1}\right)\)
            end for
        \(\theta^{t}=\arg \max _{\theta} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(h^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}^{n}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}\)
end while
    return \(\theta^{t}\)
```

$\triangleright$ The max likelihood parameter estimate.
bound on the marginal likelihood, consider the Kullback-Leibler divergence (which is always non-negative) between a 'variational' distribution $q(h \mid v)$ and the parametric model $p(h \mid v, \theta)$ :

$$
\mathrm{KL}(q(h \mid v) \mid p(h \mid v, \theta)) \equiv\langle\log q(h \mid v)-\log p(h \mid v, \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)} \geq 0
$$

The term 'variational' refers to the fact that this distribution will be a parameter of an optimisation problem. Using $p(h \mid v, \theta)=p(h, v \mid \theta) / p(v \mid \theta)$ and the fact that $p(v \mid \theta)$ does not depend on $h$,

$$
\mathrm{KL}(q(h \mid v) \mid p(h \mid v, \theta))=\langle\log q(h \mid v)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}-\langle\log p(h, v \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}+\log p(v \mid \theta) \geq 0
$$

Rearranging, we obtain a bound on the marginal likelihood ${ }^{1}$

$$
\log p(v \mid \theta) \geq \underbrace{-\langle\log q(h \mid v)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}}_{\text {Entropy }}+\underbrace{\langle\log p(h, v \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}}_{\text {Energy }}
$$

The energy term is also called the 'expected complete data log likelihood'. The bound is potentially useful since the $\theta$ dependent energy term is similar in form to the fully observed case, except that terms with missing data have their log likelihood weighted by a prefactor. Equation(11.2.3) is a marginal likelihood bound for a single training example. Under the i.i.d. assumption, the log likelihood of all training data $\mathcal{V}=\left\{v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}\right\}$ is the sum of the individual log likelihoods:

$$
\log p(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log p\left(v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

Summing over the training data, we obtain a bound on the log (marginal) likelihood

$$
\log p(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta) \geq \tilde{L}(\{q\}, \theta) \equiv \underbrace{-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}}_{\text {entropy }}+\underbrace{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(h^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}}_{\text {energy }}
$$

Note that the bound $\tilde{L}(\{q\}, \theta)$ is exact (that is, the right hand side is equal to the log likelihood) when we set $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta\right), n=1, \ldots, N$.

The bound depends both on $\theta$ and the set of variational distributions $\{q\}$. Our aim is then to try to optimise this bound w.r.t. $\theta$ and $\{q\}$; in doing so we will push up the lower bound, and hopefully increase thereby the likelihood itself. A simple iterative procedure to optimise the bound is to first fix $\theta$ and then optimise w.r.t. $\{q\}$, and then fix $\{q\}$ and optimise the bound w.r.t. $\theta$. These are known as the ' E ' and ' M ' steps and are repeated until convergence:
E-step For fixed $\theta$, find the distributions $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N$ that maximise equation (11.2.5).
M-step For fixed $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N$, find the parameters $\theta$ that maximise equation (11.2.5).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ This is analogous to a standard partition function bound in statistical physics, from where the terminology 'energy' and 'entropy' hails.

# 11.2.2 Classical EM 

In the variational E-step above, the fully optimal setting is

$$
q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta\right)
$$

Since $q$ is fixed during the M-step, performing the M-step optimisation is equivalent to maximising the energy term alone, see algorithm(11.1). From here onwards we shall use the term 'EM' to refer to the classical EM algorithm, unless otherwise stated. It is important to note that the EM algorithm cannot generally guarantee to find the fully optimal maximum likelihood solution and can get trapped in local optima, as discussed in example(11.2).

Example 11.2 (EM for a one-parameter model). We consider a model small enough that we can plot fully the evolution of the EM algorithm. The model is on a single visible variable $v$ with $\operatorname{dom}(v)=\mathbb{R}$ and single two-state hidden variable $h$ with $\operatorname{dom}(h)=\{1,2\}$. We define a model $p(v, h \mid \theta)=p(v \mid h, \theta) p(h)$ with

$$
p(v \mid h, \theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} e^{-(v-\theta h)^{2}}
$$

and $p(h=1)=p(h=2)=0.5$. For an observation $v=2.75$ our interest is to find the parameter $\theta$ that optimises the likelihood

$$
p(v=2.75 \mid \theta)=\sum_{h=1,2} p(v=2.75 \mid h, \theta) p(h)=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\pi}}\left(e^{-(2.75-\theta)^{2}}+e^{-(2.75-2 \theta)^{2}}\right)
$$

The $\log$ likelihood is plotted in fig(11.2a) with optimum at $\theta=1.325$. If the state of $h$ were given, the $\log$ likelihood would be a single bump, rather than the more complex double bump in the case of missing data. To use the EM approach to find the optimum $\theta$, we need to work out the energy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\log p(v, h \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)} & =\langle\log p(v \mid h, \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}+\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)} \\
& =-\left\langle(v-\theta h)^{2}\right\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}+\text { const. }
\end{aligned}
$$

There are two $h$ states of the $q$ distribution and using $q(h)$ as shorthand for $q(h \mid v)$, normalisation requires $q(1)+q(2)=1$. Due to the normalisation, we can fully parameterise $q$ using $q(2)$ alone. The EM procedure then iteratively optimises the lower bound

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log p(v=2.75 \mid \theta) & \geq \tilde{L}(q(2), \theta) \\
& \equiv-q(1) \log q(1)-q(2) \log q(2)-\sum_{h=1,2} q(h)(2.75-\theta h)^{2}+\text { const. }
\end{aligned}
$$

From an initial starting $\theta$, the EM algorithm finds the $q$ distribution that optimises $\tilde{L}(q(2), \theta)$ (E-step) and then updates $\theta$ (M-step). Depending on the initial $\theta$, the solution found is either a global or local optimum of the likelihood, see fig(11.2).

The M-step is easy to work out analytically in this case with $\theta^{\text {new }}=v\langle h\rangle_{q(h)} /\left\langle h^{2}\right\rangle_{q(h)}$. Similarly, the E-step sets $q^{\text {new }}(h)=p(h \mid v, \theta)$ so that

$$
q^{\text {new }}(h=2)=\frac{p(v=2.75 \mid h=2, \theta) p(h=2)}{p(v=2.75)}=\frac{e^{-(2.75-2 \theta)^{2}}}{e^{-(2.75-2 \theta)^{2}}+e^{-(2.75-\theta)^{2}}}
$$

where we used

$$
p(v=2.75)=p(v=2.75 \mid h=1, \theta) p(h=1)+p(v=2.75 \mid h=2, \theta) p(h=2)
$$

![img-146.jpeg](img-146.jpeg)

Figure 11.2: (a): The log likelihood for the model described in example(11.2). (b): Contours of the lower bound $\hat{L}(q(h=2), \theta)$. For an initial choice $\theta=1.9$, successive updates of the E (vertical) and M (horizontal) steps are plotted, with the algorithm converging to the global optimum maximum likelihood setting for $\theta$. (c): Starting at $\theta=1.95$, the EM algorithm converges to a local optimum.

Example 11.3. Consider a simple model

$$
p\left(x_{1}, x_{2} \mid \theta\right)
$$

where $\operatorname{dom}\left(x_{1}\right)=\operatorname{dom}\left(x_{2}\right)=\{1,2\}$. Assuming an unconstrained distribution

$$
p\left(x_{1}, x_{2} \mid \theta\right)=\theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}, \quad \theta_{1,1}+\theta_{1,2}+\theta_{2,1}+\theta_{2,2}=1
$$

our aim is to learn $\theta$ from the data $\mathbf{x}^{1}=(1,1), \mathbf{x}^{2}=(1,?), \mathbf{x}^{3}=(?, 2)$. The energy term for the classical EM is

$$
\log p\left(x_{1}=1, x_{2}=1 \mid \theta\right)+\left\langle\log p\left(x_{1}=1, x_{2} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{1}=1, \theta^{\text {old }}\right)}+\left\langle\log p\left(x_{1}, x_{2}=2 \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(x_{1} \mid x_{2}=2, \theta^{\text {old }}\right)}
$$

Writing out fully each of the above terms on a separate line gives the energy

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log \theta_{1,1} \\
& +p\left(x_{2}=1 \mid x_{1}=1, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \log \theta_{1,1}+p\left(x_{2}=2 \mid x_{1}=1, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \log \theta_{1,2} \\
& +p\left(x_{1}=1 \mid x_{2}=2, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \log \theta_{1,2}+p\left(x_{1}=2 \mid x_{2}=2, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \log \theta_{2,2}
\end{aligned}
$$

This expression resembles the standard log likelihood of fully observed data except that terms with missing data have their weighted log parameters. The parameters are conveniently decoupled in this bound (apart from the trivial normalisation constraint) so that finding the optimal parameters is straightforward. This is achieved by the M-step update which gives

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\theta_{1,1} \propto 1+p\left(x_{2}=1 \mid x_{1}=1, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) & \theta_{1,2} \propto p\left(x_{2}=2 \mid x_{1}=1, \theta^{\text {old }}\right)+p\left(x_{1}=1 \mid x_{2}=2, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \\
\theta_{2,1}=0 & \theta_{2,2} \propto p\left(x_{1}=2 \mid x_{2}=2, \theta^{\text {old }}\right)
\end{array}
$$

where $p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{1}, \theta^{\text {old }}\right) \propto \theta_{x_{1}, x_{2}}^{\text {old }}$ (E-step) etc. The E and M -steps are iterated till convergence.

# The EM algorithm increases the likelihood 

Whilst, by construction, the EM algorithm cannot decrease the lower bound on the likelihood, an important question is whether or not the log likelihood itself is necessarily increased by this procedure.


Figure 11.3: A database containing information about being a Smoker (1 signifies the individual is a smoker), and lung Cancer ( 1 signifies the individual has lung Cancer). Each row contains the information for an individual, so that there are 7 individuals in the database.

We use $\theta^{\prime}$ for the new parameters, and $\theta$ for the previous parameters in two consecutive iterations. Using $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta\right)$ we see that as a function of the parameters, the lower bound for a single variable pair $(v, h)$ depends on $\theta$ and $\theta^{\prime}$ :

$$
L B\left(\theta^{\prime} \mid \theta\right) \equiv-\langle\log p(h \mid v, \theta)\rangle_{p(h \mid v, \theta)}+\left\langle\log p\left(h, v \mid \theta^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle_{p(h \mid v, \theta)}
$$

From the definition of the lower bound, equation (11.2.3), we have

$$
\log p\left(v \mid \theta^{\prime}\right)=L B\left(\theta^{\prime} \mid \theta\right)+K L\left(p(h \mid v, \theta) \mid p\left(h \mid v, \theta^{\prime}\right)\right)
$$

That is, the Kullback-Leibler divergence is the difference between the lower bound and the true likelihood. We may then also write

$$
\log p(v \mid \theta)=L B(\theta \mid \theta)+\underbrace{K L(p(h \mid v, \theta) \mid p(h \mid v, \theta))}_{0}
$$

Hence

$$
\log p\left(v \mid \theta^{\prime}\right)-\log p(v \mid \theta)=\underbrace{L B\left(\theta^{\prime} \mid \theta\right)-L B(\theta \mid \theta)}_{\geq 0}+\underbrace{K L\left(p(h \mid v, \theta) \mid p\left(h \mid v, \theta^{\prime}\right)\right)}_{\geq 0}
$$

The first assertion is true since, by definition of the M-step, we search for a $\theta^{\prime}$ which has a higher value for the bound than our starting value $\theta$. The second assertion is true by the non-negative property of the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

For more than a single datapoint, we simply sum each individual bound for $\log p\left(v^{n} \mid \theta\right)$. Hence we reach the important conclusion that the EM algorithm increases, not only the lower bound on the marginal likelihood, but the marginal likelihood itself (more correctly, EM cannot decrease these quantities).

# Shared parameters and tables 

It is often the case in models that parameters are shared between components of the model. The application of EM to this shared parameter case is essentially straightforward. According to the energy term, we need to identify all those terms in which the shared parameter occurs. The objective for the shared parameter is then the sum over all energy terms containing the shared parameter.

### 11.2.3 Application to Belief networks

Conceptually, the application of EM to training Belief Networks with missing data is straightforward. The battle is more notational than conceptual. We begin the development with an example, from which intuition about the general case can be gleaned.

Example 11.4. Consider the network.

$$
p(a, c, s)=p(c \mid a, s) p(a) p(s)
$$

for which we have a set of data, but that the states of variable $a$ are never observed, see fig(11.3). Our goal is to learn the CPTs $p(c \mid a, s)$ and $p(a)$ and $p(s)$. To apply EM, algorithm(11.1) to this case, we first assume initial parameters $\theta_{a}^{0}, \theta_{s}^{0}, \theta_{c}^{0}$.

The first E-step, for iteration $t=1$ then defines a set of distributions on the hidden variables (here the hidden variable is $a$ ). For notational convenience, we write $q_{t}^{n}(a)$ in place of $q_{t}^{n}\left(a \mid v^{n}\right)$. Then

$$
q_{t=1}^{n=1}(a)=p\left(a \mid c=1, s=1, \theta^{0}\right), \quad q_{t=1}^{n=2}(a)=p\left(a \mid c=0, s=0, \theta^{0}\right)
$$

and so on for the 7 training examples, $n=2, \ldots, 7$.
We now move to the first M-step. The energy term for any iteration $t$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(\theta) & =\sum_{n=1}^{7}\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid a^{n}, s^{n}\right)+\log p\left(a^{n}\right)+\log p\left(s^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}^{n}(a)} \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{7}\left\{\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid a^{n}, s^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}^{n}(a)}+\left\langle\log p\left(a^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}^{n}(a)}+\log p\left(s^{n}\right)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

The final term is the log likelihood of the variable $s$, and $p(s)$ appears explicitly only in this term. Hence, the usual maximum likelihood rule applies, and $p(s=1)$ is simply given by the relative number of times that $s=1$ occurs in the database, giving $p(s=1)=4 / 7, p(s=0)=3 / 7$.

The contribution of parameter $p(a=1)$ to the energy occurs in the terms

$$
\sum_{n}\left\{q_{t}^{n}(a=0) \log p(a=0)+q_{t}^{n}(a=1) \log p(a=1)\right\}
$$

which, using the normalisation constraint is

$$
\log p(a=0) \sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=0)+\log (1-p(a=0)) \sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=1)
$$

Differentiating with respect to $p(a=0)$ and solving for the zero derivative we get the M-step update for $p(a=0)$

$$
p(a=0)=\frac{\sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=0)}{\sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=0)+\sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=1)}=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}(a=0)
$$

That is, whereas in the standard maximum likelihood estimate, we would have the real counts of the data in the above formula, here they have been replaced with our guessed values $q_{t}^{n}(a=0)$ and $q_{t}^{n}(a=1)$.

A similar story holds for $p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)$. Again we need to consider that normalisation means that $p(c=0 \mid a=0, s=1)$ also contributes. The contribution of this term to the energy is from those data indices $n$ for which $s=1$

$$
\sum_{n: c^{n}=1, s^{n}=1} q_{t}^{n}(a=0) \log p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)+\sum_{n: c^{n}=0, s^{n}=1} q_{t}^{n}(a=0) \log (1-p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1))
$$

Optimising with respect to $p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)$ gives

$$
p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)=\frac{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] q_{t}^{n}(a=0)}{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] q_{t}^{n}(a=0)+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=0\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] q_{t}^{n}(a=0)}
$$

For comparison, the setting in the complete data case is

$$
p(c=1 \mid a=0, s=1)=\frac{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[a^{n}=0\right]}{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[a^{n}=0\right]+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[c^{n}=0\right] \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] \mathbb{I}\left[a^{n}=0\right]}
$$

There is an intuitive relationship between these updates: in the missing data case we replace the indicators by the assumed distributions $q$. Iterating the E and M steps, these parameters will converge to a local likelihood optimum.

# 11.2.4 General case 

A belief network on a multivariate variable $x$ takes the general form

$$
p(x)=\prod_{i} p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)
$$

Some of the variables will be observed, and others hidden. We therefore partition the variable $x$ into visible and hidden multivariate parts $x=(v, h)$. Given an i.i.d. dataset $\mathcal{V}=\left\{v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}\right\}$ our interest is to learn the tables of $p(x)$ to maximise the likelihood on the visible data $\mathcal{V}$. For each datapoint index $n$, each multivariate variable $x^{n}=\left(v^{n}, h^{n}\right)$ decomposes into its visible and hidden parts; an upper variable index will typically the datapoint, and a lower index the variable number.

From equation (11.2.5), the form of the energy term for belief networks is

$$
\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}=\sum_{n} \sum_{i}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{i}^{n} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}^{n}\right)\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}
$$

Here $t$ indexes the iteration count for the EM algorithm. It is useful to define the following notation:

$$
q_{t}^{n}(x)=q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right) \delta\left(v, v^{n}\right)
$$

This means that $q_{t}^{n}(x)$ sets the visible variables in the observed state, and defines a conditional distribution on the unobserved variables. We then define the mixture distribution

$$
q_{t}(x)=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} q_{t}^{n}(x)
$$

The energy term in the left hand side of equation (11.2.35) can be written more compactly using this notation as

$$
\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}=N\left\langle\log p(x)\right\rangle_{q_{t}(x)}
$$

To see this consider the right hand side of the above

$$
N\left\langle\log p(x)\right\rangle_{q_{t}(x)}=N \sum_{x}\left[\log p(x)\right] \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n} q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right) \delta\left(v, v^{n}\right)=\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}
$$

Using this compact notation for the energy, and the structure of the belief network, we can decompose the energy as

$$
\left\langle\log p(x)\right\rangle_{q_{t}(x)}=\sum_{i}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}(x)}=\sum_{i}\left\langle\left\langle\log p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(\mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}
$$

This means that maximising the energy is equivalent to minimising

$$
\sum_{i}\left\langle\left\langle\log q_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}-\left\langle\log p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}\right\rangle_{q_{t}\left(\mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}
$$

where we added the constant first term to make this into the form of a Kullback-Leibler divergence. Since this is a sum of independent Kullback-Leibler divergences, optimally the M-step is given by setting

$$
p^{\text {new }}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)=q_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)
$$

In practice, storing the $q_{t}(x)$ over the states of all variables $x$ is prohibitively expensive. Fortunately, since the M-step only requires the distribution on the family of each variable $x_{i}$, one only requires the local distributions $q_{t}^{n}\left(x_{i}, \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)$. We may therefore dispense with the global $q_{t}(x)$ and equivalently use

$$
p^{\text {new }}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)=\frac{\sum_{n} q_{t}^{n}\left(x_{i}, \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}{\sum_{n^{\prime}} q_{t}^{n^{\prime}}\left(\mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}
$$

Algorithm 11.2 EM for Belief Networks. Input: a BN DAG and dataset on the visible variables $\mathcal{V}$. Returns the maximum likelihood estimate of the tables $p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right), i=1, \ldots, K$.

```
\(t=1\)
    Set \(p_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\) to initial values.
while \(p\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\) not converged (or likelihood not converged) do
    \(t \leftarrow t+1\)
    for \(n=1\) to \(N\) do
        \(q_{t}^{n}(x)=p_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right) \delta\left(v, v^{n}\right)\)
    end for
    for \(i=1\) to \(K\) do
        CORRECTION \(p_{t+1}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)=\frac{\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{N} q_{t}^{n}\left(x_{i}, \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}{\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{N} q_{t}^{n^{\prime}}\left(\mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}\)
    end for
end while
    return \(p_{t}\left(x_{i} \mid \mathrm{pa}\left(x_{i}\right)\right)\)
```

$\triangleright$ Iteration counter
$\triangleright$ Initialisation
$\triangleright$ Run over all datapoints
$\triangleright E$ step
$\triangleright$ Run over all variables
$\triangleright M$ step

Using the EM algorithm, the optimal setting for the E-step is to use $q_{t}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p^{o l d}\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$. With this notation, the EM algorithm can be compactly stated as in algorithm(11.2). See also EMbeliefnet.m. An illustration of the evolution of the log likelihood under EM iterations is given in fig(11.4). For readers less comfortable with the above KL-based derivation, we describe a more classical approach based on Lagrange multipliers for a specific case in example(11.5).

Example 11.5 (Another belief network example). Consider a five variable distribution with discrete variables,

$$
p\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5}\right)=p\left(x_{1} \mid x_{2}\right) p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{3}\right) p\left(x_{3} \mid x_{4}\right) p\left(x_{4} \mid x_{5}\right) p\left(x_{5}\right)
$$

in which the variables $x_{2}$ and $x_{4}$ are consistently hidden in the training data, and training data for $x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{5}$ are always present. The distribution can be represented as a belief network

The M-step is given by maximising the energy. According to the general form for the energy, equation (11.2.35), we need to consider a variational distribution $q(h \mid v)$ on the hidden variables $h=\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)$ conditioned on the visible variables $v=\left(x_{1}, x_{3}, x_{5}\right)$. Using $n$ as the datapoint index and $t$ as the EM iteration counter, we require variational distributions for each datapoint

$$
q_{t}\left(x_{2}^{n}, x_{4}^{n} \mid x_{1}^{n}, x_{3}^{n}, x_{5}^{n}\right)
$$

To keep the notation more compact, we drop here the iteration counter index and write the above as simply $q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)$. In this case, the contributions to the energy have the form

$$
\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{1}^{n} \mid x_{2}\right) p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{3}^{n}\right) p\left(x_{3}^{n} \mid x_{4}\right) p\left(x_{4} \mid x_{5}^{n}\right) p\left(x_{5}^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)}
$$

which may be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n}\langle & \left.\log p\left(x_{1}^{n} \mid x_{2}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)}+\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{3}^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)} \\
& +\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{3}^{n} \mid x_{4}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)}+\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{4} \mid x_{5}^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}, x_{4}\right)}+\sum_{n} \log p\left(x_{5}^{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

A useful property can now be exploited, namely that each term depends on only those hidden variables in the family that that term represents. Thus we may write

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n} & \left\langle\log p\left(x_{1}^{n} \mid x_{2}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}\right)}+\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{2} \mid x_{3}^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{2}\right)} \\
& +\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{3}^{n} \mid x_{4}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{4}\right)}+\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(x_{4} \mid x_{5}^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q^{n}\left(x_{4}\right)}+\sum_{n} \log p\left(x_{5}^{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The final term can be set using maximum likelihood. Let us consider therefore a more difficult table, $p\left(x_{1} \mid x_{2}\right)$. When will the table entry $p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)$ occur in the energy? This happens whenever $x_{1}^{n}$ is in state $i$. Since there is a summation over all the states of variables $x_{2}$ (due to the average), there is also a term with variable $x_{2}$ in state $j$. Hence the contribution to the energy from terms of the form $p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)$ is

$$
\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right) \log p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)
$$

where the indicator function $\mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right]$ equals 1 if $x_{1}^{n}$ is in state $i$ and is zero otherwise. To ensure normalisation of the table, we add a Lagrange term:

$$
\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right) \log p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)+\lambda\left\{1-\sum_{k} p\left(x_{1}=k \mid x_{2}=j\right)\right\}
$$

Differentiating with respect to $p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)$ and equating to zero we get

$$
\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] \frac{q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right)}{p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)}=\lambda
$$

or

$$
p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right) \propto \sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right)
$$

Hence

$$
p\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)=\frac{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right)}{\sum_{n, k} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=k\right] q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right)}
$$

From the E-step we have

$$
q^{n}\left(x_{2}=j\right)=p^{o l d}\left(x_{2}=j \mid x_{1}^{n}, x_{3}^{n}, x_{5}^{n}\right)
$$

This optimal distribution is easy to compute since this is the marginal on the family, given some evidential variables. Hence, the M-step update for the table is

$$
p^{\text {new }}\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right)=\frac{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] p^{o l d}\left(x_{2}=j \mid x_{1}^{n}, x_{3}^{n}, x_{5}^{n}\right)}{\sum_{n, k} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=k\right] p^{o l d}\left(x_{2}=j \mid x_{1}^{n}, x_{3}^{n}, x_{5}^{n}\right)}
$$

If there were no hidden data, equation (11.2.55) would read

$$
p^{\text {new }}\left(x_{1}=i \mid x_{2}=j\right) \propto \sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[x_{1}^{n}=i\right] \mathbb{I}\left[x_{2}^{n}=j\right]
$$

All that we do, therefore, in the general EM case, is to replace those deterministic functions such as $\mathbb{I}\left[x_{2}^{n}=i\right]$ by their missing variable equivalents $p^{o l d}\left(x_{2}=i \mid x_{1}^{n}, x_{3}^{n}, x_{5}^{n}\right)$.

![img-147.jpeg](img-147.jpeg)

Figure 11.4: Evolution of the log-likelihood versus iterations under the EM training procedure (from solving the Printer Nightmare with missing data, exercise(11.1)). Note how rapid progress is made at the beginning, but convergence can be slow.

# 11.2.5 Convergence 

Convergence of EM can be slow, particularly when the number of missing observations is greater than the number of visible observations. In practice, one often combines the EM with gradient based procedures to improve convergence, see section(11.6). Note also that the log likelihood is typically a non-convex function of the parameters. This means that there may be multiple local optima and the solution found often depends on the initialisation.

### 11.2.6 Application to Markov networks

Whilst our examples have been for belief networks, we may also apply the EM application to learning the parameters of Markov networks that have missing data. For a MN defined over visible and hidden variables with separate parameters $\theta_{c}$ for each clique $c$

$$
p(v, h \mid \theta)=\frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \prod_{c} \phi_{c}\left(h, v \mid \theta_{c}\right)
$$

the EM variational bound is

$$
\log p(v \mid \theta) \geq H(q)+\sum_{c}\left\langle\log \phi_{c}\left(h, v \mid \theta_{c}\right)\right\rangle_{q(h)}-\log Z(\theta)
$$

where $H(p)$ is the entropy function of a distribution, $H(p) \equiv-\langle\log p(x)\rangle_{p(x)}$. Whilst the bound decouples the clique parameters in the second term, the parameters are nevertheless coupled in the normalisation

$$
Z(\theta)=\sum_{v, h} \prod_{c=1}^{C} \phi_{c}\left(h, v \mid \theta_{c}\right), \quad \theta=\left(\theta_{1}, \ldots, \theta_{C}\right)
$$

Because of this we cannot directly optimise the above bound on a parameter by parameter basis. One approach is to use an additional bound $\log Z(\theta)$ from above, as for iterative scaling, section(9.6.4) to decouple the clique parameters in $Z$; we leave the details as an exercise for the interested reader.

### 11.3 Extensions of EM

### 11.3.1 Partial M step

It is not necessary to find the full optimum of the energy term at each iteration. As long as one finds a parameter $\theta^{\prime}$ which has a higher energy than that of the current parameter $\theta$, then the conditions required in section(11.2.2) still hold, and the likelihood cannot decrease at each iteration.

### 11.3.2 Partial E-step

The E-step requires us to find the optimum of

$$
\log p(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta) \geq-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(h^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}
$$

with respect to $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$. The fully optimal setting is

$$
q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)
$$

For a guaranteed increase in likelihood at each iteration, from section(11.2.2) we required that this fully optimal setting of $q$ is used. Unfortunately, therefore, one cannot in general guarantee that a partial E-step (in which one would only partially optimise the lower bound with respect to $q$ for fixed $\theta$ ) would always increase the likelihood. Of course, it is guaranteed to increase the lower bound on the likelihood, though not the likelihood itself. We discuss some partial E-step scenarios below.

# Intractable energy 

The EM algorithm assumes that we can calculate

$$
\langle\log p(h, v \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h \mid v)}
$$

However, there may be cases in which we cannot computationally carry out the averages with respect to the fully optimal form of $q$. In this case one may consider a restricted class $\mathcal{Q}$ of $q$-distributions for which the averages can be carried out. For example, one class for which the averages may become computationally tractable is the factorised distributions $q(h \mid v)=\prod_{j} q\left(h_{j} \mid v\right)$; another popular class are Gaussian $q$ distributions. We can then find the best distribution in the class $\mathcal{Q}$ by using a numerical optimisation routine:

$$
q^{\text {opt }}=\underset{q \in \mathcal{Q}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \operatorname{KL}(q(h) \mid p(h \mid v, \theta))
$$

Alternatively, one can assume a certain structured form for the $q$ distribution, and learn the optimal factors of the distribution by free form functional calculus. This approach is taken for example in section(28.4.2).

## Viterbi training

An extreme case of a partial E-step is to restrict $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$ to a delta-function. In this case, the entropic term $\left\langle\log q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)}$ is constant (zero for discrete $h$ ), so that the optimal delta function $q$ is to set

$$
q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=\delta\left(h^{n}, h_{*}^{n}\right)
$$

where

$$
h_{*}^{n}=\underset{h}{\operatorname{argmax}} p\left(h, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

When used in the energy, the average with respect to $q$ is trivial and the energy becomes simply

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log p\left(h_{*}^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

The corresponding bound on the log-likelihood is then

$$
\log p(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta) \geq H+\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log p\left(h_{*}^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

where $H$ is the entropy of the delta function (zero for discrete $h$ ).
As a partial justification for this technique, provided there is sufficient data, one might hope that the likelihood as a function of the parameter $\theta$ will be sharply peaked around the optimum value. This means that at convergence the approximation of the posterior $p\left(h \mid v, \theta^{\text {opt }}\right)$ by a delta function will be reasonable, and an update of EM using Viterbi training will produce a new $\theta$ approximately the same as $\theta^{\text {opt }}$. For any highly suboptimal $\theta$, however, $p(h \mid v, \theta)$ may be far from a delta function, and therefore a Viterbi update is less reliable in terms of leading to an increase in the likelihood itself. This suggests that the initialisation of $\theta$ for Viterbi training is more critical than for the standard EM. Note that since Viterbi training corresponds to a partial E-step, EM training with this restricted class of $q$ distribution is therefore only guaranteed to increase the lower bound on the log likelihood, not the likelihood itself.

This technique is popular in the speech recognition community for training HMMs, section(23.2), from where the terminology Viterbi training arises.

# Stochastic EM 

Another approximate $q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$ distribution that is popular is to use an empirical distribution formed by samples from the fully optimal distribution $p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta\right)$. That is one draws samples (see chapter(27) for a discussion on sampling) $h_{1}^{n}, \ldots, h_{L}^{n}$ from $p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}, \theta\right)$ and forms a $q$ distribution

$$
q\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)=\frac{1}{L} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \delta\left(h^{n}, h_{l}^{n}\right)
$$

The energy then becomes proportional to

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \log p\left(h_{l}^{n}, v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

so that, as in Viterbi training, the energy is always computationally tractable for this restricted $q$ class. Provided that the samples from $p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$ are reliable, stochastic training will produce an energy function with (on average) the same characteristics as the true energy under the classical EM algorithm. This means that the solution obtained from stochastic EM should tend to that from classical EM as the number of samples increases.

### 11.4 A failure case for EM

Whilst the EM algorithm is very useful, there are some cases in which it does not work. Consider a likelihood of the form

$$
p(v \mid \theta)=\int_{h} p(v \mid h, \theta) p(h), \quad \text { with } \operatorname{CORRECTION} p(v \mid h, \theta)=\delta(v, f(h \mid \theta))
$$

If we attempt an EM approach for this, this will fail (see also exercise(7.8)). To see why this happens, the M-step sets

$$
\theta_{\text {new }}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\left\langle\log p(v, h \mid \theta)\right\rangle_{p\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\left\langle\log p(v \mid h, \theta)\right\rangle_{p\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)}
$$

where we used the fact that for this model $p(h)$ is independent of $\theta$. In the case that $p(v \mid h, \theta)=\delta(v, f(h \mid \theta))$ then

$$
p\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right) \propto \delta\left(v, f\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)\right) p(h)
$$

so that optimising the energy gives the update

$$
\theta_{\text {new }}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\left\langle\log \delta(v, f(h \mid \theta))\right\rangle_{p\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)}
$$

Since $p\left(h \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)$ is zero everywhere expect that $h^{*}$ for which $v=f\left(h^{*} \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)$, then the energy term becomes $\log \delta\left(f\left(h^{*} \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right), f\left(h^{*} \mid \theta\right)\right)$. This is effectively negative infinity if $\theta \neq \theta_{\text {old }}$ and zero when $\theta=\theta_{\text {old }}$. Hence $\theta=\theta_{\text {old }}$ is optimal and the EM algorithm fails to produce a meaningful parameter update. ${ }^{2}$ This situation occurs in practice, and has been noted in particular in the context of Independent Component Analysis[239]. Whilst using a delta-function for the output is clearly extreme, a similar slowing down of parameter updates can occur when the term $p(v \mid h, \theta)$ becomes close to deterministic.

One can attempt to heal this behaviour by deriving an EM algorithm based on the distribution

$$
p_{\epsilon}(v \mid h, \theta)=(1-\epsilon) \delta(v, f(h \mid \theta))+\epsilon n(h), \quad 0 \leq \epsilon \leq 1
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{2}$ For discrete variables and the Kronecker delta, the energy attains the maximal value of zero when $\theta=\theta_{\text {old }}$. In the case of continuous variables, however, the log of the Dirac delta function is not well defined. Considering the delta function as the limit of a narrow width Gaussian, for any small but finite width, the energy is largest when $\theta=\theta_{\text {old }}$.

where $n(h)$ is an arbitrary distribution on the hidden variable $h$. The original deterministic model corresponds to $p_{0}(v \mid h, \theta)$. Defining

$$
p_{\epsilon}(v \mid \theta)=\int_{h} p_{\epsilon}(v \mid h, \theta) p(h), \quad p_{\epsilon}(v \mid \theta)=(1-\epsilon) p_{0}(v \mid \theta)+\epsilon\langle n(h)\rangle_{p(h)}
$$

an EM algorithm for $p_{\epsilon}(v \mid \theta), 0<\epsilon<1$ satisfies

$$
p_{\epsilon}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {new }}\right)-p_{\epsilon}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)=(1-\epsilon)\left(p_{0}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {new }}\right)-p_{0}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)\right)>0
$$

which implies

$$
p_{0}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {new }}\right)-p_{0}\left(v \mid \theta_{\text {old }}\right)>0
$$

This means that the EM algorithm for the non-deterministic case $0<\epsilon<1$ is guaranteed to increase the likelihood under the deterministic model $p_{0}(v \mid \theta)$ at each iteration (unless we are at convergence). See [107] for an application of this 'antifreeze' technique to learning Markov Decision Processes with EM.

# 11.5 Variational Bayes 

Variational Bayes is analogous to EM in that it helps us to deal with hidden variables; however it is a Bayesian method that returns a posterior distribution on parameters, rather than a single best $\theta$ as given by maximum likelihood. To keep the notation simple, we'll initially assume only a single datapoint with observation $v$. Our interest is then the parameter posterior

$$
p(\theta \mid v) \propto p(v \mid \theta) p(\theta) \propto \sum_{h} p(v, h \mid \theta) p(\theta)
$$

The VB approach assumes a factorised approximation of the joint hidden and parameter posterior, see fig(11.5):

$$
p(h, \theta \mid v) \approx q(h) q(\theta)
$$

The optimal settings for the factors $q(h)$ and $q(\theta)$ can be found by minimising the Kullback-Leibler divergence between $p(h, \theta \mid v)$ and $q(h) q(\theta)$ as discussed below.

## A bound on the marginal likelihood

By minimising the KL divergence,

$$
\mathrm{KL}(q(h) q(\theta) \mid p(h, \theta \mid v))=\langle\log q(h)\rangle_{q(h)}+\langle\log q(\theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)}-\langle\log p(h, \theta \mid v)\rangle_{q(h) q(\theta)} \geq 0
$$

we arrive at the bound

$$
\log p(v) \geq-\langle\log q(h)\rangle_{q(h)}-\langle\log q(\theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)}+\langle\log p(v, h, \theta)\rangle_{q(h) q(\theta)}
$$

Minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence with respect to $q(\theta)$ and $q(h)$ is equivalent to obtaining the tightest lower bound on $\log p(v)$. A simple coordinate-wise procedure in which we first fix the $q(\theta)$ and solve for $q(h)$ and then vice versa is analogous to the E and M step of the EM algorithm:

## E-step

$$
q^{\text {new }}(h)=\underset{q(h)}{\operatorname{argmin}} \mathrm{KL}\left(q(h) q^{o l d}(\theta) \mid p(h, \theta \mid v)\right)
$$

## M-step

$$
q^{\text {new }}(\theta)=\underset{q(\theta)}{\operatorname{argmin}} \mathrm{KL}\left(q^{\text {new }}(h) q(\theta) \mid p(h, \theta \mid v)\right)
$$

For a set of observations $\mathcal{V}$ and hidden variables $\mathcal{H}$, the procedure is described in algorithm(11.3). For distributions $q(\mathcal{H})$ and $q(\theta)$ which are parameterised or otherwise constrained, the best distributions in the minimal KL sense are returned. In general, each iteration of VB is guaranteed to increase the bound on the marginal likelihood, but not the marginal likelihood itself. Like the EM algorithm, VB can (and often does) suffer from local maxima issues. This means that the converged solution can be dependent on the initialisation.

Algorithm 11.3 Variational Bayes.

```
\(t=0\)
Choose an initial distribution \(q_{0}(\theta)\).
while \(\theta\) not converged (or likelihood bound not converged) do
    \(t \leftarrow t+1\)
    \(q_{t}(\mathcal{H})=\arg \min _{q(\mathcal{H})} \mathrm{KL}\left(q(\mathcal{H}) q_{t-1}(\theta) \mid p(\mathcal{H}, \theta \mid \mathcal{V})\right)\)
    \(q_{t}(\theta)=\arg \min _{q(\theta)} \mathrm{KL}\left(q_{t}(\mathcal{H}) q(\theta) \mid p(\mathcal{H}, \theta \mid \mathcal{V})\right)\)
end while
return \(q_{t}(\theta)\)
```

$\triangleright$ The posterior parameter approximation.
![img-148.jpeg](img-148.jpeg)
(a)
![img-149.jpeg](img-149.jpeg)
(b)

Figure 11.5: (a): Generic form of a model with hidden variables. (b): A factorised posterior approximation used in Variational Bayes.

# Unconstrained approximations 

For fixed $q(\theta)$ the contribution to the KL divergence equation (11.5.3) from $q(h)$ is

$$
\langle\log q(h)\rangle_{q(h)}-\langle\log p(v, h, \theta)\rangle_{q(h) q(\theta)}=\operatorname{KL}(q(h) \mid \tilde{p}(h))+\text { const. }
$$

where

$$
\tilde{p}(h) \equiv \frac{1}{\hat{Z}} \exp \left(\langle\log p(v, h, \theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)}\right)
$$

and $\hat{Z}$ is a normalising constant. Hence, for fixed $q(\theta)$, the E-step sets $q(h)$ to $\tilde{p}$,

$$
q(h) \propto \exp \langle\log p(v, h, \theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)} \propto \exp \langle\log p(v, h \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)}
$$

Similarly, for fixed $q(h)$, the M-step sets

$$
q(\theta) \propto \exp \langle\log p(v, h, \theta)\rangle_{q(h)}=p(\theta) \exp \langle\log p(v, h \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h)}
$$

These E and M-step updates are iterated to convergence.

## i.i.d. Data

Under the i.i.d. assumption, we obtain a bound on the marginal likelihood for the whole dataset $\mathcal{V}=$ $\left\{v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}\right\}$ :

$$
\log p(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta) \geq \sum_{n}\left\{-\left\langle\log q\left(h^{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n}\right)}-\langle\log q(\theta)\rangle_{q(\theta)}+\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n}, h^{n}, \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(h^{n}\right) q(\theta)}\right\}
$$

The bound holds for any $q\left(h^{n}\right)$ and $q(\theta)$ but is tightest for the converged estimates from the VB procedure. For an i.i.d. dataset, it is straightforward to show that without loss of generality we may assume

$$
q\left(h^{1}, \ldots, h^{N}\right)=\prod_{n} q\left(h^{n}\right)
$$

Under this we arrive at algorithm(11.4).

Algorithm 11.4 Variational Bayes (i.i.d. data).

```
\(t=0\)
Choose an initial distribution \(q_{0}(\theta)\).
    \(\triangleright\) Iteration counter
    while \(\theta\) not converged (or likelihood bound not converged) do
        \(t \leftarrow t+1\)
        for \(n=1\) to \(N\) do
            \(q_{t}^{n}\left(h^{n}\right) \propto \exp \left(\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n}, h^{n} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t-1}(\theta)}\right)\)
            end for
            \(q_{t}(\theta) \propto p(\theta) \exp \left(\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n}, h^{n} \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{q_{t}^{n}\left(h^{n}\right)}\right)\)
end while
    return \(q_{t}^{n}(\theta)\)
```

$\triangleright$ The posterior parameter approximation.

# 11.5.1 EM is a special case of variational Bayes 

If we wish to find a summary of the parameter posterior corresponding to only the most likely point $\theta_{*}$, then we may use a restricted $q(\theta)$ of the form

$$
q(\theta)=\delta\left(\theta, \theta_{*}\right)
$$

where $\theta_{*}$ is the single optimal value of the parameter. If we plug this assumption into equation (11.5.4) we obtain the bound

$$
\log p\left(v \mid \theta_{*}\right) \geq-\langle\log q(h)\rangle_{q(h)}+\left\langle\log p\left(v, h, \theta_{*}\right)\right\rangle_{q(h)}+\text { const. }
$$

The M-step is then given by

$$
\theta_{*}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}}(\langle\log p(v, h \mid \theta)\rangle_{q(h)}+\log p(\theta))
$$

For a flat prior $p(\theta)=$ const., this is therefore equivalent to energy maximisation in the EM algorithm. Using this single optimal value in the VB E-step update for $q\left(h^{n}\right)$ we have

$$
q_{t}^{n}(h) \propto p\left(v, h \mid \theta_{*}\right) \propto p\left(h \mid v, \theta_{*}\right)
$$

which is the standard E-step of EM. Hence EM is a special case of VB under a flat prior $p(\theta)=$ const. and delta function approximation of the parameter posterior.

### 11.5.2 An example: VB for the Asbestos-Smoking-Cancer network

In section(9.4) we showed how to apply Bayesian methods to train a belief network, giving rise to a posterior distribution over parameter. In our previous discussion, the data was fully observed. Here, however, we wish to revisit this case, now assuming however that some of the observations can be missing. This complicates the Bayesian analysis and motivates approximate methods such as VB.
Let's reconsider Bayesian learning in the binary variable asbestos-smoking-cancer network, as described in section(9.4)

$$
p(a, c, s)=p(c \mid a, s) p(a) p(s)
$$

in which we use a factorised parameter prior

$$
p\left(\theta_{c}\right) p\left(\theta_{a}\right) p\left(\theta_{s}\right)
$$

When all the data $\mathcal{V}$ is i.i.d. and observed, the parameter posterior factorises. However, as we discussed in section(11.1.1) if the state of $a$ (asbestos) is not observed, the parameter posterior no longer factorises:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(\theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c} \mid \mathcal{V}\right) & \propto p\left(\theta_{a}\right) p\left(\theta_{s}\right) p\left(\theta_{c}\right) p\left(\mathcal{V} \mid \theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c}\right) \\
& \propto p\left(\theta_{a}\right) p\left(\theta_{s}\right) p\left(\theta_{c}\right) \prod_{n} p\left(v^{n} \mid \theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c}\right) \\
& \propto p\left(\theta_{a}\right) p\left(\theta_{s}\right) p\left(\theta_{c}\right) \prod_{n} p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right) \sum_{a^{n}} p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right) p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

![img-150.jpeg](img-150.jpeg)

Figure 11.6: (a): A model for the relationship between lung Cancer, Asbestos exposure and Smoking with factorised parameter priors. Variables $c$ and $s$ are observed, but variable $a$ is consistently missing. (b): A factorised parameter posterior approximation.
where the summation over $a$ prevents the factorisation into a product of the individual table parameters. This means that it becomes more awkward to represent the posterior since we cannot exactly do this by using posterior distributions on each parameter table alone. This is a situation in which VB can be useful since it enables us to impose factorisations on the posterior. In VB we consider an approximation to the posterior over the parameters and latent variables $q(h) q(\theta)$. In this case $\theta=\left(\theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c}\right)$ and the latent variables are asbestos, $a^{n}$ (one for each datapoint). For this example the visible variables are smoking and cancer: $\mathcal{V}=\left\{s^{n}, c^{n}\right\}, n=1, \ldots, N$. The exact joint distribution over all these variables is then

$$
p\left(\theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c}, a^{1}, \ldots, a^{N} \mid \mathcal{V}\right) \propto \underbrace{p\left(\theta_{a}\right) p\left(\theta_{s}\right) p\left(\theta_{c}\right)}_{\text {prior }} \underbrace{\prod_{n} p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right) p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right) p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)}_{\text {posterior }}
$$

In VB we make a factorised assumption, splitting the parameters and latent variables:

$$
p\left(\theta, a^{1: N} \mid \mathcal{V}\right) \approx q(\theta) q\left(a^{1: N}\right)
$$

From the general results in equation (11.5.9), we have (ignoring terms that are independent of $a$ in the exponent)

$$
q\left(a^{1: N}\right) \propto \exp \left(\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{c}\right)}\right)
$$

From this we see immediately that our approximation automatically factorises

$$
q\left(a^{1: N}\right)=\prod_{n} q\left(a^{n}\right)
$$

Similarly, from equation (11.5.10) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
q(\theta) & \propto p(\theta) \exp \left(\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right) p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right) p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}\right) \\
& =p(\theta) \exp \left(\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}\right)\left\{\prod_{n} p\left(s^{n} \mid \theta_{s}\right)\right\} \exp \left(\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the parameter prior is factorised, we can collect terms in $\theta_{a}, \theta_{s}$ and $\theta_{c}$ and see that the VB assumption automatically results in a factorised parameter posterior approximation. Hence, our VB approximation is of the form, see fig(11.6),

$$
p\left(\theta_{a}, \theta_{s}, \theta_{c}, a^{1}, \ldots, a^{N} \mid \mathcal{V}\right) \approx q\left(\theta_{a}\right) q\left(\theta_{c}\right) q\left(\theta_{s}\right) \prod_{n} q\left(a^{n}\right)
$$

All that remains is to form E-step $\left(q\left(a^{n}\right)\right.$ updates) and M-step ( $q(\theta)$ updates), as described below.

# M-step: $q(\theta)$ updates 

From above we have

$$
q\left(\theta_{a}\right) \propto p\left(\theta_{a}\right) \prod_{n} \exp \left\langle\log p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}
$$

where

$$
\left\langle\log p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}=q\left(a^{n}=1\right) \log \theta_{a}+q\left(a^{n}=0\right) \log \left(1-\theta_{a}\right)
$$

Hence

$$
\exp \left\langle\log p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(a^{n}\right)}=\theta_{a}^{q\left(a^{n}=1\right)}\left(1-\theta_{a}\right)^{q\left(a^{n}=0\right)}
$$

It is convenient to use a Beta distribution prior,

$$
p\left(\theta_{a}\right)=B\left(\theta_{a} \mid \alpha, \beta\right) \propto \theta_{a}^{\alpha-1}\left(1-\theta_{a}\right)^{\beta-1}
$$

since the posterior approximation is then also a Beta distribution:

$$
q\left(\theta_{a}\right)=B\left(\theta_{a} \mid \alpha+\sum_{n} q\left(a^{n}=1\right), \beta+\sum_{n} q\left(a^{n}=0\right)\right)
$$

A similar calculation gives

$$
q\left(\theta_{s}\right)=B\left(\theta_{s} \mid \alpha+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right], \beta+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=0\right]\right)
$$

Finally, we have a table for each of the parental states of $c$. For example

$$
q\left(\theta_{c}(a=0, s=1)\right)=B\left(\theta_{c} \mid \alpha+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=1\right] q\left(a^{n}=0\right), \beta+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[s^{n}=0\right] q\left(a^{n}=1\right)\right)
$$

These are reminiscent of the standard Bayesian equations, equation (9.4.15), except that the missing data counts have been replaced by $q$ 's.

## E-step: $q\left(a^{n}\right)$ updates

From equation (11.5.24), we have

$$
q\left(a^{n}\right) \propto \exp \left(\left\langle\log p\left(c^{n} \mid s^{n}, a^{n}, \theta_{c}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{c}\right)}+\left\langle\log p\left(a^{n} \mid \theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{a}\right)}\right)
$$

For example, if assume that for datapoint $n, s$ is in state 1 and $c$ in state 0 , then

$$
q\left(a^{n}=1\right) \propto \exp \left\langle\log \left(1-\theta_{c}(s=1, a=1)\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{c}(s=1, a=1)\right)}+\left\langle\log \theta_{a}\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{a}\right)}
$$

and

$$
q\left(a^{n}=0\right) \propto \exp \left(\left\langle\log \left(1-\theta_{c}(s=1, a=0)\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{c}(s=1, a=1)\right)}+\left\langle\log \left(1-\theta_{a}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\theta_{a}\right)}\right)
$$

These updates require the Beta distribution averages $\langle\log \theta\rangle_{B(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta)}$ and $\langle\log (1-\theta)\rangle_{B(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta)}$; these are straightforward to compute, see exercise(8.17).

The complete VB procedure is then given by iterating equations (11.5.33,11.5.34,11.5.35) and (11.5.37,11.5.38) until convergence.

Given a converged factorised approximation, computing a marginal table such as $p(a=1 \mid \mathcal{V})$ is then straightforward under the approximation

$$
p(a=1 \mid \mathcal{V}) \approx \int_{\theta_{a}} q\left(a=1 \mid \theta_{a}\right) q\left(\theta_{a}\right)=\frac{\alpha+\sum_{n} q\left(a^{n}=1\right)}{\alpha+\sum_{n} q\left(a^{n}=0\right)+\beta+\sum_{n} q\left(a^{n}=1\right)}
$$

The application of VB to learning the tables in arbitrarily structured BNs is a straightforward extension of the technique outlined here. Under the factorised approximation, $q(h, \theta)=q(h) q(\theta)$, one will always obtain a simple updating equation analogous to the full data case, but with the missing data replaced by variational approximations. Nevertheless, if a variable has many missing parents, the number of states in the average with respect to the $q$ distribution can become intractable, and further constraints on the form of the approximation, or additional bounds are required.

One may readily extend the above to the case of Dirichlet distributions on multinomial variables, see exercise(11.5). Indeed, the extension to the exponential family is straightforward.

# 11.6 Optimising the Likelihood by Gradient Methods 

The EM algorithm typically works well when the amount of missing information is small compared to the complete information. In this case EM exhibits approximately the same convergence as Newton based gradient method[255]. However, if the fraction of missing information approaches unity, EM can converge very slowly. In the case of continuous parameters $\theta$, an alternative is to compute the gradient of the likelihood directly and use this as part of a standard continuous variable optimisation routine. The gradient is straightforward to compute using the following identity. Consider the log likelihood

$$
L(\theta)=\log p(v \mid \theta)
$$

The derivative can be written

$$
\partial_{\theta} L(\theta)=\frac{1}{p(v \mid \theta)} \partial_{\theta} p(v \mid \theta)=\frac{1}{p(v \mid \theta)} \partial_{\theta} \int_{h} p(v, h \mid \theta)
$$

At this point, we take the derivative inside the integral

$$
\partial_{\theta} L(\theta)=\frac{1}{p(v \mid \theta)} \int_{h} \partial_{\theta} p(v, h \mid \theta)=\int_{h} p(h \mid v, \theta) \partial_{\theta} \log p(v, h \mid \theta)=\left\langle\partial_{\theta} \log p(v, h \mid \theta)\right\rangle_{p(h \mid v, \theta)}
$$

where we used $\partial \log f(x)=(1 / f(x)) \partial f(x)$. The right hand side is the average of the derivative of the log complete likelihood. This is closely related to the derivative of the energy term in the EM algorithm, though note that the average here is performed with respect the current distribution parameters $\theta$ and not $\theta^{\text {old }}$ as in the EM case. Used in this way, computing the derivatives of latent variable models is relatively straightforward. These derivatives may then be used as part of a standard optimisation routine such as conjugate gradients[255].

### 11.6.1 Undirected models

Whilst equation (11.6.3) represents the general case, it is not always possible to easily compute the required averages. Consider an undirected model which contains both hidden and visible variables

$$
p(v, h \mid \theta)=\frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp (\phi(v, h \mid \theta))
$$

For i.i.d. data, the log likelihood on the visible variables is (assuming discrete $v$ and $h$ )

$$
L(\theta)=\sum_{n}\left(\log \sum_{h} \exp \phi\left(v^{n}, h \mid \theta\right)-\log \sum_{h, v} \exp \phi(v, h \mid \theta)\right)
$$

which has gradient

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} L=\sum_{n}\left(\underbrace{\left\langle\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \phi\left(v^{n}, h \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{p(h \mid v^{n}, \theta)}}_{\text {clamped average }}-\underbrace{\left\langle\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \phi(v, h \mid \theta)\right\rangle_{p(h, v \mid \theta)}}_{\text {free average }}\right)
$$

For a Markov Network $p$ that is intractable (the partition function $Z$ cannot be computed efficiently and averages w.r.t. $p$ cannot be computed exactly), the gradient is particularly difficult to estimate since it is the difference of two averages, each of which needs to be estimated. Even getting the sign of the gradient correct can therefore be computationally difficult. For this reason learning in general unstructured Markov networks is particularly difficult (the unstructured Boltzmann machine with hidden units being a particular case in point).

# 11.7 Summary 

- Provided the data is missing at random, we can safely learn parameters by maximising the likelihood of the observed data.
- Variational Expectation Maximisation is a general-purpose algorithm for maximum likelihood learning under missing information.
- The classical EM algorithm is a special case of V-EM and guarantees an improvement (non-decrease) in the likelihood at each iteration.
- Bayesian learning in the case of missing information is potentially problematic since the posterior is typically not factored according to the prior assumptions. In this case approximations are useful, such as variational Bayes, which assumes a factorisation between the parameters and the latent/missing variables.
- The gradient can be easily computed for latent variable models and may be used as part of an optimisation routine. This provides an alternative training approach in cases when EM is slow to converge.
