# CHAPTER 18 

The previous chapter discussed the use of linear models in classification and regression. In this chapter we discuss using priors on the parameters and the resulting posterior distribution over parameters. This represents a powerful extension since it enables us to specify in a principled way our prior knowledge and takes into account that when data is limited there will be considerable uncertainty as to which is the 'best' parameter estimate.

### 18.1 Regression With Additive Gaussian Noise

The linear models in chapter(17) were trained under maximum likelihood and do not deal with the issue that, from a probabilistic perspective, parameter estimates are inherently uncertain due to the limited available training data. Regression refers to inferring a mapping on the basis of observed data $\mathcal{D}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, y^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N\right\}$, where $\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, y^{n}\right)$ represents an input-output pair. We discuss here the scalar output case (and vector inputs $\mathbf{x}$ ) with the extension to the vector output case $\mathbf{y}$ being straightforward. We assume that each (clean) output is generated from a model $f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})$ where the parameters $\mathbf{w}$ of the function $f$ are unknown. An observed output $y$ is generated by the addition of noise $\eta$ to the clean model output,

$$
y=f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})+\eta
$$

If the noise is Gaussian distributed, $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\eta \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)$, the model generates an output $y$ for input $\mathbf{x}$ with probability

$$
p(y \mid \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x})=\mathcal{N}\left(y \mid f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}), \sigma^{2}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^{2}}} \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2 \sigma^{2}}[y-f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})]^{2}\right)
$$

Here our interest is only in modelling this output distribution, and not the distribution of the inputs. As such no parameters are used to model the inputs. If we assume that each data input-output pair is generated identically and independently, the likelihood the model generates the data is

$$
p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w})=\prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(y^{n} \mid \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x}^{n}\right) p\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)
$$

We may use a prior weight distribution $p(\mathbf{w})$ to quantify our a priori belief in the suitability of each parameter setting. Writing $\mathcal{D}=\left\{\mathcal{D}_{x}, \mathcal{D}_{y}\right\}$, the posterior weight distribution is then given by

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w}) \propto p\left(\mathcal{D}_{y} \mid \mathbf{w}, \mathcal{D}_{x}\right) p(\mathbf{w})
$$

Using the Gaussian noise assumption, and for convenience defining $\beta=1 / \sigma^{2}$, this gives

$$
\log p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})=-\frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[y^{n}-f\left(\mathbf{x}^{n} ; \mathbf{w}\right)\right]^{2}+\log p(\mathbf{w})+\frac{N}{2} \log \beta+\text { const. }
$$

![img-206.jpeg](img-206.jpeg)

Figure 18.1: Belief Network representation of a Bayesian Model for regression under the i.i.d. data assumption. The hyperparameter $\alpha$ acts as a form of regulariser, controlling the flexibility of the prior on the weights $\mathbf{w}$. The hyperparameter $\beta$ controls the level of noise on the observations.

Note the similarity between equation (18.1.5) and the regularised training error equation (17.2.17). In the probabilistic framework, we identify the choice of a sum squared error with the assumption of additive Gaussian noise. Similarly, the regularising term is identified with $\log p(\mathbf{w})$.

# 18.1.1 Bayesian linear parameter models 

Linear parameter models, as discussed in chapter(17), have the form

$$
f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_{i} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x}) \equiv \mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where the parameters $w_{i}$ are also called 'weights' and the number of basis functions is $\operatorname{dim}(\mathbf{w})=B$. Such models have a linear parameter dependence, but may represent a non-linear input-output mapping if the basis functions $\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ are non-linear in $\mathbf{x}$. Since the output scales linearly with $\mathbf{w}$, we can discourage extreme output values by penalising large weight values. A natural weight prior is thus

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \alpha^{-1} \mathbf{I}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha}{2 \pi}\right)^{\frac{B}{2}} \exp \left(-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right)
$$

where the precision $\alpha$ is the inverse variance. If $\alpha$ is large, the total squared length of the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ is encouraged to be small. The full model $p(\mathcal{D}, \mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \beta)$ is then specified, see fig(18.1). Under the Gaussian noise assumption, the posterior distribution is

$$
\log p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})=-\frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}+\text { const. }
$$

where $\Gamma=\{\alpha, \beta\}$ represents the hyperparameter set. Parameters that determine the functions $\phi$ may also be included in the hyperparameter set. Completing the square, section(8.4.1), the weight posterior is therefore a Gaussian distribution,

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})
$$

where the covariance and mean are given by

$$
\mathbf{S}=\left(\alpha \mathbf{I}+\beta \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right)^{-1}, \quad \mathbf{m}=\beta \mathbf{S} \sum_{n=1}^{N} y^{n} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)
$$

The mean prediction for an input $\mathbf{x}$ is then given by

$$
\bar{f}(\mathbf{x}) \equiv \int f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \Gamma) d \mathbf{w}=\mathbf{m}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

Similarly, the variance of the underlying estimated clean function is

$$
\operatorname{var}(f(\mathbf{x}))=\left\langle\left[\mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\right]^{2}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \Gamma)}-\bar{f}(\mathbf{x})^{2}=\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{S} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

The output variance $\operatorname{var}(f(\mathbf{x}))$ depends only on the input variables and not on the training outputs $y$. Since the additive noise $\eta$ is uncorrelated with the model outputs, the predictive variance is

$$
\operatorname{var}(y(\mathbf{x}))=\operatorname{var}(f(\mathbf{x}))+\sigma^{2}
$$

and represents the variance of the 'noisy' output for an input $\mathbf{x}$.

![img-207.jpeg](img-207.jpeg)

Figure 18.2: Along the horizontal axis we plot the input $x$ and along the vertical axis the output $y$. (a): The raw input-output training data and basis functions $\phi_{i}(x)$. (b): Prediction using regularised training and (poorly chosen) fixed hyperparameters. (c): Prediction using ML-II optimised hyperparameters. Also plotted are standard error bars on the clean underlying function, $f(x) \pm \sqrt{\operatorname{var}(f(x))}$.

Example 18.1. In fig(18.2b), we show the mean prediction on the data in fig(18.2a) using 15 Gaussian basis functions

$$
\phi_{i}(x)=\exp \left(-0.5\left(x-c_{i}\right)^{2} / \lambda^{2}\right)
$$

with width $\lambda=0.03^{2}$ and centres $c_{i}$ spread out evenly over the 1-dimensional input space from -2 to 2 . We set the other hyperparameters by hand to $\beta=100$ and $\alpha=1$. The prediction severely overfits the data, a result of a poor choice of hyperparameter settings. This is resolved in fig(18.2c) using the ML-II parameters, as described below.

# 18.1.2 Determining hyperparameters: ML-II 

The hyperparameter posterior distribution is

$$
p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma) p(\Gamma)
$$

A simple summarisation of the posterior is given by the MAP assignment which takes the single 'optimal' setting:

$$
\Gamma^{*}=\underset{\Gamma}{\operatorname{argmax}} p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D})
$$

If the prior belief about the hyperparameters is weak $(p(\Gamma) \approx$ const. $)$, this is equivalent to using the $\Gamma$ that maximises the marginal likelihood

$$
p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=\int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma) d \mathbf{w}
$$

This approach to setting hyperparameters is called 'ML-II' [33] or the Evidence Procedure[195].
In the case of Bayesian Linear Parameter models under Gaussian additive noise, computing the marginal likelihood equation (18.1.17) involves only Gaussian integration. A direct approach to deriving an expression for the marginal likelihood is to consider

$$
p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w})=\exp \left(-\frac{\beta}{2}\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right)(2 \pi \beta)^{N / 2}(2 \pi \alpha)^{B / 2}
$$

By collating terms in $\mathbf{w}$ (completing the square, section(8.4.1)), the above represents a Gaussian in $\mathbf{w}$ with additional factors. After integrating over this Gaussian we have

$$
2 \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=-\beta \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(y^{n}\right)^{2}+\mathbf{d}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{d}-\log \operatorname{det}(\mathbf{S})+B \log \alpha+N \log \beta-N \log (2 \pi)
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{d}=\beta \sum_{n} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) y^{n}
$$

See exercise(18.2) for an alternative expression.

Example 18.2. We return to the example in fig(18.2) and try to find a more appropriate setting for the hyperparameters. Using the hyperparameters $\alpha, \beta, \lambda$ that optimise expression (18.1.19) gives the results in fig(18.2c) where we plot both the mean predictions and standard predictive error bars. This demonstrates that an acceptable setting for the hyperparameters can be obtained by maximising the marginal likelihood. Generally speaking, provided the number of hyperparameters is low compared to the number of datapoints, setting hyperparameters using ML-II will not be at risk of overfitting.

# 18.1.3 Learning the hyperparameters using EM 

As described above, we can set hyperparameters $\Gamma$ by maximising the marginal likelihood equation (18.1.17). A convenient computational procedure to achieve this is to interpret the $\mathbf{w}$ as latent variables and apply the EM algorithm, section(11.2). From equation (18.1.17), the energy term is

$$
E \equiv\langle\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \Gamma) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma)\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \Gamma^{\text {old }})}
$$

According to the general EM procedure we need to maximise the energy term. For a hyperparameter $\Gamma$ the derivative of the energy is given by

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \Gamma} E \equiv\left\langle\frac{\partial}{\partial \Gamma} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \Gamma) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma)\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \Gamma^{\text {old }})}
$$

For the Bayesian LPM with Gaussian weight and noise distributions, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} E & =\frac{N}{2 \beta}-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma^{\text {old }}, \mathcal{D}\right)} \\
& =\frac{N}{2 \beta}-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{m}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}-\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{trace}\left(\mathbf{S} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{m}$ are given in equation (18.1.10). Solving for the zero derivatives gives the M-step update

$$
\frac{1}{\beta^{\text {new }}}=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{m}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}+\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S} \hat{\mathbf{S}})
$$

where

$$
\hat{\mathbf{S}} \equiv \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)
$$

Similarly, for $\alpha$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} E=\frac{B}{2 \alpha}-\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma^{\text {old }}, \mathcal{D}\right)}=\frac{B}{2 \alpha}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}\right)
$$

which, on equating to zero, gives the update

$$
\frac{1}{\alpha^{\text {new }}}=\frac{1}{B}\left(\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}\right)
$$

An alternative fixed point procedure that can be more rapidly convergent than EM is given in equation (18.1.37). Closed form updates for other hyperparameters, such as the width of the basis functions, are generally not available, and the corresponding energy term needs to be optimised numerically.

![img-208.jpeg](img-208.jpeg)

Figure 18.3: Predictions for an RBF for different widths $\lambda$. For each $\lambda$ the ML-II optimal $\alpha, \beta$ are obtained by running the EM procedure to convergence and subsequently used to form the predictions. In each panel the dots represent the training points, with $x$ along the horizontal axis and $y$ along the vertical axis. Mean predictions are plotted, along with predictive error bars of one standard deviation. According to ML-II, the best model corresponds to $\lambda=0.37$, see fig(18.4). The smaller values of $\lambda$ overfit the data, giving rise to too 'rough' functions. The largest values of $\lambda$ underfit, giving too 'smooth' functions. See demoBayesLinReg.m.

# 18.1.4 Hyperparameter optimisation : using the gradient 

To maximise equation (18.1.17) with respect to hyperparameters $\Gamma$, we can make use of the general identity from equation (11.6.3) which, in this context, is

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \Gamma} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=\left\langle\frac{\partial}{\partial \Gamma} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \Gamma) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma)\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \Gamma)}
$$

Since the likelihood is independent of $\alpha$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=\left\langle\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \log p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})}
$$

Using

$$
\log p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)=-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}+\frac{B}{2} \log \alpha+\text { const. }
$$

![img-209.jpeg](img-209.jpeg)

Figure 18.4: The log marginal likelihood $\log p\left(\mathcal{D} \mid \lambda, \alpha^{*}(\lambda), \beta^{*}(\lambda)\right)$ having found the optimal values of the hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ using ML-II. These optimal values are dependent on $\lambda$. According to ML-II, the best model corresponds to $\lambda=0.37$. From fig(18.3) we see that this gives a reasonable fit to the data.

we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle-\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}+\frac{B}{\alpha}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})}
$$

Setting the derivative to zero, the optimal $\alpha$ satisfies

$$
0=-\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})}+\frac{B}{\alpha}
$$

One may now form a fixed point equation

$$
\alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B}{\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})}}
$$

which is equivalent to an EM update, equation (18.1.27), for this model. For a Gaussian posterior, $p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle=\operatorname{trace}\left(\left\langle\mathbf{w w}^{\top}\right\rangle-\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle^{\top}+\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle^{\top}\right)=\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m} \\
& \alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B}{\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}}
\end{aligned}
$$

One may similarly find the gradient and associated fixed point update for $\beta$ which, again is equivalent to the EM update for this model.

# Gull-MacKay fixed point iteration 

From equation (18.1.32) we have

$$
0=-\alpha\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D})}+B=-\alpha \mathbf{S}-\alpha \mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}+B
$$

so that an alternative fixed point equation[135, 194] is

$$
\alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B-\alpha \operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})}{\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}}
$$

In practice this update converges more rapidly than equation (18.1.35). Similarly, one can form an alternative update for $\beta$

$$
\beta^{\text {new }}=\frac{1-\beta \operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S} \hat{\mathbf{S}})}{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[y^{n}-\mathbf{m}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right]^{2}}
$$

Example 18.3 (Learning the basis function widths). In fig(18.3) we plot the training data for a regression problem using a Bayesian LPM. A set of 10 Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) are used,

$$
\phi_{i}(x)=\exp \left(-0.5\left(x-c_{i}\right)^{2} / \lambda^{2}\right)
$$

with $c_{i}, i=1, \ldots, 10$ spread out evenly between -2 and 2 . The hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are learned by ML-II under EM updating. For a fixed width $\lambda$ we then present the predictions, each time finding the optimal $\alpha$ and $\beta$ for this width. The optimal joint $\alpha, \beta, \lambda$ hyperparameter setting is obtained as described in fig(18.4) which shows the marginal log likelihood for a range of widths. The fit resulting from the jointly optimal $\alpha, \beta, \lambda$ hyperparameter is reasonable.

# 18.1.5 Validation likelihood 

The hyperparameters found by ML-II are those which are best at explaining the training data. In principle, this is different from those that are best for prediction and, in practice therefore, it is reasonable to set hyperparameters also by validation techniques. One such method is to set hyperparameters by minimal prediction error on a validation set. Another common technique is to set hyperparameters $\Gamma$ by their likelihood on a validation set $\left\{\mathcal{X}_{\text {val }}, \mathcal{Y}_{\text {val }}\right\} \equiv\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}_{\text {val }}^{m}, y_{\text {val }}^{m}\right), m=1, \ldots, M\right\}$ :

$$
p\left(\mathcal{Y}_{\text {val }} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{X}_{\text {train }}, \mathcal{Y}_{\text {train }}, \mathcal{X}_{\text {val }}\right)=\int_{\mathbf{w}} p\left(\mathcal{Y}_{\text {val }} \mid \mathbf{w}, \Gamma\right) p\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{X}_{\text {train }}, \mathcal{Y}_{\text {train }}\right)
$$

from which we obtain (see exercise(18.3))

$$
\log p\left(\mathcal{Y}_{\text {val }} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D}_{\text {train }}, \mathcal{X}_{\text {val }}\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}\left(2 \pi \mathbf{C}_{\text {val }}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{y}_{\text {val }}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\text {val }} \mathbf{m}\right)^{\top} \mathbf{C}_{\text {val }}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{y}_{\text {val }}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\text {val }} \mathbf{m}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{y}_{\text {val }}=\left[y_{\text {val }}^{1}, \ldots, y_{\text {val }}^{M}\right]^{\top}$, covariance

$$
\mathbf{C}_{\text {val }} \equiv \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\text {val }} \mathbf{S} \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\text {val }}^{\top}+\sigma^{2} \mathbf{I}_{M}
$$

and the design matrix of explanatory variables

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\text {val }}^{\top}=\left[\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}_{\text {val }}^{1}\right), \ldots, \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}_{\text {val }}^{M}\right)\right]
$$

The optimal hyperparameters $\Gamma^{*}$ can then be found by maximising (18.1.41) with respect to $\Gamma$.

### 18.1.6 Prediction and model averaging

For fixed hyperparameters, the Bayesian LPM defines a Gaussian posterior distribution on the weights w. The distribution can be used to compute the expected predictor and also the variance of the predictor. More generally, however, we can place a prior distribution on the hyperparameters themselves and obtain a corresponding posterior

$$
p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma) p(\Gamma)
$$

The mean function predictor is then given by integrating over both the posterior weights and the hyperparameters

$$
\bar{f}(\mathbf{x})=\int f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w}, \Gamma \mid \mathcal{D}) d \mathbf{w} d \Gamma=\int\left\{\int f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma, \mathcal{D}) d \mathbf{w}\right\} p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D}) d \Gamma
$$

The term in curly brackets is the mean predictor for fixed hyperparameters. Equation(18.1.45) then weights each mean predictor by the posterior probability of the hyperparameter $p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D})$. This is a general recipe for combining model predictions, where each model is weighted by its posterior probability. However, computing the integral over the hyperparameter posterior is numerically challenging and approximations are usually required. Provided the hyperparameters are well determined by the data, we may instead approximate the above hyperparameter integral by finding the MAP hyperparameters and use

$$
\bar{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \int f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}) p\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma^{*}, \mathcal{D}\right) d \mathbf{w}
$$

Under a flat prior $p(\Gamma)=$ const., this is equivalent to using the mean predictor with hyperparameters set by ML-II. An alternative is to draw samples $\Gamma^{l}, l=1, \ldots, L$ from the posterior distribution $p(\Gamma \mid \mathcal{D})$ and form then a predictor by averaging over the samples

$$
\bar{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \frac{1}{L} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \int f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w}) p\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \Gamma^{l}, \mathcal{D}\right) d \mathbf{w}
$$

# 18.1.7 Sparse linear models 

A common interest is to attempt to explain data using as few of the inputs as possible. More generally, we can try to find the most parsimonious explanation using a limited number of features $\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})$. From a Bayesian LPM perspective, we require a prior that strongly encourages only a limited number of weights $w_{i}$ to be active, with the rest being set to zero. Formally, this corresponds to a non-Gaussian prior on the weights which hampers the use of exact Bayesian methods. Non Bayesian methods make use of penalty terms such as $L_{1}$ (lasso) regularisation $\sum_{i}\left|w_{i}\right|$ for which the objective of the LPM remains concave [291]1; this is closely related to using Laplace priors in the Bayesian setting. Here we briefly discuss some approximate methods for sparse linear regression.

## The relevance vector machine

The relevance vector machine assumes that only a small number of components of the basis function vector are relevant in determining the solution for $\mathbf{w}$. For a predictor,

$$
f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_{i} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x}) \equiv \mathbf{w}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
$$

it is often the case that some basis functions will be redundant in the sense that a linear combination of the other basis functions can reproduce the training outputs with insignificant loss in accuracy. To exploit this effect and seek a parsimonious solution we may use a more refined prior that encourages each $w_{i}$ itself to be small:

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha})=\prod_{i} p\left(w_{i} \mid \alpha_{i}\right)
$$

For computational convenience, in the RVM one typically chooses a Gaussian

$$
p\left(w_{i} \mid \alpha_{i}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(w_{i} \mid 0, \alpha_{i}^{-1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha_{i}}{2 \pi}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \exp \left(-\frac{\alpha_{i}}{2} w_{i}^{2}\right)
$$

Sparsity is then achieved by optimising over the hyperparameters $\alpha_{i}$, with large $\alpha_{i}$ effectively forcing a weight $w_{i}$ to be zero. The modifications required to the description of section(18.1.1) are to replace $\mathbf{S}$ with

$$
\mathbf{S}=\left(\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})+\beta \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)\right)^{-1}
$$

The marginal likelihood is then given by

$$
2 \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \Gamma)=-\beta \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(y^{n}\right)^{2}+\mathbf{d}^{\top} \mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{d}-\log \operatorname{det}(\mathbf{S})+\sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \alpha_{i}+N \log \beta-N \log (2 \pi)
$$

The EM update for $\beta$ is unchanged, and the EM update for each $\alpha_{i}$ is

$$
\frac{1}{\alpha_{i}^{\text {new }}}=[\mathbf{S}]_{i i}+m_{i}^{2}
$$

A potential difficulty with this approach is that there are as many hyperparameters as there are parameters and finding the optimal hyperparameters by ML-II can be problematic, resulting in overly aggressive pruning of the weights. This can be ameliorated by using a more fully Bayesian approach 294].

## Spike and slab priors

A natural alternative approach to sparse linear regression is to use binary indicators $s_{i} \in\{0,1\}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{B} s_{i} w_{i} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x}), \quad p(\mathbf{w})=\prod_{i} \mathcal{N}\left(w_{i} \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)
$$

Algorithm 18.1 Evidence Procedure for Bayesian Logistic Regression
1: Initialise $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$.
2: while Not Converged do
3: Find optimal $\mathbf{w}^{*}$ by iterating equation (18.2.16), equation (18.2.15) to convergence. $\triangleright$ E-step
4: Update $\alpha$ according to equation (18.2.9).
5: end while
so that only those weights $w_{i}$ with $s_{i}=1$ will contribute to the function. One can specify a level of sparsity by choosing a prior on the joint set $p\left(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{B}\right)$ that encourages only a small number of the $s_{i}$ to be 1 , the rest being zero. This can be achieved using a product of Bernoulli distributions

$$
p(\mathbf{s})=\prod_{i=1}^{B} \theta^{s_{i}}(1-\theta)^{1-s_{i}}
$$

where $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$ specifies the prior level of sparsity. This is equivalent to using the original LPM

$$
f(\mathbf{x} ; \mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_{i} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})
$$

with the 'spike and slab' weight prior

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{s})=\prod_{i}\left\{s_{i} \mathcal{N}\left(w_{i} \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)+\left(1-s_{i}\right) \delta\left(w_{i}\right)\right\}
$$

which places either a spike at 0 (when $s_{i}=0$ ) or a broader Gaussian 'slab' $\mathcal{N}\left(w_{i} \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)$ when $s_{i}=1$. These two formulations are equivalent and result in a non-Gaussian posterior for the weights, for which approximation methods are required. Popular approaches include Gibbs sampling, chapter(27), and variational methods chapter(28).

# 18.2 Classification 

For the logistic regression model

$$
p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x})=\sigma\left(\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_{i} \phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})\right)
$$

the maximum likelihood method returns only a single optimal $\mathbf{w}$. To deal with the inevitable uncertainty in estimating $\mathbf{w}$ we need to determine the posterior distribution. To do so we first define a prior on the weights $p(\mathbf{w})$. As for the regression case, a convenient choice is a Gaussian

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \alpha^{-1} \mathbf{I}\right)=\frac{\alpha^{B / 2}}{(2 \pi)^{B / 2}} \exp \left(-\alpha \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w} / 2\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the inverse variance (precision). Given a dataset of input-class labels, $\mathcal{D}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, c^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N\right\}$, the parameter posterior is (assuming we make no model of the input distribution)

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})=\frac{p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \alpha) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)}{p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)}=\frac{1}{p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)} p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha) \prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(c^{n} \mid \mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{w}\right)
$$

Unfortunately, this distribution is not of any standard form and exactly inferring statistics such as the mean is formally computationally intractable.

# 18.2.1 Hyperparameter optimisation 

Analogous to the regression case, hyperparameters such as $\alpha$ can be set by maximising the marginal likelihood

$$
p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)=\int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha) d \mathbf{w}=\int \prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(c^{n} \mid \mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{w}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{2 \pi}\right)^{B / 2} \exp \left(-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right) d \mathbf{w}
$$

There are several approaches one could take to approximate this integral and below we discuss the Laplace and a variational technique. Common to all approaches, however, is the form of the gradient, differing only in the statistics under an approximation to the posterior. For this reason we derive first generic hyperparameter update formulae that apply under both approximations.

To find the optimal $\alpha$, we search for the zero derivative of $\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)$. This is equivalent to the linear regression case, and we immediately obtain

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle-\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}+\frac{B}{\alpha}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})}
$$

Setting the derivative to zero, an exact equation is that the optimal $\alpha$ satisfies

$$
0=-\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})}+\frac{B}{\alpha}
$$

One may now form a fixed point equation

$$
\alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B}{\left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})}}
$$

The averages in the above expression cannot be computed exactly and are replaced by averages with respect to an approximation of the posterior $q(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})$. For a Gaussian approximation of the posterior, $q(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D})=$ $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left\langle\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right\rangle=\operatorname{trace}\left(\left\langle\mathbf{w w}^{\top}\right\rangle-\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle^{\top}+\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle^{\top}\right)=\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m} \\
& \alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B}{\operatorname{trace}(\mathbf{S})+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}}
\end{aligned}
$$

In this case the Gull-Mackay alternative fixed point equation[135, 194] is

$$
\alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{B-\alpha \mathbf{S}}{\mathbf{m}^{\top} \mathbf{m}}
$$

The hyperparameter updates (18.2.9) and (18.2.10) have the same form as for the regression model. The mean $\mathbf{m}$ and covariance $\mathbf{S}$ of the posterior in the regression and classification cases are however different. In the classification case we need to approximate the mean and covariance, as discussed below.

### 18.2.2 Laplace approximation

The Laplace approximation, section(28.2) is a simple approximation made by fitting a Gaussian locally around the most probable point of the posterior. The weight posterior for the logistic regression model is given by

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha, \mathcal{D}) \propto \exp (-E(\mathbf{w}))
$$

where

$$
E(\mathbf{w})=\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}-\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log \sigma\left(\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{h}^{n}\right), \quad \mathbf{h}^{n} \equiv\left(2 c^{n}-1\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{n}
$$

By approximating $E(\mathbf{w})$ by a quadratic function in $\mathbf{w}$, we obtain a Gaussian approximation $q(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \alpha)$ to $p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \alpha)$. To do so we first find the minimum of $E(\mathbf{w})$. Differentiating, we obtain

$$
\nabla E=\alpha \mathbf{w}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(1-\sigma^{n}\right) \mathbf{h}^{n}, \quad \sigma^{n} \equiv \sigma\left(\mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{h}^{n}\right)
$$

It is convenient to use a Newton method to find the optimum. The Hessian matrix with elements

$$
H_{i j} \equiv \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial w_{i} \partial w_{j}} E(\mathbf{w})
$$

is given by

$$
\mathbf{H}=\alpha \mathbf{I}+\underbrace{\sum_{n=1}^{N} \sigma^{n}\left(1-\sigma^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{n}\left(\boldsymbol{\phi}^{n}\right)^{\top}}_{\mathbf{J}}
$$

Note that the Hessian is positive semidefinite (see exercise(18.4)) so that the function $E(\mathbf{w})$ is convex (bowl shaped), and finding a minimum of $E(\mathbf{w})$ is numerically unproblematic. A Newton update then is

$$
\mathbf{w}^{n e w}=\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla E
$$

Given a converged $\mathbf{w}$, the posterior approximation is given by

$$
q(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}, \alpha)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S}), \quad \mathbf{S} \equiv \mathbf{H}^{-1}
$$

where $\mathbf{m}=\mathbf{w}^{*}$ is the converged estimate of the minimum point of $E(\mathbf{w})$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is the Hessian of $E(\mathbf{w})$ at this point.

# Approximating the marginal likelihood 

Using the Laplace approximation, the marginal likelihood is given by

$$
p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha)=\int_{\mathbf{w}} p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \alpha)=\int_{\mathbf{w}} \prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(c^{n} \mid \mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{w}\right)\left(\frac{\alpha}{2 \pi}\right)^{B / 2} e^{-\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{w}} \propto \int_{\mathbf{w}} e^{-E(\mathbf{w})}
$$

For an optimum value $\mathbf{m}=\mathbf{w}^{*}$, we approximate the marginal likelihood using (see section(28.2))

$$
\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha) \approx L(\alpha) \equiv-\frac{\alpha}{2}\left(\mathbf{w}^{*}\right)^{\top} \mathbf{w}^{*}+\sum_{n} \log \sigma\left(\left(\mathbf{w}^{*}\right)^{\top} \mathbf{h}^{n}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}(\alpha \mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J})+\frac{B}{2} \log \alpha
$$

Given this approximation $L(\alpha)$ to the marginal likelihood, an alternative strategy for hyperparameter optimisation is to optimise $L(\alpha)$ with respect to $\alpha$. By differentiating $L(\alpha)$ directly, the reader may show that the resulting updates are in fact equivalent to using the general condition equation (18.2.6) under a Laplace approximation to the posterior statistics.

## Making predictions

Ultimately, our interest is to classify in novel situations, averaging over posterior weight uncertainty (assuming $\alpha$ is fixed to a suitable value),

$$
p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D})=\int p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}) d \mathbf{w}
$$

The $B$ dimensional integrals over $\mathbf{w}$ cannot be computed analytically and numerical approximation is required. Using the Laplace approximation, we replace the exact posterior $p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})$ with our Laplace's method Gaussian approximation $q(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})$

$$
p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D}) \approx \int p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) q(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D}) d \mathbf{w}=\int \sigma\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S}) d \mathbf{w}
$$

![img-210.jpeg](img-210.jpeg)

Figure 18.5: Bayesian logistic regression using RBF functions $\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\exp \left(-\lambda\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{m}_{i}\right)^{2}\right)$, placing the centres $\mathbf{m}_{i}$ on a subset of the training points. The green points are training data from class 1 , and the red points are training data from class 0 . The contours represent the probability of being in class 1 . The optimal value of $\alpha$ found by ML-II is 0.45 ( $\lambda$ is set by hand to 2). See demoBayesLogRegression.m
where, for notational convenience, we write $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} \equiv \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$. To compute the predictions it would appear that we need to carry out an integral in $B$ dimensions. However, since the term $\sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \mathbf{w}\right)$ depends on $\mathbf{w}$ via the scalar product $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \mathbf{w}$, we only require the integral over the one-dimensional projection $h \equiv \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \mathbf{w}$, see exercise(18.5). That is

$$
p(c=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D}) \approx \int \sigma(h) q(h \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D}) d h
$$

Since under the Laplace approximation $\mathbf{w}$ is Gaussian distributed, then so is the linear projection $h$

$$
q(h \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathcal{D})=\mathcal{N}\left(h \mid \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \mathbf{m}, \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}\right)
$$

Predictions may then be made by numerically evaluating the one-dimensional integral over the Gaussian distribution in $h$, equation (18.2.22). Fast approximate methods for computing this are discussed below.

# Approximating the Gaussian average of a logistic sigmoid 

Predictions under a Gaussian posterior approximation require the computation of

$$
I \equiv\langle\sigma(x)\rangle_{\mathcal{N}\left(x \mid \rho, \sigma^{2}\right)}
$$

Gaussian quadrature is an obvious numerical candidate[244]. An alternative is to replace the logistic sigmoid by a suitably transformed erf function[195], the reason being that the Gaussian average of an erf function is another erf function. Using a single erf, an approximation is ${ }^{1}$

$$
\sigma(x) \approx \frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{erf}(\nu x))
$$

These two functions agree at $-\infty, 0, \infty$. A reasonable criterion is that the derivatives of these two should agree at $x=0$ since then they have locally the same slope around the origin and have globally similar shape. Using $\sigma(0)=0.5$ and that the derivative is $\sigma(0)(1-\sigma(0))$, this requires

$$
\frac{1}{4}=\frac{\nu}{\sqrt{\pi}} \Rightarrow \nu=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4}
$$

A more accurate approximation can be obtained by taking a convex combination of scaled erf functions [22], see logsigapp.m

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ Note that the definition of the erf function used here is taken to be consistent with MATLAB, namely that $\operatorname{erf}(x) \equiv$ $\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{x} e^{-t^{2}} d t$. Other authors define it to be the cumulative density function of a standard Gaussian, $\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{x} e^{-\frac{1}{2} t^{2}} d t$.

# 18.2.3 Variational Gaussian approximation 

An alternative to Laplace's method is to use a so-called variational method. Since the marginal likelihood is a key quantity that can be used for example for hyperparameter selection, it is useful to have a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood. Like in EM, one can then find the best hyperparameters by maximising this lower bound, rather than the likelihood itself. To keep the notation reasonably simple, we drop the conditioning on hyperparameters throughout and attempt to find a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood $p(\mathcal{D})$. One approach to obtaining a bound is based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence

$$
\mathrm{KL}(q(\mathbf{w}) \mid p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})) \geq 0
$$

Since $p(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathcal{D})=p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w}) / p(\mathcal{D})$ we obtain

$$
\log p(\mathcal{D}) \geq\langle\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w})\rangle_{q(\mathbf{w})}-\langle\log q(\mathbf{w})\rangle_{q(\mathbf{w})}
$$

which holds for any distribution $q(\mathbf{w})$. The angled brackets $\langle\cdot\rangle_{q}$ denote expectation with respect to $q$. Using the explicit form for the logistic regression model, the right hand side is given by ${ }^{2}$

$$
\mathcal{B}_{K L} \equiv \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log \sigma\left(s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q(\mathbf{w})}-\operatorname{KL}(q(\mathbf{w}) \mid p(\mathbf{w}))
$$

To form a tractable lower bound, we need to choose a class of distributions $q(\mathbf{w})$ for which the above expression can be evaluated, for example a Gaussian $q(\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})$. For a Gaussian prior $p(\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ then $\operatorname{KL}(q(\mathbf{w}) \mid p(\mathbf{w}))$ is straightforward. For numerical convenience, we parameterise the covariance of the approximation using a Cholesky decomposition $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{C}^{\top} \mathbf{C}$ for upper triangular $\mathbf{C}$. This gives

$$
-2 \mathrm{KL}(q(\mathbf{w}) \mid p(\mathbf{w}))=4 \sum_{i} \log C_{i i}-\log \operatorname{det}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})+\operatorname{trace}\left(\mathbf{C}^{\top} \mathbf{C} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\right)+\mathbf{m}^{\top} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{m}+B
$$

where $B=\operatorname{dim}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}})$. In computing the bound (18.2.29), the problematic remaining terms are

$$
I_{n} \equiv\left\langle\log \sigma\left(s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{S})}
$$

We define the activation $a_{n} \equiv s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}$. Since $\mathbf{w}$ is Gaussian distributed, so is the activation,

$$
p\left(a_{n}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(a_{n} \mid \tilde{\mu}_{n}, \tilde{\sigma}_{n}^{2}\right), \quad \tilde{\mu}_{n}=s_{n} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{\top} \mathbf{m}, \quad \tilde{\sigma}_{n}^{2}=\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{\top} \mathbf{C}^{\top} \mathbf{C} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}
$$

so that

$$
I_{n}=\left\langle\log \sigma\left(a_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{N}\left(a_{n} \mid \tilde{\mu}_{n}, \tilde{\sigma}_{n}^{2}\right)}=\left\langle\log \sigma\left(\tilde{\mu}_{n}+z \tilde{\sigma}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{z}
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{z}$ denotes expectation with respect to the standard normal distribution $z \sim \mathcal{N}(z \mid 0,1)$. In this way $I_{n}$ can be computed by any standard one-dimensional numerical integration method, such as Gaussian quadrature. Since the bound (18.2.29) is therefore numerically accessible for any parameters $\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{C}$ of the approximating Gaussian, we may proceed to find the optimal parameters by direct numerical maximisation of the lower bound. The gradient of the bound with respect to $\mathbf{m}$ is

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{B}_{K L}}{\partial \mathbf{m}}=-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{m}+\sum_{n=1}^{N} s_{n} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\left(1-\left\langle\sigma\left(\tilde{\mu}_{n}+z \tilde{\sigma}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{z}\right)
$$

Similarly, one may show that

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{B}_{K L}}{\partial \mathbf{C}}=\mathbf{C}^{-\top}-\mathbf{C} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}+\mathbf{C} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{\top}}{\tilde{\sigma}_{n}}\left\langle z \sigma\left(\tilde{\mu}_{n}+z \tilde{\sigma}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{z}
$$

with the understanding that only the upper triangular part of the matrix expression is to be taken. One may show that the bound equation (18.2.29) is concave in the mean and covariance[60]. These gradients may then be used as part of a general purpose optimisation routine to find the best $\mathbf{m}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ approximation parameters.

# 18.2.4 Local variational approximation 

An alternative to the KL bounding method above is to use a so-called local method that bounds each term in the integrand. To lower bound

$$
p(\mathcal{D})=\int \prod_{n} \sigma\left(s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right) p(\mathbf{w}) d \mathbf{w}
$$

we may bound the logistic sigmoid function[155], see fig(18.6),

$$
\sigma(x) \geq \sigma(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{2}(x-\xi)-\lambda(\xi)\left(x^{2}-\xi^{2}\right)\right), \quad \lambda(\xi) \equiv \frac{1}{2 \xi}\left(\sigma(\xi)-\frac{1}{2}\right)
$$

Hence

$$
\log \sigma\left(s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right) \geq \log \sigma\left(\xi_{n}\right)+\frac{1}{2} s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\frac{1}{2} \xi_{n}-\lambda\left(\xi_{n}\right)\left[\left(\mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right)^{2}-\xi_{n}^{2}\right]
$$

Using this we can write

$$
p(\mathcal{D}) \geq \int d \mathbf{w} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \prod_{n} e^{\log \sigma\left(\xi_{n}\right)+\frac{1}{2} s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}-\frac{1}{2} \xi_{n}-\lambda\left(\xi_{n}\right)\left[\left(\mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right)^{2}-\xi_{n}^{2}\right]}
$$

For fixed $\xi_{n}, n=1, \ldots, N$, the right hand side can be analytically integrated over $\mathbf{w}$, resulting in the bound

$$
\log p(\mathcal{D}) \geq \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{\operatorname{det}(\tilde{\mathbf{S}})}{\operatorname{det}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}+\frac{1}{2} \tilde{\mathbf{m}}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{m}}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[\log \sigma\left(\xi_{n}\right)-\frac{\xi_{n}}{2}+\lambda\left(\xi_{n}\right) \xi_{n}^{2}\right]
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}+2 \sum_{n=1}^{N} \lambda\left(\xi_{n}\right) \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{\top}, \quad \mathbf{b}=\sum_{n=1}^{N} \frac{1}{2} s_{n} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}, \quad \tilde{\mathbf{S}} \equiv \mathbf{A}^{-1}, \quad \tilde{\mathbf{m}} \equiv \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{b}
$$

The bound equation (18.2.39) may then be maximised with respect to the variational parameters $\xi_{n}$. At convergence, we may take the Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{m}}, \tilde{\mathbf{S}})$ as an approximation to the posterior.

## Relation to KL variational procedure

As an alternative to the numerical integration in the KL procedure described in section(18.2.3), we may instead bound the problematic term $\left\langle\log \sigma\left(s_{n} \mathbf{w}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\right)\right\rangle_{q(\mathbf{w})}$ in equation (18.2.29) using (18.2.37). As we discuss in section(28.5), this enables us to relate the KL and the local bounding procedures [60], showing that for unconstrained Cholesky parameterisation $\mathbf{C}$ the KL approach results in a provably tighter lower bound than the local approach.

As an illustration of these approximations, for two-dimensional data, $D=2$, we plot contours of the posterior and approximations in fig(18.7) which again demonstrates the over-compact nature of the local approximation. The Laplace approximation, which does not yield a bound, is plotted for comparison.

# 18.2.5 Relevance vector machine for classification 

It is straightforward to apply the sparse linear model methods of section(18.1.7) to classification. For example, in adopting the RVM prior to classification, as before we encourage individual weights to be small using

$$
p(\mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha})=\prod_{i} p\left(w_{i} \mid \alpha_{i}\right), \quad p\left(w_{i} \mid \alpha_{i}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(w_{i} \mid 0, \frac{1}{\alpha_{i}}\right)
$$

The only alterations to the previous ML-II approach is to replace equation (18.2.13) and equation (18.2.15) with

$$
[\nabla E]_{i}=\alpha_{i} w_{i}-\sum_{n}\left(1-\sigma^{n}\right) h_{i}^{n}, \quad \mathbf{H}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})+\mathbf{J}
$$

These are used in the Newton update formula as before. The update equation for the $\alpha$ 's is given by

$$
\alpha_{i}^{n e w}=\frac{1}{m_{i}^{2}+S_{i i}}
$$

Similarly, the Gull-MacKay update is given by

$$
\alpha_{i}^{n e w}=\frac{1-\alpha_{i} S_{i i}}{m_{i}^{2}}
$$

Running this procedure, one typically finds that many of the $\alpha$ 's tend to infinity and the corresponding weights are pruned from the system. The remaining weights typically correspond to basis functions (in the RBF case) in the centres of mass of clusters of datapoints of the same class, see fig(18.8). Contrast this with the situation in SVMs, where the retained datapoints tend to be on the decision boundaries. The number of training points retained by the RVM tends to be very small - smaller indeed than the number retained in the SVM framework. Whilst the RVM does not support large margins, and hence may be a less robust classifier, it does retain the advantages of a probabilistic framework[295]. A potential critique of the RVM, coupled with an ML-II procedure for learning the $\alpha_{i}$ is that it is overly aggressive in terms of pruning. Indeed, as one may verify running demoBayesLogRegRVM.m it is common to find an instance of a problem for which there exists a set of $\alpha_{i}$ such that the training data can be classified perfectly; however, after using ML-II, so many of the $\alpha_{i}$ are set to zero that the training data can no longer be classified perfectly. An alternative is to apply the spike-and-slab prior technique which suffers less from overly aggressive pruning, although requires more sophisticated approximation methods.

### 18.2.6 Multi-class case

We briefly note that the multi-class case can be treated by using the softmax function under a one-of- $m$ class coding scheme. The class probabilities are

$$
p(c=m \mid y)=\frac{e^{y_{m}}}{\sum_{m^{\prime}} e^{y_{m^{\prime}}}}
$$

![img-213.jpeg](img-213.jpeg)

Figure 18.8: Classification using the RVM with RBF $e^{-\lambda(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{m})^{2}}$, placing a basis function on a subset of the training data points. The green points are training data from class 1 , and the red points are training data from class 0 . The contours represent the probability of being in class 1. (a): Training points. (b): The training points weighted by their relevance value $1 / \alpha_{n}$. Nearly all the points have a value so small that they effectively vanish. See demoBayesLogRegRVM.m
which automatically enforces the constraint $\sum_{m} p(c=m)=1$. Naively it would appear that for $C$ classes, the cost of the Laplace approximation scales as $O\left(C^{3} N^{3}\right)$. However, one may show by careful implementation that the cost may be reduced to only $O\left(C N^{3}\right)$, analogous to the cost savings possible in the Gaussian Process classification model $[318,247]$.

# 18.3 Summary 

- A simple extension of linear regression is achieved by using a Gaussian prior on the parameters. Coupled with the assumption of additive Gaussian noise on the output, the posterior distribution is Gaussian, for which predictions can be computed readily.
- In the case of classification, no closed form Bayesian solution is obtained by using simple Gaussian priors on the parameters, and approximations are required. The parameter posterior is nevertheless well-behaved so that simple unimodal approximations may be adequate.
