# 18.5 Exercises 

Exercise 18.1. This exercise concerns Bayesian regression.

1. Show that for $f=\mathbf{w}^{T} \mathbf{x}$ and $p(\mathbf{w}) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, that $p(f \mid \mathbf{x})$ is Gaussian distributed. Furthermore, find the mean and covariance of this Gaussian.
2. Consider a target point $t=f+\epsilon$, where $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\epsilon \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)$. What is $p(f \mid t, \mathbf{x})$ ?

Exercise 18.2. A Bayesian Linear Parameter regression model is given by

$$
y^{n}=\mathbf{w}^{T} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)+\eta^{n}
$$

In vector notation $\mathbf{y}=\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}\right)^{\mathcal{T}}$ this can be written

$$
\mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\Phi} \mathbf{w}+\boldsymbol{\eta}
$$

with $\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathcal{T}}=\left[\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{1}\right), \ldots, \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^{N}\right)\right]$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ is a zero mean Gaussian distributed vector with covariance $\beta^{-1} \mathbf{I}$. An expression for the marginal likelihood of a dataset is given in equation (18.1.19). We aim to find a more compact expression for the likelihood given the hyperparameters $\Gamma$

$$
p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N} \mid \mathbf{x}^{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{N}, \Gamma\right)
$$

Since $y^{n}$ is linearly related to $\mathbf{w}$ and $p(\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \alpha^{-1} \mathbf{I}\right)$, then $\mathbf{y}$ is Gaussian distributed with mean

$$
\langle\mathbf{y}\rangle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle=\mathbf{0}
$$

and covariance matrix

$$
\mathbf{C}=\left\langle\mathbf{y} \mathbf{y}^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rangle-\langle\mathbf{y}\rangle\langle\mathbf{y}\rangle^{\mathcal{T}}=\left\langle(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \mathbf{w}+\boldsymbol{\eta})(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \mathbf{w}+\boldsymbol{\eta})^{\mathcal{T}}\right\rangle
$$

1. Show that the covariance matrix can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf{C}=\frac{1}{\beta} \mathbf{I}+\frac{1}{\alpha} \boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathcal{T}}
$$

2. Hence show that the log marginal likelihood can we written as

$$
\log p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N} \mid \mathbf{x}^{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{N}, \Gamma\right)=-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}(2 \pi \mathbf{C})-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{y}
$$

Exercise 18.3. Using exercise(18.2) as a basis, derive expression (18.1.41) for the log likelihood on a validation set.

Exercise 18.4. Consider the function $E(\mathbf{w})$ as defined in equation (18.2.12).

1. Show that the Hessian matrix which has elements,

$$
H_{i j} \equiv \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial w_{i} \partial w_{j}} E(\mathbf{w})=\left[\alpha \mathbf{I}+\sum_{n=1}^{N} \sigma^{n}\left(1-\sigma^{n}\right) \boldsymbol{\phi}^{n}\left(\boldsymbol{\phi}^{n}\right)^{\mathcal{T}}\right]_{i j}
$$

2. Show that the Hessian is positive definite.

Exercise 18.5. Show that for any function $f(\cdot)$,

$$
\int f\left(\mathbf{x}^{T} \mathbf{w}\right) p(\mathbf{w}) d \mathbf{w}=\int f(h) p(h) d h
$$

where $p(h)$ is the distribution of the scalar $\mathbf{x}^{T} \mathbf{w}$. The significance is that any high-dimensional integral of the above form can be reduced to a one-dimensional integral over the distribution of the 'field' $h[22]$.

Exercise 18.6. This exercise concerns Bayesian Logistic Regression. Our interest is to derive the optimal regularisation parameter $\alpha$ based on the Laplace approximation in section(18.2.2) to the marginal log-likelihood given by

$$
\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \alpha) \approx L(\alpha) \equiv-\frac{\alpha}{2}(\mathbf{w})^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{w}+\sum_{n} \log \sigma\left((\mathbf{w})^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{h}^{n}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}(\alpha \mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J})+\frac{B}{2} \log \alpha
$$

The Laplace procedure finds first an optimal $\mathbf{w}^{*}$ that minimises $\alpha \mathbf{w}^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{w} / 2-\sum_{n} \log \sigma\left(\mathbf{w}^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{h}^{n}\right)$, as in equation (18.2.12) which will depend on the setting of $\alpha$. Formally, therefore, in finding the $\alpha$ that optimises $L(\alpha)$ we should make use of the total derivative formula

$$
\frac{d L}{d \alpha}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha}+\sum_{i} \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{i}} \frac{\partial w_{i}}{\partial \alpha}
$$

However, when evaluated at $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}^{*}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{0}$. This means that in order to compute the derivative with respect to $\alpha$, we only need consider the terms with an explicit $\alpha$ dependence. Equating the derivative to zero and using

$$
\partial \log \operatorname{det}(\mathbf{M})=\operatorname{trace}\left(\mathbf{M}^{-1} \partial \mathbf{M}\right)
$$

show that the optimal $\alpha$ satisfies the fixed point equation

$$
\alpha^{\text {new }}=\frac{N}{\left(\mathbf{w}^{*}\right)^{\mathcal{T}} \mathbf{w}^{*}+\operatorname{trace}\left((\alpha \mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J})^{-1}\right)}
$$

In Bayesian linear parameter models, we saw that the only relevant quantities are related to the scalar product of data vectors. In Gaussian Processes we use this to motivate a prediction method that does not necessarily correspond to any 'parametric' model of the data. Such models are flexible Bayesian predictors.

# 19.1 Non-Parametric Prediction 

Gaussian Processes are flexible Bayesian models that fit well within the probabilistic modelling framework. In developing GPs it is useful to first step back and see what information we need to form a predictor. Given a set of training data

$$
\mathcal{D}=\left\{\left(x^{n}, y^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N\right\}=\mathcal{X} \cup \mathcal{Y}
$$

where $x^{n}$ is the input for datapoint $n$ and $y^{n}$ the corresponding output (a continuous variable in the regression case and a discrete variable in the classification case), our aim is to make a prediction $y^{*}$ for a new input $x^{*}$. In the discriminative framework no model of the inputs $x$ is assumed and only the outputs are modelled, conditioned on the inputs. Given a joint model

$$
p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}, y^{*} \mid x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}, x^{*}\right)=p\left(\mathcal{Y}, y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right)
$$

we may subsequently use conditioning to form a predictor $p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{D}\right)$. In previous chapters we've made much use of the i.i.d. assumption that each datapoint is independently sampled from the same generating distribution. In this context, this might appear to suggest the assumption

$$
p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}, y^{*} \mid x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}, x^{*}\right)=p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right) \prod_{n} p\left(y^{n} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right)
$$

However, this is clearly of little use since the predictive conditional is simply $p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{D}, x^{*}\right)=p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right)$ meaning the predictions make no use of the training outputs. For a non-trivial predictor we therefore need to specify a joint non-factorised distribution over outputs.

### 19.1.1 From parametric to non-parametric

If we revisit our i.i.d. assumptions for parametric models, we used a parameter $\theta$ to make a model of the input-output distribution $p(y \mid x, \theta)$. For a parametric model predictions are formed using

$$
p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{D}\right) \propto p\left(y^{*}, x^{*}, \mathcal{D}\right)=\int_{\theta} p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y}, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \theta\right) \propto \int_{\theta} p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid \theta, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right) p\left(\theta \mid \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{X}\right)
$$

![img-214.jpeg](img-214.jpeg)
(a)
![img-215.jpeg](img-215.jpeg)
(b)

Figure 19.1: (a): A parametric model for prediction assuming i.i.d. data. (b): The form of the model after integrating out the parameters $\theta$. Our non-parametric model will have this structure.

Under the assumption that, given $\theta$, the data is i.i.d., we obtain

$$
p\left(y^{* \mid x^{*}}, \mathcal{D}\right) \propto \int_{\theta} p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \theta\right) p(\theta) \prod_{n} p\left(y^{n} \mid \theta, x^{n}\right) \propto \int_{\theta} p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \theta\right) p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})
$$

where

$$
p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\theta) \prod_{n} p\left(y^{n} \mid \theta, x^{n}\right)
$$

After integrating over the parameters $\theta$, the joint data distribution is given by

$$
p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right)=\int_{\theta} p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \theta\right) p(\theta) \prod_{n} p\left(y^{n} \mid \theta, x^{n}\right)
$$

which does not in general factorise into individual datapoint terms, see fig(19.1). The idea of a nonparametric approach is to specify the form of the dependencies $p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right)$ without reference to an explicit parametric model. One route towards a non-parametric model is to start with a parametric model and integrate out the parameters. In order to make this tractable, we use a simple linear parameter predictor with a Gaussian parameter prior. For regression this leads to closed form expressions, although the classification case will require numerical approximation.

# 19.1.2 From Bayesian linear models to Gaussian processes 

To develop the GP, we briefly revisit the Bayesian linear parameter model of section(18.1.1). For parameters $\mathbf{w}$ and basis functions $\phi_{i}(x)$ the output is given by (assuming zero output noise)

$$
y=\sum_{i} w_{i} \phi_{i}(x)
$$

If we stack all the $y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}$ into a vector $\mathbf{y}$, then we can write the predictors as

$$
\mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\Phi} \mathbf{w}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}=\left[\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{1}\right), \ldots, \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{N}\right)\right]^{\top}$ is the design matrix. Assuming a Gaussian weight prior

$$
p(\mathbf{w})=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{w} \mid \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}}\right)
$$

the joint output

$$
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})=\int_{\mathbf{w}} \delta(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol{\Phi} \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w})
$$

is Gaussian distributed with mean

$$
\langle\mathbf{y}\rangle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\langle\mathbf{w}\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w})}=\mathbf{0}
$$

and covariance

$$
\left\langle\mathbf{y} \mathbf{y}^{\top}\right\rangle=\boldsymbol{\Phi}\left\langle\mathbf{w} \mathbf{w}^{\top}\right\rangle_{p(\mathbf{w})} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\top}=\left(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\top}
$$

From this we see that the $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}}$ can be absorbed into $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ using its Cholesky decomposition. In other words, without loss of generality we may assume $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{I}$. Hence, after integrating out the weights, the Bayesian linear regression model induces a Gaussian distribution on any set of outputs $\mathbf{y}$ as

$$
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K})
$$

where the covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$ depends on the training inputs alone via

$$
[\mathbf{K}]_{n, n^{\prime}}=\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{n}\right)^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{n^{\prime}}\right), \quad n, n^{\prime}=1, \ldots, N
$$

Since the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is formed as the scalar product of vectors, it is by construction positive semidefinite, see section(19.4.2). After integrating out the weights, the only thing the model directly depends on is the covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$. In a Gaussian process we directly specify the joint output covariance $\mathbf{K}$ as a function of two inputs, rather than specifying a linear model with parameters $\mathbf{w}$. Specifically we need to define the $n, n^{\prime}$ element of the covariance matrix for any two inputs $x^{n}$ and $x^{n^{\prime}}$. This is achieved using a covariance function $k\left(x^{n}, x^{n^{\prime}}\right)$

$$
[\mathbf{K}]_{n, n^{\prime}}=k\left(x^{n}, x^{n^{\prime}}\right)
$$

The matrix $\mathbf{K}$ formed from a covariance function $k$ is called the Gram matrix. The required form of the function $k\left(x^{n}, x^{n^{\prime}}\right)$ is very special - when applied to create the elements of the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ it must produce a positive definite matrix. We discuss how to create such covariance functions in section(19.3). One explicit straightforward construction is to form the covariance function from the scalar product of the basis vector $\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{n}\right)$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{n^{\prime}}\right)$. For finite-dimensional $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ this is known as a finite dimensional Gaussian Process. Given any covariance function we can always find a corresponding basis vector representation - that is, for any GP, we can always relate this back to a parametric Bayesian LPM. However, for many commonly used covariance functions, the basis functions corresponds to infinite dimensional vectors. It is in such cases that the advantages of using the GP framework are particularly evident since we would not be able to compute efficiently with the corresponding infinite dimensional parametric model.

# 19.1.3 A prior on functions 

The nature of many machine learning applications is such that the knowledge about the true underlying mechanism behind the data generation process is limited. Instead one relies on generic 'smoothness' assumptions; for example we might wish that for two inputs $x$ and $x^{\prime}$ that are close, the corresponding outputs $y$ and $y^{\prime}$ should be similar. Many generic techniques in machine learning can be viewed as different characterisations of smoothness. An advantage of the GP framework in this respect is that the mathematical smoothness properties of the functions are well understood, giving confidence in the procedure.

For a given covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$, equation (19.1.14) specifies a distribution on functions ${ }^{1}$ in the following sense: we specify a set of input points $\mathbf{x}=\left(x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}\right)$ and a $N \times N$ covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$. Then we draw a vector $\mathbf{y}=\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}\right)$ from the Gaussian defined by equation (19.1.14). We can then plot the sampled 'function' at the finite set of points $\left(x^{n}, y^{n}\right), n=1, \ldots, N$. What kind of function does a GP correspond to? In fig(19.2a) we show three sample functions drawn from a Squared Exponential covariance function defined over 500 points uniformly spaced from -2 to 3 . Each sampled function looks reasonably smooth. Conversely, for the Ornstein Uhlenbeck covariance function, the sampled functions fig(19.2c) look locally rough. These smoothness properties are related to the form of the covariance function, as discussed in section(19.4.1).

Consider two scalar inputs, $x^{i}$ and $x^{j}$ and corresponding sampled outputs $y^{i}$ and $y^{j}$. For a covariance function with large $k\left(x^{i}, x^{j}\right)$, we expect $y^{i}$ and $y^{j}$ to be very similar since they are highly correlated. Conversely, for a covariance function that has low $k\left(x^{i}, x^{j}\right)$, we expect $y^{i}$ and $y^{j}$ to be effectively independent. In general, we would expect the correlation between $y_{i}$ and $y_{j}$ to decrease the further apart $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ are ${ }^{2}$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ The term 'function' is potentially confusing since we do not have an explicit functional form for the input output-mapping. For any finite set of inputs $x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}$ the values for the 'function' are given by the outputs at those points $y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}$.
    ${ }^{2}$ For periodic functions one can have high correlation even if the inputs are far apart.

The zero mean assumption implies that if we were to draw a large number of such 'functions', the mean across these functions at a given point $x$ tends to zero. Similarly, for any two points $x$ and $x^{\prime}$ if we compute the sample covariance between the corresponding $y$ and $y^{\prime}$ for all such sampled functions, this will tend to the covariance function value $k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)$. The zero-mean assumption can be easily relaxed by defining a mean function $m(x)$ to give $p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{K})$. In many practical situations one typically deals with 'detrended' data in which such mean trends have been already removed. For this reason much of the development of GPs in the machine learning literature is for the zero mean case.

# 19.2 Gaussian Process Prediction 

For a dataset $\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ and novel input $x^{*}$, a zero mean GP makes a Gaussian model of the joint outputs $y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}, y^{*}$ given the joint inputs $x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}, x^{*}$. For convenience we write this as

$$
p\left(\mathbf{y}, y^{*} \mid \mathbf{x}, x^{*}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{y}, y^{*} \mid \mathbf{0}_{N+1}, \mathbf{K}^{+}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{0}_{N+1}$ is an $N+1$ dimensional zero-vector. The covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}^{+}$is a block matrix with elements
![img-216.jpeg](img-216.jpeg)
where $\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}$ is the covariance matrix of the training inputs $\mathbf{x}=\left(x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}\right)$ - that is

$$
\left[\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}\right]_{n, n^{\prime}} \equiv k\left(x^{n}, x^{n^{\prime}}\right), \quad n, n^{\prime}=1, \ldots, N
$$

The $N \times 1$ vector $\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}$ has elements

$$
\left[\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}\right]_{n, *} \equiv k\left(x^{n}, x^{*}\right) \quad n=1, \ldots, N
$$

$\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}}$ is the transpose of the above vector. The scalar covariance is given by

$$
\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}} \equiv k\left(x^{*}, x^{*}\right)
$$

The predictive distribution $p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\right)$ is obtained by Gaussian conditioning using result(8.4), giving a Gaussian distribution

$$
p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{D}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(y^{*} \mid \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}-\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}\right)
$$

GP regression is an exact method and there are no issues with local minima. Furthermore, GPs are attractive since they automatically model uncertainty in the predictions. However, the computational complexity for making a prediction is $O\left(N^{3}\right)$ due to the requirement of performing the matrix inversion (or solving the corresponding linear system by Gaussian elimination). This can be prohibitively expensive for large datasets and a large body of research on efficient approximations exists. A discussion of these techniques is beyond the scope of this book, and the reader is referred to [247].

### 19.2.1 Regression with noisy training outputs

To prevent overfitting to noisy data it is useful to assume that a training output $y^{n}$ is the result of some clean Gaussian process $f^{n}$ corrupted by independent additive Gaussian noise,

$$
y^{n}=f^{n}+\epsilon^{n}, \quad \text { where } \quad \epsilon^{n} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\epsilon^{n} \mid 0, \sigma^{2}\right)
$$

In this case our interest is to predict the clean signal $f^{*}$ for a novel input $x^{*}$. Then the distribution $p\left(\mathbf{y}, f^{*} \mid \mathbf{x}, x^{*}\right)$ is a zero mean Gaussian with block covariance matrix

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}+\sigma^{2} \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}} \\
\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} & \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}
\end{array}\right)
$$

so that $\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}$ is replaced by $\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}+\sigma^{2} \mathbf{I}$ in forming the prediction, equation (19.2.5). This follows since

$$
\left\langle y^{n}\right\rangle=\left\langle f^{n}\right\rangle+\left\langle\epsilon^{n}\right\rangle=0+0
$$

and, using the assumed independence of the noise with the clean signal, $f^{m} \Perp \epsilon^{n}$ and the independence of two noise components, $\epsilon^{m} \Perp \epsilon^{n}, m \neq n$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle y^{m} y^{n}\right\rangle & =\left\langle\left(f^{m}+\epsilon^{m}\right)\left(f^{n}+\epsilon^{n}\right)\right\rangle \\
& =\underbrace{\left\langle f^{m} f^{n}\right\rangle}_{k\left(x^{m}, x^{n}\right)}+\underbrace{\left\langle f^{m} \epsilon^{n}\right\rangle}_{\left\langle f^{m}\right\rangle\left\langle\epsilon^{n}\right\rangle}+\left\langle f^{n} \epsilon^{m}\right\rangle_{\left\langle f^{n}\right\rangle\left\langle\epsilon^{m}\right\rangle}+\left\langle\epsilon^{m} \epsilon^{n}\right\rangle_{\sigma^{2} \delta_{m, n}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using $\left\langle\epsilon^{m}\right\rangle=0$ we obtain the form in equation (19.2.7).

Example 19.1. Training data from a one-dimensional input $x$ and one dimensional output $y$ are plotted in fig(19.2b,d), along with the mean regression function fit, based on two different covariance functions. Note how the smoothness of the prior translates into smoothness of the prediction. The smoothness of the function space prior is a consequence of the choice of covariance function. Naively, we can partially understand this by the behaviour of the covariance function at the origin, section(19.4.1). An intuitive way to think about GP regression is to sample an 'infinite' number of functions from the prior; these are then 'filtered' by how well they fit the data by the likelihood term, leaving a posterior distribution on the functions. See demoGPreg.m

# The marginal likelihood and hyperparameter learning 

For a set of $N$ one-dimensional training inputs represented by the $N \times 1$ dimensional vector $\mathbf{y}$ and a covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$ defined on the inputs $\mathbf{x}=\left(x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}\right)$, the log marginal likelihood is

$$
\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})=-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}(2 \pi \mathbf{K})
$$

One can learn any free (hyper)parameters of the covariance function by maximising the marginal likelihood. For example, a squared exponential covariance function may have parameters $\lambda, v_{0}$ :

$$
k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)=v_{0} \exp \left\{-\frac{1}{2} \lambda\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)^{2}\right\}
$$

The $\lambda$ parameter in equation (19.2.11) specifies the appropriate length-scale of the inputs, and $v_{0}$ the variance of the function. The dependence of the marginal likelihood (19.2.10) on the parameters is typically complex and no closed form expression for the maximum likelihood optimum exists; in this case one resorts to numerical optimisation techniques such as conjugate gradients.

## Vector inputs

For regression with vector inputs and scalar outputs we need to define a covariance as a function of the two vectors, $k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)$. Using the multiplicative property of covariance functions, definition(19.3), a simple way to do this is to define

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=\prod_{i} k\left(x_{i}, x_{i}^{\prime}\right)
$$

![img-217.jpeg](img-217.jpeg)

Figure 19.2: The input space from -2 to 3 is split evenly into 1000 points $x^{1}, \ldots, x^{1000}$.
(a): Three samples from a GP prior with Squared Exponential (SE) covariance function, $\lambda=2$. The $1000 \times 1000$ covariance matrix $\mathbf{K}$ is defined using the SE kernel, from which the samples are drawn using mvrandn(zeros(1000,1),K,3).
(b): Prediction based on training points. Plotted is the posterior predicted function based on the SE covariance. The central line is the mean prediction, with standard errors bars on either side. The log marginal likelihood is $\approx 70$.
(c): Three samples from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck GP prior with $\lambda=2$.
(d): Posterior prediction for the OU covariance. The log marginal likelihood is $\approx 3$, meaning that the SE covariance is much more heavily supported by the data than the rougher OU covariance.

For example, for the squared exponential covariance function this gives

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=e^{-\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)^{2}}
$$

though 'correlated' forms are possible as well, see exercise(19.6). We can generalise the above using parameters:

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=v_{0} \exp \left\{-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{l=1}^{D} \lambda_{l}\left(x_{l}-x_{l}^{\prime}\right)^{2}\right\}
$$

where $x_{l}$ is the $l$ th component of $\mathbf{x}$ and $\theta=\left(v_{0}, \lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{D}\right)$ are the parameters. The $\lambda_{l}$ in equation (19.2.14) allow a different length scale on each input dimension and can be learned by numerically maximising the marginal likelihood. For irrelevant inputs, the corresponding $\lambda_{l}$ will become small, and the model will ignore the $l^{\text {th }}$ input dimension.

# 19.3 Covariance Functions 

Covariance functions $k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)$ are special in that they define elements of a positive definite matrix. These functions are also referred to as 'kernels', particulary in the machine learning literature.

Definition 19.1 (Covariance function). Given any collection of points $x^{1}, \ldots, x^{M}$, a covariance function $k\left(x^{i}, x^{j}\right)$ defines the elements of an $M \times M$ matrix

$$
[\mathbf{C}]_{i, j}=k\left(x^{i}, x^{j}\right)
$$

such that $\mathbf{C}$ is positive semidefinite.

# 19.3.1 Making new covariance functions from old 

The following rules (see exercise(19.1)) generate new covariance functions from existing covariance functions $k_{1}, k_{2}[196],[247]$.

Definition 19.2 (Sum).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)+k_{2}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)
$$

Definition 19.3 (Product).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right) k_{2}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)
$$

Definition 19.4 (Product Spaces). For $\mathbf{z}=\binom{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{y}}$,

$$
k\left(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}^{\prime}\right)=k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)+k_{2}\left(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{y}^{\prime}\right)
$$

and

$$
k\left(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}^{\prime}\right)=k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right) k_{2}\left(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{y}^{\prime}\right)
$$

Definition 19.5 (Vertical Rescaling).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=a(\mathbf{x}) k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right) a\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)
$$

for any function $a(\mathbf{x})$.

Definition 19.6 (Warping and Embedding).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=k_{1}\left(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{u}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)\right)
$$

for any mapping $\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})$, where the mapping $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})$ has arbitrary dimension.

A small collection of covariance functions commonly used in machine learning is given below. We refer the reader to [247] and [117] for further popular covariance functions.

### 19.3.2 Stationary covariance functions

Definition 19.7 (Stationary Kernel). A kernel $k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)$ is stationary if the kernel depends only on the separation $\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$. That is

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=k\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)
$$

For a stationary covariance function we may write $k(\mathbf{d})$, where $\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$. This means that for functions drawn from the GP, on average, the functions depend only on the distance between inputs and not on the absolute position of an input. In other words, the functions are on average translation invariant. For isotropic covariance functions, the covariance is defined as a function of the distance $|\mathbf{d}|$. Such covariance functions are, by construction, rotationally invariant.

Definition 19.8 (Squared Exponential).

$$
k(\mathbf{d})=\exp \left(-|\mathbf{d}|^{2}\right)
$$

The Squared Exponential is one of the most common covariance functions. There are many ways to show that this is a covariance function. An elementary technique is to consider

$$
\exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}-\mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}-\mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)\right)=\exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}\left|\mathbf{x}^{n}\right|^{2}\right) \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}\left|\mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right|^{2}\right) \exp \left(\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)
$$

The first two factors on the right above form a kernel of the form $\phi\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right) \phi\left(\mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)$. In the final term $k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)=$ $\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}\right)^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}$ is the linear kernel. Taking the exponential and writing the power series expansion of the exponential, we have

$$
\exp \left(k_{1}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{i!} k_{1}^{i}\left(\mathbf{x}^{n}, \mathbf{x}^{n^{\prime}}\right)
$$

this can be expressed as a series of integer powers of $k_{1}$, with positive coefficients. By the product (with itself) and sum rules above, this is therefore a kernel as well. We then use the fact that equation (19.3.9) is the product of two kernels, and hence also a kernel.

Definition 19.9 ( $\gamma$-Exponential).

$$
k(\mathbf{d})=\exp \left(-|\mathbf{d}|^{\gamma}\right), \quad 0<\gamma \leq 2
$$

When $\gamma=2$ we have the squared exponential covariance function. When $\gamma=1$ this is the OrnsteinUhlenbeck covariance function.

Definition 19.10 (Matérn).

$$
k(\mathbf{d})=|\mathbf{d}|^{\nu} K_{\nu}(|\mathbf{d}|)
$$

where $K_{\nu}$ is a modified Bessel function, $\nu>0$.

Definition 19.11 (Rational Quadratic).

$$
k(\mathbf{d})=\left(1+|\mathbf{d}|^{2}\right)^{-\alpha}, \quad \alpha>0
$$

Definition 19.12 (Periodic). For 1-dimensional $x$ and $x^{\prime}$, a stationary (and isotropic) covariance function can be obtained by first mapping $x$ to the two dimensional vector $\mathbf{u}(x)=(\cos (x), \sin (x))$ and then using the SE covariance $\exp \left(-\left(\mathbf{u}(x)-\mathbf{u}\left(x^{\prime}\right)\right)^{2}\right)[196]$

$$
k\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)=\exp \left(-\lambda \sin ^{2}\left(\omega\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)\right)\right), \quad \lambda>0
$$

See fig(19.4a).

![img-218.jpeg](img-218.jpeg)

Figure 19.3: (a): Plots of the Gamma-Exponential covariance $e^{-|x|^{\gamma}}$ versus $x$. The case $\gamma=2$ corresponds to the SE covariance function. The drop in the covariance is much more rapid as a function of the separation $x$ for small $\gamma$, suggesting that the functions corresponding to smaller $\gamma$ will be locally rough (though possess relatively higher long range correlation). (b): As for (a) but zoomed in towards the origin. For the SE case, $\gamma=2$, the derivative of the covariance function is zero, whereas the OU covariance $\gamma=1$ has a first order contribution to the drop in the covariance, suggesting that locally OU sampled functions will be much rougher than SE functions.

# 19.3.3 Non-stationary covariance functions 

Definition 19.13 (Linear).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=\mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{\prime}
$$

Definition 19.14 (Neural Network).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=\arcsin \left(\frac{2 \mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{1+2 \mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbf{x}} \sqrt{1+2 \mathbf{x}^{\prime}} \mathbf{x}^{\prime}}\right)
$$

The functions defined by this covariance always go through the origin. To shift this, one may use the embedding $\mathbf{x} \rightarrow(1, \mathbf{x})$ where the 1 has the effect of a 'bias' from the origin. To change the scale of the bias and non-bias contributions one may use additional parameters $\mathbf{x} \rightarrow(b, \lambda \mathbf{x})$. The NN covariance function can be derived as a limiting case of a neural network with infinite hidden units[317], and making use of exact integral results in [21]. See fig(19.4b).

Definition 19.15 (Gibbs).

$$
k\left(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)=\prod_{i}\left(\frac{r_{i}(\mathbf{x}) r_{i}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}{r_{i}^{2}(\mathbf{x})+r_{i}^{2}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \exp \left(-\frac{\left(x_{i}-x_{i}^{\prime}\right)^{2}}{r_{i}^{2}(\mathbf{x})+r_{i}^{2}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}\right)
$$

for functions $r_{i}(\mathbf{x})>0[122]$.

### 19.4 Analysis of Covariance Functions

### 19.4.1 Smoothness of the functions

We examine local smoothness for a translation invariant kernel $k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)=k\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)$. For two one-dimensional points $x$ and $x^{\prime}$, separated by a small amount $\delta \ll 1, x^{\prime}=x+\delta$, the covariance between the outputs $y$ and

![img-219.jpeg](img-219.jpeg)

Figure 19.4: Samples from a GP prior for $500 x$ points uniformly placed from -20 to 20 . (a): Samples from the periodic covariance function $\exp \left(-2 \sin ^{2} 0.5\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)\right)$. (b): Samples from the Neural Network covariance function with bias $b=5$ and $\lambda=1$.
$y^{\prime}$ is, by Taylor expansion,

$$
k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right) \approx k(0)+\left.\delta \frac{d k}{d x}\right|_{x=0}+O\left(\delta^{2}\right)
$$

so that the change in the covariance at the local level is dominated by the first derivative of the covariance function. For the SE covariance $k(x)=e^{-x^{2}}$,

$$
\frac{d k}{d x}=-2 x e^{-x^{2}}
$$

is zero at $x=0$. This means that for the SE covariance function, the first order change in the covariance is zero, and only higher order $\delta^{2}$ terms contribute.

For the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck covariance, $k(x)=e^{-|x|}$, the right derivative at the origin is

$$
\lim _{\delta \rightarrow 0} \frac{k(\delta)-k(0)}{\delta}=\lim _{\delta \rightarrow 0} \frac{e^{-\delta}-1}{\delta}=-1
$$

where this result is obtained using L'Hôpital's rule. Hence for the OU covariance function, there is a first order negative change in the covariance; at the local level, this decrease in the covariance is therefore much more rapid than for the SE covariance, see fig(19.3). Since low covariance implies low dependence (in Gaussian distributions), locally the functions generated from the OU process are rough, whereas they are smooth in the SE case. A more formal treatment for the stationary case can be obtained by examining the eigenvalue-frequency plot of the covariance function (spectral density), section(19.4.3). For rough functions the density of eigenvalues for high frequency components is higher than for smooth functions.

# 19.4.2 Mercer kernels 

Consider the function

$$
k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)=\boldsymbol{\phi}(x)^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}\left(x^{\prime}\right)=\sum_{s=1}^{B} \phi_{s}(x) \phi_{s}\left(x^{\prime}\right)
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(x)$ is a vector with component functions $\phi_{1}(x), \phi_{2}(x), \ldots, \phi_{B}(x)$. Then for a set of points $x^{1}, \ldots, x^{P}$, we construct the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ with elements

$$
[\mathbf{K}]_{i j}=k\left(x^{i}, x^{j}\right)=\sum_{s=1}^{B} \phi_{s}\left(x^{i}\right) \phi_{s}\left(x^{j}\right)
$$

We claim that the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ so constructed is positive semidefinite and hence a valid covariance matrix. Recalling that a matrix is positive semidefinite if for any non zero vector $\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}^{\top} \mathbf{K z} \geq 0$. Using the definition

of $\mathbf{K}$ above we have

$$
\mathbf{z}^{\top} \mathbf{K z}=\sum_{i, j=1}^{P} z_{i} K_{i j} z_{j}=\sum_{s=1}^{B} \underbrace{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{P} z_{i} \phi_{s}\left(x^{i}\right)\right]}_{\gamma_{s}} \underbrace{\left[\sum_{j=1}^{P} \phi_{s}\left(x^{j}\right) z_{j}\right]}_{\gamma_{s}}=\sum_{s=1}^{B} \gamma_{s}^{2} \geq 0
$$

Hence any function of the form equation (19.4.4) is a covariance function. We can generalise the Mercer kernel to complex functions $\boldsymbol{\phi}(x)$ using

$$
k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)=\boldsymbol{\phi}(x)^{\top} \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\dagger}\left(x^{\prime}\right)
$$

where ${ }^{\dagger}$ represents the complex conjugate. Then the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ formed from inputs $x^{i}, i=1, \ldots, P$ is positive semidefinite since for any real vector $\mathbf{z}$,

$$
\mathbf{z}^{\top} \mathbf{K z}=\sum_{s=1}^{B} \underbrace{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{P} z_{i} \phi_{s}\left(x^{i}\right)\right]}_{\gamma_{s}} \underbrace{\left[\sum_{j=1}^{P} \phi_{s}^{\dagger}\left(x^{j}\right) z_{j}\right]}_{\gamma_{s}^{\dagger}}=\sum_{s=1}^{B}\left|\gamma_{s}\right|^{2} \geq 0
$$

where we made use of the general result for a complex variable $x x^{\dagger}=|x|^{2}$. A further generalisation is to write

$$
k\left(x, x^{\prime}\right)=\int f(s) \phi(x, s) \phi^{\dagger}\left(x^{\prime}, s\right) d s
$$

for real $f(s) \geq 0$, and scalar complex functions $\phi(x, s)$. Then replacing summations with integration (and assuming we can interchange the sum over the components of $\mathbf{z}$ with the integral over $s$ ), we obtain

$$
\mathbf{z}^{\top} \mathbf{K z}=\int f(s) \underbrace{\left[\sum_{i=1}^{P} z_{i} \phi\left(x^{i}, s\right)\right]}_{\gamma(s)} \underbrace{\left[\sum_{j=1}^{P} \phi^{\dagger}\left(x^{j}, s\right) z_{j}\right]}_{\gamma^{\dagger}(s)} d s=\int f(s)|\gamma(s)|^{2} d s \geq 0
$$

# 19.4.3 Fourier analysis for stationary kernels 

For a function $g(x)$ with Fourier transform $\tilde{g}(s)$, we may use the inverse Fourier transform to write

$$
g(x)=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int \tilde{g}(s) e^{-\mathrm{i} x s} d s
$$

where $\mathrm{i} \equiv \sqrt{-1}$. For a stationary kernel $k(x)$ with Fourier transform $\tilde{k}(s)$, we can therefore write

$$
k\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int \tilde{k}(s) e^{-\mathrm{i}\left(x-x^{\prime}\right) s} d s=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int \tilde{k}(s) e^{-\mathrm{i} x s} e^{\mathrm{i} x^{\prime} s} d s
$$

which is of the same form as equation (19.4.9) where the Fourier transform $\tilde{k}(s)$ is identified with $f(s)$ and $\phi(x, s)=e^{-\mathrm{i} s x}$. Hence, provided the Fourier transform $\tilde{k}(s)$ is positive, the translation invariant kernel $k\left(x-x^{\prime}\right)$ is a covariance function. Bochner's Theorem[247] asserts the converse that any translation invariant covariance function must have such a Fourier representation.

## Application to the squared exponential kernel

For the translation invariant squared exponential kernel, $k(x)=e^{-\frac{1}{2} x^{2}}$, its Fourier transform is

$$
\tilde{k}(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\frac{1}{2} x^{2}+\mathrm{i} s x} d x=e^{-\frac{s^{2}}{2}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x+\mathrm{i} s)^{2}} d x=\sqrt{2 \pi} e^{-\frac{s^{2}}{2}}
$$

Hence the Fourier transform of the SE kernel is a Gaussian. Since this is positive the SE kernel is a covariance function.

![img-220.jpeg](img-220.jpeg)

Figure 19.5: GP classification. The GP induces a Gaussian distribution on the latent activations $y_{1}, \ldots, y^{N}, y^{*}$, given the observed values of $c^{1}, \ldots, c^{N}$. The classification of the new input $x^{*}$ is then given via the correlation induced by the training points on the latent activation $y^{*}$.

# 19.5 Gaussian Processes for Classification 

Adapting the GP framework to classification requires replacing the Gaussian regression term $p(y \mid x)$ with a corresponding classification term $p(c \mid x)$ for a discrete label $c$. To do so we will use the GP to define a latent continuous space $y$ which will then be mapped to a class probability using

$$
p(c \mid x)=\int p(c \mid y, x) p(y \mid x) d y=\int p(c \mid y) p(y \mid x) d y
$$

Given training data inputs $\mathcal{X}=\left\{x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}\right\}$, corresponding class labels $\mathcal{C}=\left\{c^{1}, \ldots, c^{N}\right\}$, and a novel input $x^{*}$, then

$$
p\left(c^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X}\right)=\int p\left(c^{*} \mid y^{*}\right) p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) d y^{*}
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) & \propto p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}\right) \\
& =\int p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right) d \mathcal{Y} \\
& =\int p(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{Y}) p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}\right) d \mathcal{Y} \\
& =\int \underbrace{\left\{\prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(c^{n} \mid y^{n}\right)\right\}}_{\text {class mapping }} \underbrace{p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}, y^{*} \mid x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}, x^{*}\right)}_{\text {Gaussian Process }} d y^{1}, \ldots, d y^{N}
\end{aligned}
$$

The graphical structure of the joint class and latent $y$ distribution is depicted in fig(19.5.) The posterior marginal $p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right)$ is the marginal of a Gaussian Process, multiplied by a set of non-Gaussian maps from the latent activations to the class probabilities. We can reformulate the prediction problem more conveniently as follows:

$$
p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) \propto p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{C} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right) \propto p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{Y}, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right) p(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X})
$$

where

$$
p(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X}) \propto\left\{\prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(c^{n} \mid y^{n}\right)\right\} p\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N} \mid x^{1}, \ldots, x^{N}\right)
$$

In equation (19.5.4) the term $p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{Y}, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right)$ does not contain any class label information and is simply a conditional Gaussian. The advantage of the above description is that we can therefore form an approximation to $p(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X})$ and then reuse this approximation in the prediction for many different $x^{*}$ without needing to rerun the approximation[318, 247].

### 19.5.1 Binary classification

For the binary class case we will use the convention that $c \in\{1,0\}$. We therefore need to specify $p(c=1 \mid y)$ for a real valued activation $y$. A convenient choice is the logistic transfer function ${ }^{3}$

$$
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{3}$ We will also refer to this as 'the sigmoid function'. More strictly a sigmoid function refers to any 's-shaped' function (from the Greek for 's').

Then

$$
p(c \mid y)=\sigma((2 c-1) y)
$$

is a valid distribution since $\sigma(-x)=1-\sigma(x)$, ensuring that the sum over the class states is 1 . A difficulty is that the non-linear class mapping term makes the computation of the posterior distribution equation (19.5.3) difficult since the integrals over $y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}$ cannot be carried out analytically. There are many approximate techniques one could apply in this case, including variational methods analogous to that described in section(18.2.3). Below we describe the straightforward Laplace method, leaving the more sophisticated methods for further reading[247].

# 19.5.2 Laplace's approximation 

In the Laplace method, section(28.2), we approximate the non-Gaussian distribution (19.5.5) by a Gaussian ${ }^{4}$ $q(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X})$

$$
p(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X}) \approx q(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X})
$$

From equation (19.5.4), approximate predictions can then be formed through the joint Gaussian

$$
p\left(y^{*}, \mathcal{Y} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) \approx p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathcal{Y}, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right) q(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{X})
$$

We will then marginalise this Gaussian to find the Gaussian distribution on $y^{*}$ alone, and then use this to form the prediction via $p\left(c^{*} \mid y^{*}\right)$.
For compactness we define the class label vector, and outputs

$$
\mathbf{c}=\left(c^{1}, \ldots, c^{N}\right)^{\top}, \quad \mathbf{y}=\left(y^{1}, \ldots, y^{N}\right)^{\top}
$$

and notationally drop the (ever present) conditioning on the inputs $x$. Also for convenience, we define

$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\left(\sigma\left(y^{1}\right), \ldots, \sigma\left(y^{N}\right)\right)^{\top}
$$

## Finding the mode

The Laplace approximation, section(28.2), corresponds to a second order expansion around the mode of the distribution. Our task is therefore to find the maximum of

$$
p(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{c}) \propto p(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{c})=\exp (\Psi(\mathbf{y}))
$$

where

$$
\Psi(\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{c}^{\top} \mathbf{y}-\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log \left(1+e^{y_{n}}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}\right)-\frac{N}{2} \log 2 \pi
$$

The maximum needs to be found numerically, and it is convenient to use the Newton method [132, 318, 247].

$$
\mathbf{y}^{n e w}=\mathbf{y}-(\nabla \nabla \Psi)^{-1} \nabla \Psi
$$

Differentiating equation 19.5.13 with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ we obtain the gradient and Hessian

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \Psi & =(\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma})-\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y} \\
\nabla \nabla \Psi & =-\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}-\mathbf{D}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the 'noise' matrix is given by

$$
\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{1}\left(1-\sigma_{1}\right), \ldots, \sigma_{N}\left(1-\sigma_{N}\right)\right)
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ Some authors use the term Laplace approximation solely for approximating an integral. Here we use the term to refer to a Gaussian approximation of a non-Gaussian distribution.

Using these expressions in the Newton update, (19.5.14) gives

$$
\mathbf{y}^{n e w}=\mathbf{y}+\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}+\mathbf{D}\right)^{-1}\left(\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}-\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}\right)
$$

To avoid unnecessary inversions, one may rewrite this in the form

$$
\mathbf{y}^{n e w}=\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{D} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}\right)^{-1}(\mathbf{D} \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma})
$$

For an initial guess of $\mathbf{y}$, we repeatedly apply equation (19.5.19) until convergence. This is guaranteed to converge since the Hessian is negative definite and has a unique maximum.

# Making predictions 

Given a converged solution $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$ we have found a Gaussian approximation

$$
q\left(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}, \mathcal{C}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{y} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{y}},\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}+\mathbf{D}\right)^{-1}\right)
$$

We now have Gaussians for $p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathbf{y}\right)$ and $q\left(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}, \mathcal{C}\right)$ in equation (19.5.9). Predictions are then made using

$$
p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) \approx \int p\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathbf{y}\right) q\left(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathcal{X}, x^{*}, \mathcal{C}\right) d \mathbf{y}
$$

where, by conditioning, section(8.4.2),

$$
p\left(y^{*} \mid \mathbf{y}, x^{*}, \mathcal{X}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(y^{*} \mid \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}-\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}\right)
$$

We can also write this as a linear system

$$
y^{*}=\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}+\eta
$$

where $\eta \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\eta \mid 0, \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}-\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}\right)$. Using equation (19.5.23) and equation (19.5.20) and averaging over $\mathbf{y}$ and the noise $\eta$, we obtain

$$
\left\langle y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right\rangle \approx \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}))
$$

Similarly, the variance of the latent prediction is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{var}\left(y^{*} \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) & \approx \mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}+\mathbf{D}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}+\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}-\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}} \\
& =\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, x^{*}}-\mathbf{K}_{x^{*}, \mathbf{x}}\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}+\mathbf{D}^{-1}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, x^{*}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where the last line is obtained using the Matrix Inversion Lemma, definition(29.11).
The class prediction for a new input $x^{*}$ is then given by

$$
p\left(c^{*}=1 \mid x^{*}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{C}\right) \approx\left\langle\sigma\left(y^{*}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{N}\left(y^{*} \mid\left\langle y^{*}\right\rangle, \operatorname{var}\left(y^{*}\right)\right)}
$$

In order to calculate the Gaussian integral over the logistic sigmoid function, we use an approximation of the sigmoid function based on the error function $\operatorname{erf}(x)$, see section(18.2.2) and avsigmaGauss.m.

Example 19.2. An example of binary classification is given in fig(19.6) in which one-dimensional input training data with binary class labels is plotted along with the class probability predictions on a range of input points. In both cases the covariance function is of the form $2 \exp \left(\left|x_{i}-x_{j}\right|^{\gamma}\right)+0.001 \delta_{i j}$. The square exponential covariance produces a smoother class prediction than the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck covariance function. See demoGPclass1D.m and demoGPclass.m.

![img-221.jpeg](img-221.jpeg)

Figure 19.6: Gaussian Process classification. The $x$-axis are the inputs, and the class is the $y$-axis. Green points are training points from class 1 and red from class 0 . The dots are the predictions $p\left(c=1 \mid x^{*}\right)$ for points $x^{*}$ ranging across the $x$ axis. (a): Square exponential covariance $(\gamma=2)$. (b): OU covariance $(\gamma=1)$. See demoGPclass1D.m.

# Marginal likelihood 

The marginal likelihood is given by

$$
p(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})=\int_{\mathcal{Y}} p(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{Y}) p(\mathcal{Y} \mid \mathcal{X})
$$

Under the Laplace approximation, the marginal likelihood is approximated by

$$
p(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}) \approx \int_{\mathbf{y}} \exp (\Psi(\hat{\mathbf{y}})) \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})^{\top} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{A}=-\nabla \nabla \Psi$. Integrating over $\mathbf{y}$ gives

$$
\log p(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}) \approx \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}) & =\Psi(\hat{\mathbf{y}})-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}(2 \pi \mathbf{A}) \\
& =\Psi(\hat{\mathbf{y}})-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1}+\mathbf{D}\right)+\frac{N}{2} \log 2 \pi \\
& =\mathbf{c}^{\top} \hat{\mathbf{y}}-\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log \left(1+\exp \left(\tilde{y}_{n}\right)\right)-\frac{1}{2} \hat{\mathbf{y}}^{\top} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \hat{\mathbf{y}}-\frac{1}{2} \log \operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{D}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the converged iterate of equation 19.5.18. One can also simplify the above using that at convergence $\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{y})$.

### 19.5.3 Hyperparameter optimisation

The approximate marginal likelihood can be used to assess hyperparameters $\theta$ of the kernel. A little care is required in computing derivatives of the approximate marginal likelihood since the optimum $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ depends on $\theta$. We use the total derivative formula [25]

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{d}{d \theta} \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})=\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})+\sum_{i} \frac{\partial}{\partial \tilde{y}_{i}} \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X}) \frac{d}{d \theta} \tilde{y}_{i} \\
& \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\left[\mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}^{-1} \mathbf{y}+\log \operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{D}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

which can be evaluated using the standard results for the derivative of a matrix determinant and inverse. Since the derivative of $\Psi$ is zero at $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, and noting that $\mathbf{D}$ depends explicitly on $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{y}_{i}} \log q(\mathcal{C} \mid \mathcal{X})=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{y}_{i}} \log \operatorname{det}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{D}\right)
$$

The implicit derivative is obtained from using the fact that at convergence

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{y}))
$$

to give

$$
\frac{d}{d \theta} \hat{\mathbf{y}}=\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}} \mathbf{D}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \mathbf{K}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{c}-\boldsymbol{\sigma})
$$

These results are substituted into equation (19.5.34) to find an explicit expression for the derivative. See exercise(19.7).

# 19.5.4 Multiple classes 

The extension of the preceding framework to multiple classes is essentially straightforward and may be achieved using the softmax function

$$
p(c=m \mid y)=\frac{e^{y_{m}}}{\sum_{m^{\prime}} e^{y_{m^{\prime}}}}
$$

which automatically enforces the constraint $\sum_{m} p(c=m)=1$. Naively it would appear that for $C$ classes, the cost of implementing the Laplace approximation for the multiclass case scales as $O\left(C^{3} N^{3}\right)$. However, one may show by careful implementation that the cost is only $O\left(C N^{3}\right)$, and we refer the reader to $[318,247]$ for details.

### 19.6 Summary

- Gaussian Processes are powerful regression models and mathematically well understood.
- The computational complexity of the prediction is cubic in the number of datapoints. This can be prohibitive for large datasets and approximate implementations are required.
- Gaussian Process classification is analytically intractable and approximations are required. The posterior is log concave so that simple unimodal approximation schemes can provide satisfactory results.
- Many classical models in statistics and physics are related to Gaussian Processes. For example, one can view linear dynamical systems, chapter(24), as specially constrained GPs.

Gaussian Processes have been heavily developed within the machine learning community over recent years and finding efficient approximations for both regression and classification remains an active research topic. We direct the interested reader to [262] and [247] for further discussion.

# CHAPTER 20 

Mixture models assume that the data is essentially clustered with each component in the mixture representing a cluster. In this chapter we view mixture models from the viewpoint of learning with missing data and discuss some of the classical algorithms, such as EM training of Gaussian mixture models. We also discuss more powerful models which allow for the possibility that an object can be a member of more than one cluster. These models have applications in areas such as document modelling.

### 20.1 Density Estimation Using Mixtures

A mixture model is one in which a set of component models is combined to produce a richer model:

$$
p(v)=\sum_{h=1}^{H} p(v \mid h) p(h)
$$

The variable $v$ is 'visible' or 'observable' and the discrete variable $h$ with $\operatorname{dom}(h)=\{1, \ldots, H\}$ indexes each component model $p(v \mid h)$, along with its weight $p(h)$. The variable $v$ can be either discrete or continuous. Mixture models have natural application in clustering data, where $h$ indexes the cluster. This interpretation can be gained from considering how to generate a sample datapoint $v$ from the model equation (20.1.1). First we sample a cluster $h$ from $p(h)$, and then draw a visible state $v$ from $p(v \mid h)$.

For a set of i.i.d. data $v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}$, a mixture model is of the form, fig(20.1),

$$
p\left(v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}, h^{1}, \ldots, h^{n}\right)=\prod_{n=1}^{N} p\left(v^{n} \mid h^{n}\right) p\left(h^{n}\right)
$$

from which the observation likelihood is given by

$$
p\left(v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}\right)=\prod_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{h^{n}} p\left(v^{n} \mid h^{n}\right) p\left(h^{n}\right)
$$

Finding the most likely assignment of datapoints to clusters is achieved by inference of

$$
\underset{h^{1}, \ldots, h^{N}}{\operatorname{argmax}} p\left(h^{1}, \ldots, h^{N} \mid v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}\right)
$$

which, thanks to the factorised form of the distribution is equivalent to computing $\arg \max _{h^{n}} p\left(h^{n} \mid v^{n}\right)$ for each datapoint.

![img-222.jpeg](img-222.jpeg)

Figure 20.1: A mixture model has a graphical representation as a DAG with a single hidden node, $h$ which indexes the mixture component; given a setting of $h$, we then generate an observation $v$ from $p(v \mid h)$. Independence of the $N$ observations means the model is replicated by the plate. The parameters are assumed common across all datapoints.

In most applications, however, the 'location' of the clusters is a priori unknown and the parameters $\theta$ of the model need to be learned to locate where these clusters are. Explicitly writing the dependence on the parameters, the model for a single datapoint $v$ and its corresponding cluster index $h$ is

$$
p(v, h \mid \theta)=p\left(v \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right) p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}\right)
$$

The optimal parameters $\theta_{v \mid h}, \theta_{h}$ of a mixture model are then most commonly set by maximum likelihood,

$$
\theta_{\text {opt }}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}} p\left(v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N} \mid \theta\right)=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmax}} \prod_{n} p\left(v^{n} \mid \theta\right)
$$

Numerically this can be achieved using an optimisation procedure such as gradient based approaches. Alternatively, by treating the component indices as latent variables, one may apply the EM algorithm, as described in the following section, which in many classical models produces simple update formulae.

Example 20.1. The data in fig(20.2) naturally has two clusters and can be modelled with a mixture of two two-dimensional Gaussians, each Gaussian describing one of the clusters. Here there is a clear visual interpretation of the meaning of 'cluster', with the mixture model placing two datapoints in the same cluster if they are both likely to be generated by the same model component. A priori we don't know the location of these two clusters and need to find the parameters; the Gaussian mean and covariance for each cluster $\mathbf{m}_{h}, \mathbf{C}_{h}, h=1,2$. This can be achieved using maximum likelihood.

# 20.2 Expectation Maximisation for Mixture Models 

Our task is to find the parameters $\theta$ that maximise the likelihood of the observations $v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N}$

$$
p\left(v^{1}, \ldots, v^{N} \mid \theta\right)=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\left\{\sum_{h} p\left(v^{n} \mid h, \theta\right) p(h \mid \theta)\right\}
$$

By treating the index $h$ as a missing variable, mixture models can be trained using the EM algorithm, section(11.2). There are two sets of parameters $-\theta_{v \mid h}$ for each component model $p\left(v \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right)$ and $\theta_{h}$ for the mixture weights $p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}\right)$. According to the general approach for i.i.d. data of section(11.2), for the M-step
![img-223.jpeg](img-223.jpeg)

Figure 20.2: Two dimensional data which displays clusters. In this case a Gaussian mixture model $1 / 2 \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{m}_{1}, \mathbf{C}_{1}\right)+1 / 2 \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{m}_{2}, \mathbf{C}_{2}\right)$ would fit the data well for suitable means $\mathbf{m}_{1}, \mathbf{m}_{2}$ and covariances $\mathbf{C}_{1}, \mathbf{C}_{2}$. To the human eye, identifying these clusters is an easy task; however, we will be interested in automatic methods that can cluster potentially very high dimensional data, for which the cluster solutions may be far less obvious.

we need to consider the energy term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(\theta) & =\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n}, h \mid \theta\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)} \\
& =\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n} \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

and maximise (20.2.3) with respect to the parameters $\theta_{v \mid h}, \theta_{h}, h=1, \ldots, H$. The E-step results in the update

$$
p^{\text {new }}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right) \propto p\left(v^{n} \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}^{o l d}\right) p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}^{o l d}\right)
$$

For initial parameters $\theta$, one then updates the E and M -steps until convergence. This is a general approach for training mixture models. Below we flesh out how these updates work for some specific models.

# 20.2.1 Unconstrained discrete tables 

Here we consider training a simple belief network $p\left(v \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right) p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}\right), \operatorname{dom}(v)=\{1, \ldots, V\}, \operatorname{dom}(h)=\{1, \ldots, H\}$ in which the tables are unconstrained. This is a special case of the more general framework discussed in section(11.2), although it is instructive to see how the EM algorithm can be derived for this specific case.

## M-step: $p(h)$

If no constraint is placed on $p\left(h \mid \theta_{h}\right)$ we may write the parameters as simply $p(h)$, with the understanding that $0 \leq p(h) \leq 1$ and $\sum_{h} p(h)=1$. Isolating the dependence of equation (20.2.3) on $p(h)$ we obtain

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}=\sum_{h} \log p(h) \sum_{n=1}^{N} p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)
$$

We now wish to maximise equation (20.2.5) with respect to $p(h)$ under the constraint that $\sum_{h} p(h)=$ 1. There are different ways to perform this constrained optimisation. One approach is to use Lagrange multipliers, see exercise(20.4). Another, arguably more elegant approach is to use the techniques described in section(11.2) based on the similarity of the above to a Kullback-Leibler divergence. First we define the distribution

$$
\tilde{p}(h) \equiv \frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N} p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}{\sum_{h} \sum_{n=1}^{N} p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)
$$

Then maximising equation (20.2.5) is equivalent to maximising

$$
\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}=\underbrace{\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}-\langle\log \tilde{p}(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}}_{-\operatorname{KL}(\tilde{p} \mid p)}+\langle\log \tilde{p}(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}
$$

since equation (20.2.5) is related to $\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}$ by the constant factor $N$. By subtracting the $\theta$ independent term $\langle\log \tilde{p}(h)\rangle_{\tilde{p}(h)}$ from equation (20.2.7), we obtain the negative Kullback-Leibler divergence $\operatorname{KL}(\tilde{p} \mid p)$. This means that the optimal $p(h)$ is that distribution which minimises the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Optimally, therefore $p(h)=\tilde{p}(h)$, so that the M-step is given by

$$
p^{\text {new }}(h)=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)
$$

![img-224.jpeg](img-224.jpeg)

Figure 20.3: Mixture of a product of Bernoulli distributions. In a Bayesian Treatment, a parameter prior is used. In the text we simply set the parameters using maximum likelihood.

# M-step : $p(v \mid h)$ 

The dependence of equation (20.2.3) on $p(v \mid h)$ is

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle\log p\left(v^{n} \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)}=\sum_{v} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=v\right] p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right) \log p(v \mid h)
$$

If the distributions $p\left(v \mid h, \theta_{v \mid h}\right)$ are not constrained, we can apply a similar Kullback-Leibler method, as we did in section(11.2) and above for $p(h)$. As an alternative to that approach, we describe here how the Lagrange method works in this case. We need to ensure that $p(v \mid h)$ is a distribution for each of the mixture states $h=1, \ldots, H$. This can be achieved using a set of Lagrange multipliers, giving the Lagrangian:

$$
\mathcal{L} \equiv \sum_{v=1}^{V} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=v\right] p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right) \log p(v \mid h)+\sum_{h=1}^{H} \lambda(h)\left(1-\sum_{v=1}^{V} p(v \mid h)\right)
$$

Differentiating with respect to $p(v=i \mid h=j)$ and equating to zero,

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p(v=i \mid h=j)}=\sum_{n=1}^{N} \frac{\mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=i\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid v^{n}=i\right)}{p(v=i \mid h=j)}-\lambda(h=j)=0
$$

Solving this, we have

$$
p(v=i \mid h=j)=\frac{1}{\lambda(h=j)} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=i\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid v^{n}=i\right)
$$

Using the normalisation requirement, $\sum_{v} p(v=i \mid h=j)=1$ shows that $\lambda(h=j)$ is just the numerator of the above equation, summed over $v$. Hence the M-step update is given by

$$
p^{n e w}(v=i \mid h=j)=\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=i\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid v^{n}=i\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{V} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbb{I}\left[v^{n}=i\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid v^{n}=i\right)}
$$

## E-step

According to the general EM procedure, section(11.2), optimally we set $p^{\text {new }}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)=p^{o l d}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)$ :

$$
p^{n e w}\left(h \mid v^{n}\right)=\frac{p^{o l d}\left(v^{n} \mid h\right) p^{o l d}(h)}{\sum_{h} p^{o l d}\left(v^{n} \mid h\right) p^{o l d}(h)}
$$

Equations (20.2.8,20.2.13,20.2.14) are repeated until convergence and guarantee that the likelihood equation (20.2.1) cannot decrease. The initialisation of the tables and mixture probabilities can severely affect the quality of the solution found since the likelihood often has local optima. If random initialisations are used, it is recommended to record the converged value of the likelihood itself, to see which parameters have the higher likelihood. The solution with the highest likelihood is to be preferred.

# 20.2.2 Mixture of product of Bernoulli distributions 

As an example mixture model, and one that can be used for practical clustering, see example(20.2), we describe a simple mixture model that can be used to cluster binary vectors, $\mathbf{v}=\left(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{D}\right)^{\mathrm{T}}, v_{i} \in\{0,1\}$. The mixture of Bernoulli products ${ }^{1}$ model is given by

$$
p(\mathbf{v})=\sum_{h=1}^{H} p(h) \prod_{i=1}^{D} p\left(v_{i} \mid h\right)
$$

where each term $p\left(v_{i} \mid h\right)$ is a Bernoulli distribution. The model is depicted in fig(20.3) and has parameters $p(h)$ and $p\left(v_{i}=1 \mid h\right), \operatorname{dom}(h)=\{1 \ldots, H\}$. One way to understand the model is to imagine drawing samples. In this case, for each datapoint $n$, we draw a cluster index $h \in\{1, \ldots, H\}$ from $p(h)$. Then for each $i=1, \ldots, D$, we draw a state $v_{i} \in\{0,1\}$ from $p\left(v_{i} \mid h\right)$.

## EM training

To train the model under maximum likelihood it is convenient to use the EM algorithm which, as usual, may be derived by writing down the energy:

$$
\sum_{n}\left\langle\log p\left(\mathbf{v}^{n}, h\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}=\sum_{n} \sum_{i}\left\langle\log p\left(v_{i}^{n} \mid h\right)\right\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}+\sum_{n}\langle\log p(h)\rangle_{p^{o l d}\left(h \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}
$$

and then performing the maximisation over the table entries. From our general results, section(11.2), we know that the M-step is equivalent to maximum likelihood when all variables are observed, and then replacing the unobserved variables $h$ by the conditional distribution $p(h \mid v)$. Using this we can write down immediately the M-step as

$$
\begin{aligned}
p^{n e w}\left(v_{i}=1 \mid h=j\right) & =\frac{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[v_{i}^{n}=1\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}{\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[v_{i}^{n}=1\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)+\sum_{n} \mathbb{I}\left[v_{i}^{n}=0\right] p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)} \\
p^{n e w}(h=j) & =\frac{\sum_{n} p^{o l d}\left(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}{\sum_{h^{\prime}} \sum_{n} p^{o l d}\left(h^{\prime} \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the E-step by

$$
p^{n e w}\left(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right) \propto p^{o l d}(h=j) \prod_{i=1}^{D} p^{o l d}\left(v_{i}^{n} \mid h=j\right)
$$

Equations (20.2.17,20.2.18) are iterated until convergence.
If an attribute $i$ is missing for datapoint $n$, one needs to sum over the states of the corresponding $v_{i}^{n}$. The effect of performing the summation for this model is simply to remove the corresponding factor $p\left(v_{i}^{n} \mid h\right)$ from the algorithm, see exercise(20.1).

## Initialisation

The EM algorithm can be very sensitive to initial conditions. Consider the following initialisation: $p\left(v_{i}=\right.$ $1 \mid h=j)=0.5$, with $p(h)$ set arbitrarily. This means that at the first iteration, $p^{\text {old }}(h=j \mid \mathbf{v}^{n})=p(h=j)$. The subsequent M-step updates are

$$
p^{n e w}(h)=p^{o l d}(h), \quad p^{n e w}\left(v_{i} \mid h=j\right)=p^{n e w}\left(v_{i} \mid h=j^{\prime}\right)
$$

for any $j, j^{\prime}$. This means that the parameters $p(v \mid h)$ immediately become independent of $h$ and the model is numerically trapped in a symmetric solution. It makes sense, therefore, to initialise the parameters in a non-symmetric fashion.

The model is readily extendable to more than two output class, and this is left as an exercise for the interested reader.

[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ This is similar to the Naive Bayes classifier in which the class labels are always hidden.

Example 20.2 (Questionnaire). A company sends out a questionnaire containing a set of $D$ 'yes/no' questions to a set of customers. The binary responses of a customer are stored in a vector $\mathbf{v}=\left(v_{1}, \ldots, v_{D}\right)^{\top}$. In total $N$ customers send back their questionnaires, $\mathbf{v}^{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{v}^{N}$, and the company wishes to perform an analysis to find what kinds of customers it has. The company assumes there are $H$ essential types of customer for which the profile of responses is defined by only the customer type.

Data from a questionnaire containing 5 questions, with 150 respondents is presented in fig(20.4). The data has a large number of missing values. We assume there are $H=2$ kinds of respondents and attempt to assign each respondent into one of the two clusters. Running the EM algorithm on this data, with random initial values for the tables, produces the results in fig(20.5). Based on assigning each datapoint $\mathbf{v}^{n}$ to the cluster with maximal posterior probability $h^{n}=\arg \max _{h} p\left(h \mid \mathbf{v}^{n}\right)$, given a trained model $p(\mathbf{v} \mid h) p(h)$, the model assigns $90 \%$ of the data to the correct cluster (which is known in this simulated case). See MIXprodBern.m.

Example 20.3 (Handwritten digits). We have a collection of 5000 handwritten digits which we wish to cluster into 20 groups, fig(20.6). Each digit is a $28 \times 28=784$ dimensional binary vector. Using a mixture of Bernoulli products, trained with 50 iterations of EM (with random initialisation), the clusters are presented in fig(20.6). As we see, the method captures natural clusters in the data - for example, there are two kinds of 1 , one slightly more slanted than the other, two kinds of 4 , etc.
