# CHAPTER 25 

## Switching Linear Dynamical Systems

Hidden Markov models assume that the underlying process is discrete; linear dynamical systems that the underlying process is continuous. However, there are scenarios in which the underlying system might jump from one continuous regime to another. In this chapter we discuss a class of models that can be used in this situation. Unfortunately the technical demands of this class of models are somewhat more involved than in previous chapters, although the models are correspondingly more powerful.

### 25.1 Introduction

Complex timeseries which are not well described globally by a single Linear Dynamical System may be divided into segments, each modelled by a potentially different LDS. Such models can handle situations in which the underlying model 'jumps' from one parameter setting to another. For example a single LDS might well represent the normal flows in a chemical plant. When a break in a pipeline occurs, the dynamics of the system changes from one set of linear flow equations to another. This scenario can be modelled using a set of two linear systems, each with different parameters. The discrete latent variable at each time $s_{t} \in\{$ normal, pipe broken $\}$ indicates which of the LDSs is most appropriate at the current time. This is called a Switching LDS and is used in many disciplines, from econometrics to machine learning[12, 63, 59, $235,324,189]$.

### 25.2 The Switching LDS

At each time $t$, a switch variable $s_{t} \in 1, \ldots, S$ describes which of a set of LDSs is to be used. The continuous observation (or 'visible') variable $\mathbf{v}_{t}, \operatorname{dim}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t}\right)=V$ is linearly related to the continuous hidden variable $\mathbf{h}_{t}$, $\operatorname{dim}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right)=H$ by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{t}=\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t}+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{v}\left(s_{t}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\eta}^{v}\left(s_{t}\right) \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{v}\left(s_{t}\right) \mid \overline{\mathbf{v}}\left(s_{t}\right), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}\left(s_{t}\right)\right)
$$

Here $s_{t}$ describes which one from the set of emission matrices $\{\mathbf{B}(1), \ldots, \mathbf{B}(S)\}$ is active at time $t$. The observation noise $\boldsymbol{\eta}^{v}\left(s_{t}\right)$ is drawn from a Gaussian with mean $\overline{\mathbf{v}}\left(s_{t}\right)$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}\left(s_{t}\right)$. The transition dynamics of the continuous hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ is linear,

$$
\mathbf{h}_{t}=\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\eta}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right) \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right) \mid \overline{\mathbf{h}}\left(s_{t}\right), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h}\left(s_{t}\right)\right)
$$

and the switch variable $s_{t}$ selects a single transition matrix from the available set $\{\mathbf{A}(1), \ldots, \mathbf{A}(S)\}$. The Gaussian transition noise $\boldsymbol{\eta}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right)$ also depends on the switch variable. The dynamics of $s_{t}$ itself is Markovian, with transition $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}\right)$. For the more general 'augmented' aSLDS model the switch $s_{t}$ is dependent on

![img-287.jpeg](img-287.jpeg)

Figure 25.1: The independence structure of the aSLDS. Square nodes $s_{t}$ denote discrete switch variables; $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ are continuous latent/hidden variables, and $\mathbf{v}_{t}$ continuous observed/visible variables. The discrete state $s_{t}$ determines which Linear Dynamical system from a finite set of Linear Dynamical systems is operational at time $t$. In the SLDS links from $h$ to $s$ are not normally considered.
both the previous $s_{t-1}$ and $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$. The model defines a joint distribution (see fig(25.1))

$$
p\left(\mathbf{v}_{1: T}, \mathbf{h}_{1: T}, s_{1: T}\right)=\prod_{t=1}^{T} p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}\right)
$$

with

$$
p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \overline{\mathbf{v}}\left(s_{t}\right)+\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}\left(s_{t}\right)\right), \quad p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \overline{\mathbf{h}}\left(s_{t}\right)+\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h}\left(s_{t}\right)\right)
$$

At time $t=1, p\left(s_{1} \mid \mathbf{h}_{0}, s_{0}\right)$ denotes the initial switch distribution $p\left(s_{1}\right)$, and $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{1} \mid \mathbf{h}_{0}, s_{1}\right)$ denotes the initial Gaussians $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{1} \mid s_{1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{1} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\pi}\left(s_{1}\right), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\pi}\left(s_{1}\right)\right)$.

The SLDS can be thought of as a marriage between a hidden Markov model and a Linear Dynamical System. The SLDS is also called a Jump Markov model/process, switching Kalman Filter, Switching Linear Gaussian State Space model, Conditional Linear Gaussian Model.

# 25.2.1 Exact inference is computationally intractable 

Both exact filtered and smoothed inference in the SLDS is intractable, scaling exponentially with time. As an informal explanation, consider filtered posterior inference for which, by analogy with equation (23.2.9), the forward pass is

$$
p\left(s_{t+1}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)=\sum_{s_{t}} \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t}} p\left(s_{t+1}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1}\right) p\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

At timestep 1, $p\left(s_{1}, \mathbf{h}_{1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1}\right)=p\left(\mathbf{h}_{1} \mid s_{1}, \mathbf{v}_{1}\right) p\left(s_{1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1}\right)$ is an indexed set of Gaussians. At timestep 2, due to the summation over the states $s_{1}, p\left(s_{2}, \mathbf{h}_{2} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: 2}\right)$ will be an indexed set of $S$ Gaussians; similarly at timestep 3 , it will be $S^{2}$ and, in general, gives rise to $S^{t-1}$ Gaussians at time $t$. Even for small $t$, the number of components required to exactly represent the filtered distribution is therefore computationally intractable. Analogously, smoothing is also intractable. The origin of the intractability of the SLDS differs from 'structural intractability' that we've previously encountered. In the SLDS, in terms of the cluster variables $x_{1: T}$, with $x_{t} \equiv\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t}\right)$ and visible variables $\mathbf{v}_{1: T}$, the graph of the distribution is singly-connected. From a purely graph theoretic viewpoint, one would therefore envisage little difficulty in carrying out inference. Indeed, as we saw above, the derivation of the filtering algorithm is straightforward since the graph is singly-connected. However, the numerical implementation of the algorithm is intractable since the description of the messages requires an exponentially increasing number of terms.

In order to deal with this intractability, several approximation schemes have been introduced [105, 120, 188, 174, 173]. Here we focus on techniques which approximate the switch conditional posteriors using a limited mixture of Gaussians. Since the exact posterior distributions are mixtures of Gaussians, albeit with an exponentially large number of components, the aim is to drop low weight components such that the resulting approximation accurately represents the posterior.

### 25.3 Gaussian Sum Filtering

Equation(25.2.4) describes the exact filtering recursion and generates an exponentially increasing number of components with time. In general, however, the influence of ancient observations will be much less relevant

than that of recent observations. This suggests that the 'effective time' is limited and that therefore a corresponding limited number of components in the Gaussian mixture may suffice to accurately represent the filtered posterior [6]. Our aim is to form a recursion for $p\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ based on a Gaussian mixture approximation of $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$. Given an approximation of the filtered distribution $p\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) \approx q\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$, the exact recursion equation (25.2.4) is approximated by

$$
q\left(s_{t+1}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)=\sum_{s_{t}} \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t}} p\left(s_{t+1}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1}\right) q\left(s_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

This approximation to the filtered posterior at the next timestep will contain $S$ times more components than in the previous timestep and, to prevent an exponential explosion in mixture components, we will need to subsequently collapse the mixture $q\left(s_{t+1}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ in a suitable way. It is useful to break the filtered approximation for equation (25.2.4) into continuous and discrete parts:

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)=q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

and derive separate filtered update formulae, as described below.

# 25.3.1 Continuous filtering 

The exact representation of $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is a mixture with $O\left(S^{t-1}\right)$ components. To retain computational feasibility we therefore approximate this with a limited $I$-component mixture

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)=\sum_{i_{t}=1}^{I} q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

where $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is a Gaussian parameterised with mean $\mathbf{f}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)$ and covariance $\mathbf{F}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)$. Strictly speaking, we should use the notation $\mathbf{f}_{t}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)$ since, for each time $t$, we have a set of means indexed by $i_{t}, s_{t}$, although we drop these dependencies in the notation used here.

An important remark is that many techniques approximate $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ using a single Gaussian, one for each state of $s_{t}$. Naturally, this gives rise to a mixture of Gaussians for $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)=\sum_{s_{t}} p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$. However, in making a single Gaussian approximation to $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ the representation of the posterior may be poor. Our aim here is to maintain an accurate approximation to $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ by using a mixture of Gaussians.

To find a recursion for the approximating distribution we first assume that we know the filtered approximation $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ and then propagate this forwards using the exact dynamics. To do so consider first the relation

$$
\begin{aligned}
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) & =\sum_{s_{t}, i_{t}} q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t}, i_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) \\
& =\sum_{s_{t}, i_{t}} q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) q\left(s_{t}, i_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Wherever possible we now substitute the exact dynamics and evaluate each of the two factors above. The usefulness of decomposing the update in this way is that the new filtered approximation is of the form of a Gaussian mixture, where $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ is Gaussian and $q\left(s_{t}, i_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ are the weights or mixing proportions of the components. We describe below how to compute these terms explicitly. Equation(25.3.4) produces a new Gaussian mixture with $I \times S$ components which we will collapse back to $I$ components at the end of the computation.

Evaluating $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$
We aim to find a filtering recursion for $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$. Since this is conditional on switch states and components, this corresponds to a single LDS forward step which can be evaluated by considering first the joint distribution

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)=\int_{\mathbf{h}_{t}} p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{H}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, \mathrm{~s}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

and subsequently conditioning on $\mathbf{v}_{t+1}$. In the above we use the exact dynamics where possible. To ease the burden on notation we derive this for $\dot{\mathbf{h}}_{t}, \dot{\mathbf{v}}_{t} \equiv 0$ for all $t$. The exact forward dynamics is then given by

$$
\mathbf{h}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t}+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{h}\left(s_{t+1}\right), \quad \mathbf{v}_{t+1}=\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t+1}+\boldsymbol{\eta}^{v}\left(s_{t+1}\right)
$$

Given the mixture component index $i_{t}$,

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}, i_{t}, s_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{f}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right), \mathbf{F}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)\right)
$$

we propagate this Gaussian with the exact dynamics equation (25.3.6). Then $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is a Gaussian with covariance and mean elements

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h h}=\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{F}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right) \mathbf{A}^{\top}\left(s_{t+1}\right)+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h}\left(s_{t+1}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v v}=\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h h} \mathbf{B}^{\top}\left(s_{t+1}\right)+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \\
& \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v h}=\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h h}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h v}^{\top}, \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}_{v}=\mathbf{B}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{A}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{f}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}_{h}=\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t+1}\right) \mathbf{f}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

These results are obtained from integrating the forward dynamics, equations (25.2.1,25.2.2) over $\mathbf{h}_{t}$, using result(8.3). To find $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ we now condition $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ on $\mathbf{v}_{t+1}$ using the standard Gaussian conditioning formulae, result(8.4), to obtain

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{h \mid v}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h \mid v}\right)
$$

with

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{h \mid v}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{h}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h v} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v v}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{v}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h \mid v}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h h}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h v} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v v}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v h}
$$

where the quantities required are defined in equation (25.3.8).

# Evaluating the mixture weights $q\left(s_{t}, i_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ 

Up to a normalisation constant the mixture weight in equation (25.3.4) can be found from

$$
q\left(s_{t}, i_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) \propto q\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

The first factor in equation (25.3.11), $q\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is Gaussian with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{v}$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{v v}$, as given in equation (25.3.8). The last two factors $q\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ and $q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ are given from the previous filtered iteration. Finally, $q\left(s_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is found from

$$
q\left(s_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)= \begin{cases}\left\langle p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)} & \text { augmented SLDS } \\ p\left(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t}\right) & \text { standard SLDS }\end{cases}
$$

In the aSLDS, the term in equation (25.3.12) will generally need to be computed numerically. A simple approximation is to evaluate equation (25.3.12) at the mean value of the distribution $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$. To take covariance information into account an alternative would be to draw samples from the Gaussian $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ and thus approximate the average of $p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right)$ by sampling. Note that this does not equate Gaussian Sum filtering for the augmented SLDS with a sequential sampling procedure, such as Particle Filtering, section(27.6.2). The sampling here is exact, for which no convergence issues arise.

## Closing the recursion

We are now in a position to calculate equation (25.3.4). For each setting of the variable $s_{t+1}$, we have a mixture of $I \times S$ Gaussians. To prevent the number of components increasing exponentially with time, we numerically collapse $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ back to $I$ Gaussians to form

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) \rightarrow \sum_{i_{t+1}=1}^{I} q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid i_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) q\left(i_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)
$$

The numerical collapse then generates the new Gaussian components and corresponding mixture weights. Any method of choice may be supplied to collapse a mixture to a smaller mixture. A straightforward approach is to repeatedly merge low-weight components, as explained in section(25.3.4). In this way the new mixture coefficients $q\left(i_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right), i_{t+1} \in 1, \ldots, I$ are defined. This completes the description of how to form a recursion for the continuous filtered posterior approximation $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ in equation (25.3.2).

![img-288.jpeg](img-288.jpeg)

Figure 25.2: Gaussian Sum Filtering. The leftmost column depicts the previous Gaussian mixture approximation $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, i_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ for two states $S=2$ (red and blue) and three mixture components $I=3$, with the mixture weight represented by the area of each oval. There are $S=2$ different linear systems which take each of the components of the mixture into a new filtered state, the colour of the arrow indicating which dynamic system is used. After one time-step each mixture component branches into a further $S$ components so that the joint approximation $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$ contains $S^{2} I$ components (middle column). To keep the representation computationally tractable the mixture of Gaussians for each state $s_{t+1}$ is collapsed back to $I$ components. This means that each coloured set of Gaussians needs to be approximated by a smaller $I$ component mixture of Gaussians. There are many ways to achieve this. A naive but computationally efficient approach is to simply ignore the lowest weight components, as depicted on the right column, see mix2mix.m.

# 25.3.2 Discrete filtering 

A recursion for the switch variable distribution in equation (25.3.2) is

$$
q\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right) \propto \sum_{i_{t}, s_{t}} q\left(s_{t+1}, i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

The r.h.s. of the above equation is proportional to

$$
\sum_{s_{t}, i_{t}} q\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

for which all terms have been computed during the recursion for $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$. We therefore now have all the quantities required to compute the Gaussian Sum approximation of the filtering forward pass. A schematic representation of Gaussian Sum filtering is given in fig(25.2) and the pseudo code is presented in algorithm(25.1). See also SLDSforward.m.

### 25.3.3 The likelihood $p\left(\mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$

The likelihood $p\left(\mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ may be found from

$$
p\left(\mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1} p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

where

$$
p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) \approx \sum_{i_{t}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}} q\left(\mathbf{v}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

In the above expression, all terms have been computed in forming the recursion for the filtered posterior $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t+1}\right)$.

### 25.3.4 Collapsing Gaussians

A central part of the above filtering recursion is the collapse of a mixture of Gaussians to a smaller number of Gaussians. That is, given a mixture of $N$ Gaussians

$$
p(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_{i} \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}\right)
$$

we wish to collapse this to a smaller $K<N$ mixture of Gaussians. We describe a simple method which has the advantage of computational efficiency, but the disadvantage that no spatial information about the

Also return the approximate log-likelihood $L \equiv \log p\left(\mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) . I_{t}$ are the number of components in each Gaussian mixture approximation. for $s_{1} \leftarrow 1$ to $S$ do

$\alpha_{1} \leftarrow p\left(s_{1}\right) \hat{p}$
end for
for $t \leftarrow 2$ to $T$ do
for $s_{t} \leftarrow 1$ to $S$ do
for $i \leftarrow 1$ to $I_{t-1}$, and $s \leftarrow 1$ to $S$ do
$\left\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x \mid y}(i, s), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x \mid y}(i, s), \hat{p}\right\}=\operatorname{LDSFORWARD}\left(\mathbf{f}_{t-1}(i, s), \mathbf{F}_{t-1}(i, s), \mathbf{v}_{t} ; \theta\left(s_{t}\right)\right)$
$p^{*}\left(s_{t} \mid i, s\right) \equiv\left\langle p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}=s\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1} \mid i_{t-1}=i, s_{t-1}=s, \mathbf{v}_{1: t-1}\right)}$
$p^{\prime}\left(s_{t}, i, s\right) \leftarrow w_{t-1}(i, s) p^{*}\left(s_{t} \mid i, s\right) \alpha_{t-1}(s) \hat{p}$
end for
Collapse the $I_{t-1} \times S$ mixture of Gaussians defined by $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{x \mid y}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{x \mid y}$, and weights $p\left(i, s \mid s_{t}\right) \propto p^{\prime}\left(s_{t}, i, s\right)$ to a Gaussian with $I_{t}$ components, $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) \approx$ $\sum_{i_{t}=1}^{I_{t}} p\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, i_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$. This defines the new means $\mathbf{f}_{t}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)$, covariances $\mathbf{F}_{t}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right)$ and mixture weights $w_{t}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}\right) \equiv p\left(i_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$
Compute $\alpha_{t}\left(s_{t}\right) \propto \sum_{i, s} p^{\prime}\left(s_{t}, i, s\right)$
end for
normalise $\alpha_{t}$
$L \leftarrow L+\log \sum_{s_{t}, i, s} p^{\prime}\left(s_{t}, i, s\right)$
end for
mixture is used[297]. First we describe how to collapse a mixture to a single Gaussian. This can be achieved by finding the mean and covariance of the mixture distribution (25.3.17). These are

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}=\sum_{i} p_{i} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\sum_{i} p_{i}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\right)-\boldsymbol{\mu} \boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathrm{T}}
$$

To collapse a mixture then to a $K$-component mixture we may first retain the $K-1$ Gaussians with the largest mixture weights. The remaining $N-K+1$ Gaussians are simply merged to a single Gaussian using the above method. Alternative heuristics such as recursively merging the two Gaussians with the lowest mixture weights are also reasonable.

More sophisticated methods which retain some spatial information would clearly be potentially useful. The method presented in [188] is a suitable approach which considers removing Gaussians which are spatially similar (and not just low-weight components), thereby retaining a sense of diversity over the possible solutions. In applications with many thousands of timesteps, speed can be a factor in determining which method of collapsing Gaussians is to be preferred.

# 25.3.5 Relation to other methods 

Gaussian Sum Filtering can be considered a form of 'analytical particle filtering', section(27.6.2), in which instead of point distributions (delta functions) being propagated, Gaussians are propagated. The collapse operation to a smaller number of Gaussians is analogous to resampling in Particle Filtering. Since a Gaussian is more expressive than a delta-function, the Gaussian Sum filter is generally an improved approximation technique over using point particles. See [17] for a numerical comparison.

### 25.4 Gaussian Sum Smoothing

Approximating the smoothed posterior $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ is more involved than filtering and requires additional approximations. For this reason smoothing is more prone to failure since there are more assumptions that need to be satisfied for the approximations to hold. The route we take here is to assume that a Gaussian Sum

filtered approximation has been carried out, and then approximate the $\gamma$ backward pass, analogous to that of section(23.2.4). By analogy with the RTS smoothing recursion equation (23.2.20), the exact backward pass for the SLDS reads

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t+1}} p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

where $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ is composed of the discrete and continuous components of the smoothed posterior at the next time step. The recursion runs backwards in time, beginning with the initialisation $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{T}, s_{T} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ set by the filtered result (at time $t=T$, the filtered and smoothed posteriors coincide). Apart from the fact that the number of mixture components will increase at each step, computing the integral over $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$ in equation (25.4.1) is problematic since the conditional distribution term is non-Gaussian in $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$. For this reason it is more useful to derive an approximate recursion by beginning with the exact relation

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

which can be expressed more directly in terms of the SLDS dynamics as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)\left\langle p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}, \underline{\mathbf{v}}_{t+1: T}\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)} \\
& \times\left\langle p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

In forming the recursion we assume access to the distribution $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ from the future timestep. However, we also require the distribution $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ which is not directly known and needs to be inferred, in itself a computationally challenging task. In the Expectation Correction (EC) approach [17] one assumes the approximation (see fig(25.3))

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

resulting in an approximate recursion for the smoothed posterior,

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx \sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)\left\langle p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathbf{h}_{t+1}}\left\langle p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)\right\rangle_{\mathbf{h}_{t+1}}
$$

where $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathbf{h}_{t+1}}$ represents averaging with respect to the distribution $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$. In carrying out the approximate recursion, (25.4.5) we will end up with a mixture of Gaussians that grows at each timestep. To avoid the exponential explosion problem, we use a finite mixture approximation, $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ :

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

and plug this into the approximate recursion above. From equation (25.4.5) a recursion for the approximation is given by

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} q\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \underbrace{\left\langle q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}}_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)} \underbrace{\left\langle q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}}_{q\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}
$$

As for filtering, wherever possible, we replace approximate terms by their exact counterparts and parameterise the posterior using

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

To reduce the notational burden here we outline the method only for the case of using a single component approximation in both the forward and backward passes. The extension to using a mixture to approximate each $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ is conceptually straightforward and deferred to section(25.4.4). In the single Gaussian case we assume we have a Gaussian approximation available for

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{g}\left(s_{t+1}\right), \mathbf{G}\left(s_{t+1}\right)\right)
$$

Figure 25.3: The EC backpass approximates $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ by $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$. The motivation for this is that $s_{t}$ influences $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$ only indirectly through $\mathbf{h}_{t}$. However, $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ will most likely be heavily influenced by $\mathbf{v}_{1: t}$, so that not knowing the state of $s_{t}$ is likely to be of secondary importance. # 25.4.1 Continuous smoothing 

For given $s_{t}, s_{t+1}$, an RTS style recursion for the smoothed continuous distribution is obtained from equation (25.4.7), giving

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\int_{\mathbf{h}_{t+1}} p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

To compute equation (25.4.10) we then perform a single update of the LDS backward recursion, section(24.4.2).

### 25.4.2 Discrete smoothing

The second average in equation (25.4.7) corresponds to a recursion for the discrete variable and is given by

$$
\left\langle q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)} \equiv q\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

The average of $q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ with respect to $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ cannot be achieved in closed form. A simple approach is to approximate the average by evaluation at the mean ${ }^{1}$

$$
\left\langle q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)} \approx q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\left|\mathbf{h}_{t+1}=\left\langle\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right\rangle\right.
$$

where $\left\langle\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right\rangle$ is the mean of $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$ with respect to $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$.
Replacing $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$ by its mean gives the approximation

$$
\left\langle q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)} \approx \frac{1}{Z} \frac{e^{-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{z}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{T}}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1}\right) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) \mathbf{z}_{t+1}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1}\right)}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{det}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right)}} q\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{z}_{t+1}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1}\right) \equiv\left\langle\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right\rangle-\left\langle\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right\rangle
$$

and $Z$ ensures normalisation over $s_{t} . \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is the filtered covariance of $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}$ given $s_{t}, s_{t+1}$ and the observations $\mathbf{v}_{1: t}$, which may be taken from $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{b h}$ in equation (25.3.8). Approximations which take covariance information into account can also be considered, although the above simple (and fast) method may suffice in practice $[17,207]$.

### 25.4.3 Collapsing the mixture

From section(25.4.1) and section(25.4.2) we now have all the terms in equation (25.4.8) to compute the approximation to equation (25.4.7). Due to the summation over $s_{t+1}$ in equation (25.4.7), the number of mixture components is multiplied by $S$ at each iteration. To prevent an exponential explosion of components, the mixture equation (25.4.7) is then collapsed to a single Gaussian

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \rightarrow q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

The collapse to a mixture is discussed in section(25.4.4).

This routine needs the results from algorithm(25.1). The routine LDSBACKWARD is found in algorithm(24.2).

$$
\mathbf{G}_{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{F}_{T}, \mathbf{g}_{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{f}_{T}, u_{T} \leftarrow w_{T}
$$

for $t \leftarrow T-1$ to 1 do
for $s \leftarrow 1$ to $S, s^{\prime} \leftarrow 1$ to $S, i \leftarrow 1$ to $I_{t}, j^{\prime} \leftarrow 1$ to $J_{t+1}$ do
$(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\left(i, s, j^{\prime}, s^{\prime}\right)=\operatorname{LDSBACKWARD}\left(\mathbf{g}_{t+1}\left(j^{\prime}, s^{\prime}\right), \mathbf{G}_{t+1}\left(j^{\prime}, s^{\prime}\right), \mathbf{f}_{t}(i, s), \mathbf{F}_{t}(i, s), \theta\left(s^{\prime}\right)\right)$
$p\left(i_{t}, s_{t} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, v_{1: T}\right)=\left\langle p\left(s_{t}=s, i_{t}=i \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, s_{t+1}=s^{\prime}, j_{t+1}=j^{\prime}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}=s^{\prime}, j_{t+1}=j^{\prime}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}$
$p\left(i, s, j^{\prime}, s^{\prime} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \leftarrow p\left(s_{t+1}=s^{\prime} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) u_{t+1}\left(j^{\prime}, s^{\prime}\right) p\left(i_{t}, s_{t} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, v_{1: T}\right)$
end for

Collapse the mixture defined by weights $p\left(i_{t}=i, s_{t+1}=s^{\prime}, j_{t+1}=j^{\prime} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1_{T}}\right) \propto$ $p\left(i, s_{t}, j^{\prime}, s^{\prime} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$, means $\boldsymbol{\mu}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}\right)$ and covariances $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\left(i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}\right)$ to a mixture with $J_{t}$ components. This defines the new means $\mathbf{g}_{t}\left(j_{t}, s_{t}\right)$, covariances $\mathbf{G}_{t}\left(j_{t}, s_{t}\right)$ and mixture weights $u_{t}\left(j_{t}, s_{t}\right)$.
$p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \leftarrow \sum_{i_{t}, j^{\prime}, s^{\prime}} p\left(i_{t}, s_{t}, j^{\prime}, s^{\prime} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$

# 25.4.4 Using mixtures in smoothing 

The extension to the mixture case is straightforward based on the representation

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx \sum_{j_{t}=1}^{J} q\left(j_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, j_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

Analogously to the case with a single component,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{i_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(j_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \\
& \times\left\langle q\left(i_{t}, s_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)\right\rangle_{q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The average in the last line of the above equation can be tackled using the same techniques as outlined in the single Gaussian case. To approximate $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, i_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ we consider this as the marginal of the joint distribution

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, \mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t+1}, i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

As in the case of a single mixture, the problematic term is $q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$. Analogously to equation (25.4.4), we make the assumption

$$
q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \mid j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

meaning that information about the current switch state $s_{t}, i_{t}$ is ignored. We can then form

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{i_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}} p\left(i_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid i_{t}, s_{t}, j_{t+1}, s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

This mixture can then be collapsed to a smaller mixture using any method of choice, to give

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx \sum_{j_{t}} q\left(j_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) q\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid j_{t}, s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

The resulting procedure is sketched in algorithm(25.2), including using mixtures in both the forward and backward passes.

# 25.4.5 Relation to other methods 

A classical smoothing approximation for the SLDS is generalised pseudo Bayes (GPB) [12, 173, 172]. In GPB one starts from the exact recursion

$$
p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t}, s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)=\sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
$$

The quantity $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ is difficult to obtain and GPB makes the approximation

$$
p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \approx p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)
$$

Plugging this into equation (25.4.22) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) & \approx \sum_{s_{t+1}} p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right) p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right) \\
& =\sum_{s_{t+1}} \frac{p\left(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)}{\sum_{s_{t}} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)} p\left(s_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The recursion is initialised with the approximate filtered $p\left(s_{T} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$. Computing the smoothed recursion for the switch states in GPB is then equivalent to running the RTS backward pass on a hidden Markov model, independently of the backward recursion for the continuous variables. The only information the GPB method uses to form the smoothed distribution $p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ from the filtered distribution $p\left(s_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is the Markov switch transition $p\left(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t}\right)$. This approximation drops information from the future since information passed via the continuous variables is not taken into account. In contrast to GPB, the EC Gaussian smoothing technique preserves future information passing through the continuous variables. GPB forms an approximation for $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ by using the recursion (25.4.8) where $q\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: T}\right)$ is replaced by $q\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$. In SLDSbackward.m one may choose to use either EC or GBP.

Example 25.1 (Traffic Flow). A illustration of modelling and inference with a SLDS is to consider a simple network of traffic flow, fig(25.4). Here there are 4 junctions $a, b, c, d$ and traffic flows along the roads in the direction indicated. Traffic flows into the junction at $a$ and then goes via different routes to $d$. Flow out of a junction must match the flow into a junction (up to noise). There are traffic light switches at junctions $a$ and $b$ which, depending on their state, route traffic differently along the roads. Using $\phi$ to denote the clean (noise free) flow, we model the flows using the switching linear system:

$$
\left.\begin{array}{c}
\phi_{a}(t) \\
\phi_{a \rightarrow d}(t) \\
\phi_{a \rightarrow b}(t) \\
\phi_{b \rightarrow d}(t) \\
\phi_{b \rightarrow c}(t) \\
\phi_{c \rightarrow d}(t)
\end{array}\right\}= \begin{cases}\phi_{a}(t-1) \\
\phi_{a}(t-1)\left(0.75 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{a}(t)=1\right]+1 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{a}(t)=2\right]\right) \\
\phi_{a}(t-1)\left(0.25 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{a}(t)=1\right]+1 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{a}(t)=3\right]\right) \\
\phi_{a \rightarrow b}(t-1) 0.5 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{b}(t)=1\right] \\
\phi_{a \rightarrow b}(t-1)\left(0.5 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{b}(t)=1\right]+1 \times \mathbb{I}\left[s_{b}(t)=2\right]\right) \\
\phi_{b \rightarrow c}(t-1)\end{cases}
$$

By identifying the flows at time $t$ with a 6 dimensional vector hidden variable $\mathbf{h}_{t}$, we can write the above flow equations as

$$
\mathbf{h}_{t}=\mathbf{A}\left(s_{t}\right) \mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{\eta}_{t}^{h}
$$

for a set of suitably defined matrices $\mathbf{A}(s)$ indexed by the switch variable $s=s_{a} \bigotimes s_{b}$, which takes $3 \times 2=6$ states. We additionally include noise terms to model cars parking or de-parking during a single timestep. The covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{h}$ is diagonal with a larger variance at the inflow point $a$ to model that the total volume of traffic entering the system can vary.

Noisy measurements of the flow into the network are taken at $a$

$$
v_{1, t}=\phi_{a}(t)+\eta_{1}^{v}(t)
$$

![img-290.jpeg](img-290.jpeg)

Figure 25.4: A representation of the traffic flow between junctions at $a, b, c, d$, with traffic lights at $a$ and $b$. If $s_{a}=1 a \rightarrow d$ and $a \rightarrow b$ carry 0.75 and 0.25 of the flow out of $a$ respectively. If $s_{a}=2$ all the flow from $a$ goes through $a \rightarrow d$; for $s_{a}=3$, all the flow goes through $a \rightarrow b$. For $s_{b}=1$ the flow out of $b$ is split equally between $b \rightarrow d$ and $b \rightarrow c$. For $s_{b}=2$ all flow out of $b$ goes along $b \rightarrow c$.
![img-291.jpeg](img-291.jpeg)

Figure 25.5: Time evolution of the traffic flow measured at two points in the network. Sensors measure the total flow into the network (upper panel) $\phi_{a}(t)$ and the total flow out of the network (lower panel), $\phi_{d}(t)=\phi_{a \rightarrow d}(t)+\phi_{b \rightarrow d}(t)+$ $\phi_{c \rightarrow d}(t)$. The total inflow at $a$ undergoes a random walk. Note that the flow measured at $d$ can momentarily drop to zero if all traffic is routed through $a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c$ in two consecutive time steps.
along with a noisy measurement of the total flow out of the system at $d$,

$$
v_{2, t}=\phi_{a \rightarrow d}(t)+\phi_{b \rightarrow d}(t)+\phi_{c \rightarrow d}(t)+\eta_{2}^{v}(t)
$$

The observation model can be represented by $\mathbf{v}_{t}=\mathbf{B} \mathbf{h}_{t}+\boldsymbol{\eta}_{t}^{v}$ using a constant $2 \times 6$ projection matrix $\mathbf{B}$. The switch variables follow a simple Markov transition $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}\right)$ which biases the switches to remain in the same state in preference to jumping to another state. See demoSLDStraffic.m for details.

Given the above system and a prior which initialises all flow at $a$, we draw samples from the model using forward (ancestral) sampling which form the observations $\mathbf{v}_{1: 100}$, fig(25.5). Using only the observations and the known model structure we then attempt to infer the latent switch variables and traffic flows using Gaussian Sum filtering and smoothing (EC method) with 2 mixture components per switch state, fig(25.6).

We note that a naive HMM approximation based on discretising each continuous flow into 20 bins would contain $2 \times 3 \times 20^{6}$ or 384 million states. Even for modest size problems, a naive approximation based on discretisation is therefore impractical.

Example 25.2 (Following the price trend). The following is a simple model of the price trend of a stock, which assumes that the price tends to continue going up (or down) for a while before it reverses direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_{1, t} & =h_{1, t-1}+h_{2, t-1}+\eta_{1}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right) \\
h_{2}(t) & =\mathbb{I}\left[s_{t}=1\right] h_{2, t-1}+\eta_{2}^{h}\left(s_{t}\right) \\
v_{t} & =h_{1, t}+\eta^{v}\left(s_{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

here $h_{1}$ represents the 'clean' price and $h_{2}$ the direction. There is only a single observation variable at each time, which is the clean price plus a small amount of noise. There are two switch states, $\operatorname{dom}\left(s_{t}\right)=\{1,2\}$. When $s_{t}=1$, the model functions normally, with the direction being equal to the previous direction plus a small amount of noise $\eta_{2}^{h}\left(s_{t}=1\right)$. When $s_{t}=2$ however, the direction is sampled from a Gaussian with a large variance. The transition $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}\right)$ is set so that normal dynamics is more likely, and when $s_{t}=2$ it is likely to go back to normal dynamics the next timestep. Full details are in SLDSpricemodel.mat. In fig(25.7) we plot some samples from the model and also smoothed inference of the switch distribution, showing how we can analyse the series to infer the points of likely change in the stock price direction. See also exercise(25.1).

![img-292.jpeg](img-292.jpeg)

(a): The correct latent flows through time along with the switch variable state used to generate the data. The colours corresponds to the flows at the corresponding coloured edges/nodes in fig(25.4). (b): Filtered flows based on a $I=2$ Gaussian Sum forward pass approximation. Plotted are the 6 components of the vector $\left\langle\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right\rangle$ with the posterior distribution of the $s_{a}$ and $s_{b}$ traffic light states $p\left(s_{t}^{a} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right), p\left(s_{t}^{b} \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ plotted below. # 25.5 Reset Models 

Reset models are special switching models in which the switch state isolates the present from the past, resetting the position of the latent dynamics (these are also known as changepoint models). Whilst these models are rather general, it can be helpful to consider a specific model, and here we consider the SLDS changepoint model with two states. We use the state $s_{t}=0$ to denote that the LDS continues with the standard dynamics. With $s_{t}=1$, however, the continuous dynamics is reset to a prior:

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right)= \begin{cases}p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}\right) & s_{t}=0 \\ p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right) & s_{t}=1\end{cases}
$$

where

$$
p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{A} \mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\boldsymbol{\mu}^{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{0}\right), \quad p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}^{1}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1}\right)
$$

Similarly we write

$$
p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right)= \begin{cases}p^{0}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) & s_{t}=0 \\ p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) & s_{t}=1\end{cases}
$$

For simplicity we assume the switch dynamics are first order Markov with transition $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}\right)$, see fig(25.8). Under this model the dynamics follows a standard LDS, but when $s_{t}=1, \mathbf{h}_{t}$ is reset to a value drawn from

![img-294.jpeg](img-294.jpeg)

Figure 25.8: The independence structure of a reset model. Square nodes $s_{t}$ denote the binary reset variables and $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ the continuous state. The $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ are continuous variables, and $\mathbf{v}_{t}$ continuous observations. If the dynamics resets, $s_{t}=1$, the dependence of the continuous $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ on the past is cut.
a Gaussian distribution, independent of the past. Such models are of interest in prediction where the timeseries is following a trend but suddenly changes and the past is forgotten. Whilst this may not seem like a big change to the model, this model is computationally more tractable, exact filtered inference scaling with $O\left(T^{2}\right)$, compared to $O\left(T 2^{T}\right)$ in the general two-state SLDS. To see this, consider the filtering recursion

$$
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) \propto \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} \sum_{s_{t-1}} p\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}\right)
$$

We now consider the two cases

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=0\right) & \propto \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} \sum_{s_{t-1}} p^{0}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}\right) p\left(s_{t}=0 \mid s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}\right) \\
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=1\right) & \propto p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right) \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} \sum_{s_{t-1}} p\left(s_{t}=1 \mid s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}\right) \\
& \propto p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right) \sum_{s_{t-1}} p\left(s_{t}=1 \mid s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(s_{t-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Equation(25.5.6) shows that $p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=1 \mid \mathbf{v}_{1: t}\right)$ is not a mixture model in $\mathbf{h}_{t}$, but contains only a single component proportional to $p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}\right)$. If we use this information in equation (25.5.5) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=0\right) \propto \int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} p^{0}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) & p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}\right) p\left(s_{t}=0 \mid s_{t-1}=0\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}=0\right) \\
& +\int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} p^{0}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}\right) p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}\right) p\left(s_{t}=0 \mid s_{t-1}=1\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}=1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming $\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}=0\right)$ is a mixture distribution with $K$ components, then $\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=0\right)$ will be a mixture with $K+1$ components. In general, therefore, $\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=0\right)$ will contain $T$ components and $\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}=1\right)$ a single component. As opposed to the full SLDS case, the number of components therefore grows only linearly with time, as opposed to exponentially. This means that the computational effort to perform exact filtering scales as $O\left(T^{2}\right)$. Smoothing can be achieved using the $\alpha-\beta$ approach, see exercise(25.3). Despite this reduction in complexity over the SLDS, for long timeseries $T \gg 1$, filtering and smoothing for these reset models can still be computationally expensive. See [51] for approximations based on retaining only a limited number of mixture components, reducing the complexity to linear in $T$.

# Run-length formalism 

One may also describe reset models using a 'run-length' formalism defining at each time $t$ a latent variable $r_{t}$ which describes the length of the current segment[3]. If there is a change, the run-length variable is reset to zero, otherwise it is increased by 1 :

$$
p\left(r_{t} \mid r_{t-1}\right)= \begin{cases}P_{c p} & r_{t}=0 \\ 1-P_{c p} & r_{t}=r_{t-1}+1\end{cases}
$$

where $P_{c p}$ is the probability of a reset (or 'changepoint'). The joint distribution is given by

$$
p\left(v_{1: T}, r_{1: T}\right)=\prod_{t} p\left(r_{t} \mid r_{t-1}\right) p\left(v_{t} \mid v_{1: t-1}, r_{t}\right), \quad p\left(v_{t} \mid v_{1: t-1}, r_{t}\right)=p\left(v_{t} \mid v_{t-r_{t}: t-1}\right)
$$

with the understanding that if $r_{t}=0$ then $p\left(v_{t} \mid v_{t-r_{t}: t-1}\right)=p\left(v_{t}\right)$. The graphical model of this distribution is awkward to draw since the number of links depends on the run-length $r_{t}$. Predictions can be made using

$$
p\left(v_{t+1} \mid v_{1: t}\right)=\sum_{r_{t}} p\left(v_{t+1} \mid v_{t-r_{t}: t}\right) p\left(r_{t} \mid v_{1: t}\right)
$$

where the filtered 'run-length' $p\left(r_{t} \mid v_{1: t}\right)$ is given by the forward recursion:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(r_{t}, v_{1: t}\right) & =\sum_{r_{t-1}} p\left(r_{t}, r_{t-1}, v_{1: t-1}, v_{t}\right)=\sum_{r_{t-1}} p\left(r_{t}, v_{t} \mid r_{t-1}, v_{1: t-1}\right) p\left(r_{t-1}, v_{1: t-1}\right) \\
& =\sum_{r_{t-1}} p\left(v_{t} \mid r_{t}, \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{T}, v_{1: t-1}\right) p\left(r_{t} \mid r_{t-1}, \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{T}\right) p\left(r_{t-1}, v_{1: t-1}\right) \\
& =\sum_{r_{t-1}} p\left(r_{t} \mid r_{t-1}\right) p\left(v_{t} \mid v_{t-r_{t}: t-1}\right) p\left(r_{t-1}, v_{1: t-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that filtered inference scales with $O\left(T^{2}\right)$.

# 25.5.1 A Poisson reset model 

The changepoint structure is not limited to conditionally Gaussian cases only. To illustrate this, we consider the following model ${ }^{2}$ : At each time $t$, we observe a count $y_{t}$ which we assume is Poisson distributed with an unknown positive intensity $h$. The intensity is constant, but at certain unknown times $t$, it jumps to a new value. The indicator variable $c_{t}$ denotes whether time $t$ is such a changepoint or not. Mathematically, the model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p\left(h_{0}\right) & =\mathcal{G}\left(h_{0} ; a_{0}, b_{0}\right) \\
p\left(c_{t}\right) & =\mathcal{B E}\left(c_{t} ; \pi\right) \\
p\left(h_{t} \mid h_{t-1}, c_{t}\right) & =\mathbb{I}\left[c_{t}=0 \mid \delta\left(h_{t}, h_{t-1}\right)+\mathbb{I}\left[c_{t}=1\right] \mathcal{G}\left(h_{t} ; \nu, b\right)\right. \\
p\left(v_{t} \mid h_{t}\right) & =\mathcal{P O}\left(v_{t} ; h_{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The symbols $\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{B E}$ and $\mathcal{P O}$ denote the Gamma, Bernoulli and the Poisson distributions respectively:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{G}(h ; a, b) & =\exp ((a-1) \log h-b h-\log \Gamma(a)+a \log b) \\
\mathcal{B E}(c ; \pi) & =\exp (c \log \pi+(1-c) \log (1-\pi)) \\
\mathcal{P O}(v ; h) & =\exp (v \log h-h-\log \Gamma(v+1))
\end{aligned}
$$

Given observed counts $v_{1: T}$, the task is to find the posterior probability of a change and the associated intensity levels for each region between two consecutive changepoints. Plugging the above definitions in the generic updates equation (25.5.5) and equation (25.5.6), we see that $\alpha\left(h_{t}, c_{t}=0\right)$ is a Gamma potential, and that $\alpha\left(g_{t}, c_{t}=1\right)$ is a mixture of Gamma potentials, where a Gamma potential is defined as

$$
\phi(h)=e^{l} \mathcal{G}(h ; a, b)
$$

via the triple $(a, b, l)$. For the corrector update step we need to calculate the product of a Poisson term with the observation model $p\left(v_{t} \mid h_{t}\right)=\mathcal{P O}\left(v_{t} ; h_{t}\right)$. A useful property of the Poisson distribution is that, given the observation, the latent variable is Gamma distributed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{P O}(v ; h) & =v \log h-h-\log \Gamma(v+1) \\
& =(v+1-1) \log h-h-\log \Gamma(v+1) \\
& =\mathcal{G}(h ; v+1,1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the update equation requires multiplication of two Gamma potentials. A nice property of the Gamma density is that the product of two Gamma densities is also a Gamma potential:

$$
\left(a_{1}, b_{1}, l_{1}\right) \times\left(a_{2}, b_{2}, l_{2}\right)=\left(a_{1}+a_{2}-1, b_{1}+b_{2}, l_{1}+l_{2}+g\left(a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}\right)\right)
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{2}$ This example is due to Taylan Cemgil.

where

$$
g\left(a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}\right) \equiv \log \frac{\Gamma\left(a_{1}+a_{2}-1\right)}{\Gamma\left(a_{1}\right) \Gamma\left(a_{2}\right)}+\log \left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right)+a_{1} \log \left(b_{1} /\left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right)\right)+a_{2} \log \left(b_{2} /\left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right)\right)
$$

The $\alpha$ recursions for this reset model are therefore closed in the space of a mixture of Gamma potentials, with an additional Gamma potential in the mixture at each timestep. A similar approach can be used to form the smoothing recursions, see exercise(25.3).

Example 25.3 (Coal mining disasters). We illustrate the Poisson reset model on the coal mining disaster dataset [157]. The data set consists of the number of deadly coal-mining disasters in England per year over a time span of 112 years from 1851 to 1962. It is widely agreed in the statistical literature that a change in the intensity (the expected value of the number of disasters) occurs around the year 1890, after new health and safety regulations were introduced. In fig(25.9) we show the marginals $p\left(h_{t} \mid y_{1: T}\right)$ along with the filtering density. Note that we are not constraining the number of changepoints and in principle allow any number. The smoothed density suggests a sharp decrease around $t=1890$.
![img-295.jpeg](img-295.jpeg)

Figure 25.9: Estimation of change points. (Top) coal mining disaster dataset. (Middle) Filtered estimate of the marginal intensity $p\left(h_{t} \mid v_{1: t}\right)$ and (Bottom) smoothed estimate $p\left(h_{t} \mid v_{1: T}\right)$. Here, darker color means higher probability.

# 25.5.2 Reset-HMM-LDS 

The reset model defined by equations (25.5.1,25.5.3) above is useful in many applications, but is limited since only a single dynamical model is considered. An extension is to consider a set of available dynamical models, indexed by $s_{t} \in\{1, \ldots, S\}$, with a reset that cuts dependency of the continuous variable on the past $[100,59]:$

$$
p\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}, c_{t}\right)= \begin{cases}p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right) & c_{t}=0 \\ p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}\right) & c_{t}=1\end{cases}
$$

The states $s_{t}$ follow a Markovian dynamics $p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right)$, see fig(25.10). A reset occurs if the state $s_{t}$ changes, otherwise, no reset occurs:

$$
p\left(c_{t}=1 \mid s_{t}, s_{t-1}\right)=\mathbb{I}\left[s_{t} \neq s_{t-1}\right]
$$

The computational complexity of filtering for this model is $O\left(S^{2} T^{2}\right)$ which can be understood by analogy with the reset $\alpha$ recursions, equations(25.5.5,25.5.6) on replacing $h_{t}$ by $\left(h_{t}, s_{t}\right)$. To see this we consider the filtering recursion for the two cases

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}, c_{t}=0\right) & =\int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} \sum_{s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}} p^{0}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p^{0}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right) p\left(c_{t}=0 \mid s_{t}, s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right) \\
\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}, c_{t}=1\right) & =\int_{\mathbf{h}_{t-1}} \sum_{s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}} p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}, c_{t}\right) p\left(c_{t}=1 \mid s_{t}, s_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right) \\
& =p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}\right) \sum_{s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}} p\left(c_{t}=1 \mid s_{t}, s_{t-1}\right) p\left(s_{t} \mid s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right) \alpha\left(s_{t-1}, c_{t-1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

![img-296.jpeg](img-296.jpeg)

Figure 25.10: The independence structure of a reset-HMMLDS model. Square nodes $c_{t} \in\{0,1\}$ denote reset variables; $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ are continuous latent variables, and $\mathbf{v}_{t}$ continuous observations. The discrete state $s_{t} \in\{1, \ldots, S\}$ determines which Linear Dynamical system from a finite set of Linear Dynamical systems is operational at time $t$.

From equation (25.5.27) we see that $\alpha\left(\mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}, c_{t}=1\right)$ contains only a single component proportional to $p^{1}\left(\mathbf{v}_{t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{t}, s_{t}\right) p^{1}\left(\mathbf{h}_{t} \mid s_{t}\right)$. This is therefore exactly analogous to the standard reset model, except that we need now to index a set of messages with $s_{t}$, therefore each message taking $O(S)$ steps to compute. The computational effort to perform exact filtering scales as $O\left(S^{2} T^{2}\right)$.

# 25.6 Summary 

- The switching linear dynamical system is a marriage of a discrete state HMM with the continuous latent state linear dynamical system. It is able to model discrete jumps in an underlying continuous process, finding application in a large variety of domains from finance to speech processing.
- The classical inference problems in the SLDS are formally intractable since representing the messages requires an exponential amount of space.
- Many approximation methods have been developed for the SLDS and in this chapter we described a robust deterministic method based on a mixture of Gaussians representation.
- Reset models are such that the continuous variable forgets the past when reset. Unlike the SLDS such models are much more amenable to exact inference. Extensions include the reset-HMM which allows for a set of discrete and continuous states in which a special discrete state resets the continuous states.

where $p\left(h_{t} \mid v_{1: t}\right)=\sum_{s_{t}} p\left(h_{t}, s_{t} \mid v_{1: t}\right)$.

1. Compute the mean prediction error
mean_abs_pred_error=mean(abs(vpred(2:200)-v(2:200)))
2. Compute the mean naive prediction error
mean_abs_pred_error_naive=mean(abs(v(1:199)-v(2:200)))
which corresponds to saying that tomorrow's price will be the same as today's.

Exercise 25.2. The data in fig(25.11) are observed prices from an intermittent mean-reverting process, contained in meanrev.mat. There are two states $S=2$. There is a true (latent) price $p_{t}$ and an observed price $v_{t}$ (which is plotted). When $s=1$, the true underlying price reverts back towards the mean $m=10$ with rate $r=0.9$. Otherwise the true price follows a random walk:

$$
p_{t}= \begin{cases}r\left(p_{t-1}-m\right)+m+\eta_{t}^{p} & s_{t}=1 \\ p_{t-1}+\eta_{t}^{p} & s_{t}=2\end{cases}
$$

where

$$
\eta_{t}^{p} \sim \begin{cases}\mathcal{N}\left(\eta_{t}^{p} \mid 0,0.0001\right) & s_{t}=1 \\ \mathcal{N}\left(\eta_{t}^{p} \mid 0,0.01\right) & s_{t}=2\end{cases}
$$

The observed price $v_{t}$ is related to the unknown price $p_{t}$ by

$$
v_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(v_{t} \mid p_{t}, 0.001\right)
$$

It is known that $95 \%$ of the time $s_{t+1}$ is in the same state as at time $t>1$ and that at time $t=1$ either state of $s_{1}$ is equally likely. Also at $t=1, p_{1} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(p_{1} \mid m, 0.1\right)$. Based on this information, and using Gaussian Sum filtering with $I=2$ components (use SLDSforward.m), what is the probability at time $t=280$ that the dynamics is following a random walk, $p\left(s_{280}=2 \mid v_{1: 280}\right)$ ?
